Indian socialism is better called statism: it places state above society.

This state, as an essay in this volume will prove, is a predatory
state, a kleptocracy: the rule of thieves. After fighting for and obtaining
political freedom from a colonial regime, India needs to fight again
for freedom from the socialist state.

Freedom rests on three pillars: the political freedom of democracy;
the economic freedom of the market; and liberal education—that
which teaches the value of freedom.

We need to fight for economic freedom. Today, we are ranked 120
in the World Economic Freedom Index. ‘Mostly Unfree’ is the
category in which we are placed. From this index, it is easy to see
why many countries are poor: their people are not free and their
states are kleptocratic.

We also need to fight for liberal education. I often lecture to
students of economics and never cease to be surprised at their total
ignorance of the dominant themes in the philosophy of freedom.
They are being trained to see the state as the solution. This is not
knowledge, it is propaganda. The essays in this volume will disprove
many of the false ideas taught by the socialist Indian state in its
universities. The task ahead will be to get the state out of education.
The human mind is the most precious resource we have. We cannot
continue to allow the destruction of this resource.

These essays have been written for the enjoyment of those who
take citizenship seriously. The housewife, the copywriter, the ad
executive, the manager, the student, the journalist—they are the target
audience. The style is journalistic, not academic. These are simply
essays, these are not theses.

I enjoyed writing these essays and if these provide enjoyment to
my reader, I will be doubly rewarded.

1. POPULATION!
—or How people cause prosperity
People who need people are the luckiest people in the world.
—Barbra Streisand

Economics is the study of prosperity. Adam Smith studied the ‘wealth
of nations’. Unfortunately, since then, we have had too many
economists studying poverty—and prescribing the state as the way
out. They also see population to be a cause of poverty—and prescribe
state-conceived, -financed and -directed population control
programmes; which are often coercive. In India the state teaches
children, through high school economics textbooks, that our
population is a cause of our poverty. This essay seeks to establish the
fact that population causes prosperity. This can be proved in four
words: Urban Areas Are Rich. Every urban area, all over the world,
is densely populated and quite rich. What else are dots on the map?
This is seen throughout history: the story of civilization is a story of
cities—-all densely populated and all quite rich. We need to remind
ourselves that humans are the only species capable of creating wealth.
An increase in our numbers can only cause prosperity! That is why
in the old days they said, ‘May your tribe increase.’ Was it meant as
a curse?
THE MORE THE MERRIER
What is prosperity? It can be symbolically represented as follows—
in what I call ‘The More the Merrier Equation’:

It is particularly mortifying for me to begin a collection of essays
with what looks suspiciously like a mathematical equation typically
used by economists to impress, beguile and confuse people—including
their students. Commenting on the takeover of economics by
mathematicians, John Kenneth Galbraith said:

Mathematical accomplishment in economic theory did attain a certain
objective value as a ticket of admission to the economics profession, a
device for keeping out those with purely verbal talent.'

But unfortunately, the prosperity equation is the only place to
begin this essay, and indeed this book. That is because, once we
understand prosperity, we know the causes of our poverty—and the
definite fact that population is not one of them.

So what is PK + 3TC + F + S = Prosperity?

P is a Person, a Human Being

This equation is based on the basic fact that human beings alone are
economic, and hence create prosperity. There is a bird whose faecal
matter is high-value fertilizer. It shits money—but isn’t rich itself.
Humans harvest its droppings and become rich because of one main
reason: we have the ability to trade—the ‘natural propensity’ Adam
Smith spoke of, ‘to truck, barter and exchange’. Since we are the
only species with this ability, it follows that only human beings can
create wealth. How can an increase in the number of human beings
cause poverty?

K is Knowledge

Thus, PK is a person with knowledge: of skills, of markets, or
whatever. Even to harvest the bird-shit above, a P will have to have
knowledge of its worth, the location of those who value it and those

with whom he can trade. A P must have K of the market. But what is
knowledge?

For the answer to that question, we must turn to Friedrich August
von Hayek, the philosopher of freedom who won the 1974 Nobel

Prize for Economics. His theory of knowledge disproved the method
of central economic planning. Knowledge, Hayek said, could be both
codifiable and uncodifiable. There is little that can be codified about
how to ride a bicycle, or climb a coconut tree. The market relies on
all these kinds of knowledge and no institution that seeks to replace
the market can gather all the knowledge required for the task. How
does a planner collect uncodifiable knowledge? Planning is bound to
fail, Hayek said, because the knowledge required for the purpose
cannot be collected.

Anyone who is ‘economic’—who trades some good or service in

' the market—possesses knowledge of some kind. The skills of the
butcher, the vegetable vendor, the housemaid, the cab driver—all
these are based on ‘knowledge’. Each kind of knowledge commands
some price in the market and it is not true that academic knowledge
obtains the highest reward: no professor of economics earns as much
as Sachin Tendulkar.
3TC stands for Trade, Towns, Transport and Communications
This is ‘the more the merrier’ part of the equation. These are the
methods by which you get access to more human beings. To create
prosperity, a PK must meet or interact with other PKs. 3TC gets him
to other PKs and is, therefore, vital to prosperity.

Trade is the basic economic activity of human beings that gave
rise to civilization. Indeed, we are the only species capable of it—
Homo economicus. As Adam Smith noted, only human beings can
strike ‘bargains’; no dog can exchange one bone for another. Among
humans, this ability to trade is innate and should be celebrated. Little
children gainfully trade toys and food amongst themselves: give me
some chips and have a sip of my cola. Trade is a ‘positive sum
game’: with trade, both sides are better off than before. When A
gives up a little cola for some chips, she is better off; and B, who
gives up some chips for a sip, is also better off. Barter led to the
invention of money as a ‘medium of exchange’—perhaps the greatest
creation of the human mind. Socialism does not value trade. It

emphasizes manufacture. It believes that by restricting trade the state
can create ‘industrialization’. This is what Hayek called the ‘fatal
conceit’ of socialism.

Towns are where PKs are concentrated. You are more likely to
strike a deal in a town than in the wide open countryside. Civilization
is based on towns and cities. The root of the word ‘civilization’ is
civitas, which means ‘city’. These are the dots we see on the map.
Human beings create these colonies for themselves just as ants build
anthills. These are all densely populated—and prosperous.

There is a specific reason why towns are critical to the economics
of prosperity. ‘Economics is the study of the production of wealth
through the division of labour,’ said Prof. George Reisman who, like
Hayek, studied under the great Austrian economist, Ludwig von
Mises. The division of labour is maximum in an urban area: you
cannot be a receptionist, dentist, barber or taxi driver in a village.
Of course, this division of labour is also based on the division of
knowledge; so we could improve Professor Reisman’s definition
somewhat by saying that: Economics is the study of the production
of wealth through the division of labour and knowledge. Thus,
urbanization is critical to economics because in urban areas there is
maximum scope for division of labour and knowledge. Further,
‘planning’ is not economics, because it is not a study of the division
of labour and knowledge.

Transport and Communications allow the economic pulse of an
urban conglomerate to generate prosperity through a vast hinterland.
They also allow these urban superpowers—and the vast numbers of
PKs in them—to interconnect: the more the merrier. That, I believe,
is the economic theory of the Internet. Adam Smith had clearly
observed the importance of transportation. He saw that ‘good roads,
canals and navigable rivers, by diminishing the expense of carriage,
put the remote parts of the country more nearly upon a level with
those in the neighbourhood of the town.’ He added that these newly
developed modes of transportation were the ‘greatest of all
improvements’.

F is Freedom, the vital ingredient
Without economic freedom, the rest is useless. Each human being—
each PK—is looking out for his own economic benefit. He or she is

. POPULATION / 5
the best judge of how that gain is to be obtained—and should therefore
be left free to get it. Indians possess very little economic freedom. In
the 1999 World Freedom Index, India is ranked 120: ‘mostly unfree’
is what we are. The state has cornered vast economic powers. Indians
willingly gave the state these powers, asking it to occupy the
‘commanding heights of the economy’. This is the basic reason why
India is still poor, for the state does not create wealth: it only taxes
and spends. PKs create wealth—when they are left free.

S is Security

This is the standard public good supposed to be supplied by the
Hobbesian state. Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679) wrote Leviathan in
1651, in which he put forward the political theory that (if not
absolutist) justified government absolutely—while saying it should
be limited. The difference between the ‘state of nature’ in which
there is no state and man is at war with every man,’ and the situation
in which sovereignty has been granted to the monarch, are
distinguished only by the security brought about by the installation
of this sovereign power. Of course, it should be examined, especially
where states fail to provide citizens with adequate security, whether
there are better methods of providing local collective security. But of
that, later.

With this equation, we can judge why some Ps are poor. In our
case, it is easy to see that poverty is because all the other factors—K,
the 3Ts, C, F and S—have been largely missing. The priorities of a
poor nation seeking prosperity become clear.

URBANIZATION AND POPULATION

Population causes prosperity. Urban areas—densely populated cities
and towns—possess more cars, cellphones and millionaires than vacant
rural countrysides. Further, urbanization is a growing phenomenon
—-proving that more and more people are finding it ‘economic’ to
live in places where the density of population is high. Why? Because
these generate wealth. They follow the prosperity equation. Hong
Kong, Singapore, Tokyo, New York, London... the list is endless.
? This is a highly contestable assumption. There are many stateless societies in
Africa as well as India wherein anarchy does not mean chaos, simply because
the market is there to motivate human beings to be ‘moral’ and maintain order.

These are the anthills humans build. These are where humans are
most concentrated, and they are the generators of prosperity.

Of course, it is ridiculous to suggest that this process of adding on
human population ad infinitum will continue to generate prosperity.
No one wants a situation in which we are left with only standing
room. But the prosperity equation has an in-built stabilizer. People
who urbanize find it ‘economic’ to opt for small families. A small
family is a globally accepted urban ‘value’. Thus, urbanization and
globalization—the spread of this value—will do more to bring down
our numbers than the expensive strategies pursued by governments
today.

This calls for a radical rethinking of accepted beliefs regarding
the so-called ‘population problem’. Today, school children are taught,
through government-approved economics textbooks, that population
is a cause of poverty. The elected as well as appointed personnel of
the state wax eloquent on the insurn.ountable dimensions of this
perceived problem. The strategies pursued by the state to tackle this
‘problem’ involve huge expenditures which cost the taxpayer dear
without much reciprocal benefit.

These strategies—at their ludicrous extreme—even went to the
extent of using force. Sanjay Gandhi’s programme of mass sterilization
is fresh in our memory. The use of force is, of course, anathema to
those who believe in freedom. There is greater reason to challenge it
when this force is used on the basis of completely false conceptions
of both the ‘problem’ as well as the ‘cure’. The use of force by the
state is sometimes justified on the grounds that the issue at stake is
the promotion of ‘public good’. In this instance, the state cannot
claim to have used force towards such ends.

Lord Bauer said that increased commercial contact between
countries would lower birth rates faster than anything governments
could think of. Others have often opined—and this opinion is
particularly popular in India—that ‘development is the best
contraceptive.’ What both are saying is that if we follow the prosperity
equation, the growth of our numbers will also stabilize. Urbanization
brings down high population growth rates. There is no need for the
state to bother about population. Let it look after its basic tasks like
law and order.

It is quite ‘irrational’ on the part of the state to consider population
to be a problem, because more the people the more it can tax: that is

; POPULATION /7
why Mughal emperors went under the title Jahanpanah or ‘Refuge
of the World.’ If someone abandoned the protection of a
neighbourhood king and settled down under Akbar the Great, the
Mughal exchequer gained. So what sense do immigration restrictions
make: none whatsoever. They are not ‘rational’; they are based on
xenophobia. Those who practice immigration restrictions do not
appreciate the fact that human beings are generators of wealth; that
countries which see a human influx gain in the long run, and that
countries which see an exodus lose heavily: their greatest resource is
depleted.

The equation tells us numerous reasons why many of our Ps are
poor. They don’t have adequate modern Knowledge. Transport and
Communications are rudimentary. Free trade is not practised.
Economic Freedom is in low supply. Security is likewise. But what
about Towns? What can be said about the manner in which India has
been urbanizing? Quite a lot, actually.

URBANIZATION EXAMINED

David Clark, Head of the Department of Geography, University of
Coventry, has studied the phenomenon of urbanization in depth,
especially over recent decades.’ He says that not till 1899, when
Adna Ferrin Weber published The Growth of Cities in the Nineteenth
Century, did urban study become ‘a central focus of inquiry in the
newly emerging discipline of geography.’ Urbanization was a limited
phenomenon then but ‘in the last thirty years it has become valid to
talk about an urban world: a world in which urban places and urban
living are the norm rather than the exception.’ The year 1996 has
‘marked a major watershed in the evolution of human settlement’,
for today it can be said that more than half the world’s population
lives in towns and cities. Over 2.6 billion people worldwide are
urbanites. ‘No longer are towns and cities exceptional settlement
forms in predominantly rural societies—the world has become an
urban place.’

If we look at the Indian scenario, a likely picture emerges. The
richest states of India—Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka,
Punjab, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala—report levels of

urbanization that are higher than the all-India average of 30 per cent.
Maharashtra and Gujarat report urban growth rates in excess of 3 per
cent: significantly higher than their growth rates of population.
Extrapolating from the latest figures available,* it would be safe to
assert that these two states are approaching the world average of 50
per cent urbanization. The poorest areas of India—like Bihar and
Assam-—report levels of urbanization that barely touch double digits.
(From Census data.)

Thus, statistical evidence from our own country supports the thesis
that population causes prosperity. It also supports the belief that
urbanization brings down population growth rates. Kerala, the state
with the lowest population growth rate,°> reports the highest urban
growth rate in India—almost 5 per cent annually. It is undoubtedly
true that the high level of literacy in Kerala has a lot to do with its
low population growth rate—the K factor—but the role played by its
huge migrant community in transmitting urban values should not be
overlooked.

Where will all this lead? David Clark believes that the population
of the world will stabilize at 85 per cent urban—living on just 7 per
cent of the earth’s land. The forces of globalization will power the
process. As his study reveals, unlike an earlier period in the evolution
of the global economy, today’s globalization is sending
industrialization to the periphery. In an earlier age, when the industrial
revolution had just begun and the world economy was controlled by
imperialist forces, manufacturing would tend to restrict itself to the
core of the empire. Today things are the other way round. Globalization
has also come to mean that the world is not only the market, it is also
the factory. Examples abound. There is an American toy company
that has a small office in New York which designs and markets its
products—all manufactured on contract by small! firms in Korea,
Taiwan and China. A leading manufacturer of athletic footwear
operates much the same way. There are western publishing firms
which do their specialized jobs like editing and proof-reading at home,
leaving ‘labour-intensive’ work like typesetting and printing to
‘‘Habitat II’, India National Report, 1996.
> Kerala has controlled its population growth very well, but has not attained high
prosperity. This disproves the notion that population growth causes poverty and
that prosperity can be attained simply by controlling the growth of numbers.

contracted parties in South-East Asia. During the past 30 years—and
especially the last 10 years—these forces have led to greater
industrialization as well as increased urbanization in the periphery
of the global economic system. These processes are now accelerating.

Herein lie the opportunities and the challenges—especially for the
‘Third World’. The cities of the Third World are particularly notable
as environmental disaster zones. India is no exception. Bombay, Delhi,
Calcutta, Madras, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Poona... these great cities
which boasted a high quality of life have now become gaping sores
on the earth’s environment. The quality of air in all these cities has
become unacceptable. Standards of civic hygiene are abysmal. Matters
of great environmental concern—like sewage treatment and garbage
disposal—do not obtain sufficient public investment. Environmentally
friendly systems of rapid mass transportation do not exist. None of

‘these great cities have effective municipal organization. They are
usually seats of state governments—and these higher levels of
government hold all the powers. Delhi is unique. Power over its affairs
is shared by the central government, the state government, a lieutenant
governor and a host of unaccountable statal bodies like the Delhi
Development Authority.

Apart from these big cities, Indians live in hundreds of big towns
and thousands of small towns. The conditions in these are much
worse. Untreated sewage from these towns pollutes every major
riverine system. None of these towns have an administratively
competent, financially solvent and publicly accountable system of
municipal organization. Unlike the prefects of provincial France, the
Indian Administrative Service has never fostered institutions of urban
democracy. A typical district is headquartered in a big town, and has
a host of smaller towns within its jurisdiction. All these urban areas
are on the brink of disintegration.

The gross mismanagement of urban areas, which generate wealth,
is the greatest failure of a state that has viewed population to be as
huge a ‘problem’ as urbanization. This has always been referred to
as the ‘rural-urban migration problem’, and its implications have
not been understood. It is fairly obvious that human beings are guided
to do things that earn them more money—they are economically
‘rational’. They prefer gains to losses. Thus, if many are choosing to
shift from thinly populated countrysides to crowded towns, then surely
there must be some economic rationale that explains this behaviour.

It is glaringly evident, in this case, that urban areas generate prosperity
and that people come flocking to them hoping for a share of that
prosperity. If you want to tackle poverty sincerely, you must look
upon urbanization as a process that will help you along the way.
This, unfortunately, the Indian state has never considered. China, on
the other hand, has a pronounced urban vision. Its two top leaders,
Jiang Zemin and Zhu Rongji have both been mayors of big cities like
Shanghai. They ran them well, and helped rebuild them. A Chinese
mayor was quoted in the Time magazine as saying that the crane
should be made China’s national bird—and he was referring to
construction cranes! China has made the connection between
prosperity and urbanization; India has not. The BJP-led government
which took over in 1998 wanted to invest 60 per cent of total state
outlay on ‘rural development’! At the 1998 Economic Editors’
Conference, the head of India’s Planning Commission said that his
greatest desire was to ensure that no villager would migrate to a city.
PRIMACY

To fully understand the dimensions of urbanization and rural—urban
migration, let us once again turn to David Clark.

Clark cites various studies which have looked into the manner in
which secondary and tertiary towns develop around primary cities.
The growth of these smaller urban centres is extremely important to
the understanding of the urbanization process. In India, what is clearly
visible is that these secondary and tertiary towns are not developing—
we are all crowding into cities. This is the phenomenon of ‘primacy’
—one city becoming overly important in the urban scheme. Reporting
on primacy, Clark says:

The evidence suggests, however, that primacy exists in countries in which
the principal city is more strongly linked to and integrated within the
global urban system than it is to the domestic urban hierarchy.®
The fact that we inhabit a country whose urbanization has been
severely lopsided, creating primacy, in which the ‘principal city is
more strongly linked to and integrated within the global urban system
than it is to the domestic urban hierarchy’ can be illustrated by an
Clark, D., op. cit., p. 29.

account of my recent visit to Dehra Dun, a town of tourism interest,
with many elite residential public schools, a military academy, a
forestry institute and the preferred place of retirement of innumerable
senior military and civil officers. Dehra Dun, at the foothills, is the
gateway to the Garhwal mountains. About 30 km uphill and you are
in Mussoorie, once called ‘the queen of hill stations.’

Dehra Dun is just 250 km from Delhi. The highway is the same
one that takes you to Hardwar, Rishikesh and ultimately Uttarkashi—
it is heavily used by the devout. But the highway no longer exists.
Some years ago I might have called it a ‘bad road’. But today, one
can only say ‘no road’. So it takes over 6 hours—if you drive with
maximum emphasis on safety—to reach Dehra Dun from Delhi. You
can fly to Dubai or Hong Kong in much less time. The principal city
is better linked to the global urban system than it is to the domestic

‘urban hierarchy: QED.

All along the drive, this urban hierarchy confronts you. Ghaziabad,
Meerut, Modinagar, Khatauli, Muzaffarnagar, Roorkee—these are
all towns, or urban areas. But they lack sound links to their primary
city. If these links were in place, the urban picture would be different.
Delhi would decongest; the surrounds would ‘develop’.

Some statistics from Gujarat, one of the most urbanized and
prosperous states of India, can be quoted to support the thesis of
primacy.’

Class One urban centres are those with a population above
1,00,000. In 1981, Gujarat had 13 of these; in 1991, the figure rose
to 21—a more than 50 per cent jump. The total population in Class
One urban areas as a percentage of total urban population rose from
57.9 to 66.4 during 1981-91—-an almost 10 per cent increase.

Class Two urban centres are those with a population between
50,000 and 99,000. During 1981-91, the number of such urban
centres just nudged up from 23 to 27. The percentage of total urban
population in Class Two towns actually fell from 14.5 to 12.7 per cent.

Class Three urban centres have a population between 20,000 and
49,000. During 1981-91, the number of Class Three urban centres
increased marginally from 46 to SO, and the percentage of total urban

In 1991, while there were 350 urban centres in all in Gujarat,
two-thirds of the entire urban population was concentrated in 21 cities.
The figure must be higher now. This is primacy.

It is because of primacy that our big cities are growing beyond
sustainable levels, while the innumerable small towns that surround
them are not developing. The transportation links between surrounding
towns and the primary city are grossly inadequate. Clark speaks of
various studies which show that, with sound transportation links,
primacy ceases and what may be called ‘normal’ or ‘market-driven’
urban development ensues. Market-driven urban development is what
India must pursue. For this, massive investments in transportation
are essential. Of course, laws which restrict real estate development,
like land ceilings and rent control, must go. Great emphasis must be
laid on the systems by which property is registered and bought and
sold. It must be made quick and foolproof, so that good economics
is not thwarted by crooks and babus. And the housing finance system
must be streamlined with quick rules for foreclosure.

Market-driven urbanization will not only control population, it
will also deal with the greatest practical problem faced by citizens of

Transportation adds to the supply of land. Connect Village X to

Pluralism believed in a world of open and competing groups with no

democracy. Unfortunately, the world is not such, and the hollowness

Pluralism—the notion that there are many groups and none really
dominant—was challenged by two other schools of thought: the Elite
Theorists and the Marxists. The Elite Theorists look upon the state
as being an instrument in the hands of a ‘power elite’. They coined
the expression ‘military-industrial complex’. Marxists, similarly,
believe the state (and they too are looking at the western liberal

the capitalists. Thus, both the Elite Theorists and the Marxists disagree
with the analyses of the Pluralists. They do not see the open and
competing groups that Pluralists see; they see, instead, an elite
controlling the state in its own interests. Thereafter, the Elite Theorists
and the Marxists disagree on what should be done, but that’s another
story.

Pluralist analyses were further disproved by many successive studies

nature of the group formation process. Mancur Olson, in 1965,
published The Logic of Collective Action which inquired into the
economic reasons why groups form, how they are maintained and
how and when they act. Pluralists, with their belief in ‘open and
competing groups’, had overlooked inquiring into the economic
reasons of group formation. Olson showed how important was the
role of economic incentives and disincentives in maintaining groups—
you cannot run any trade union without them—and also how particular
kinds of groups were more likely to form than others. This is one of
the many reasons why most Pluralists redefined themselves as ‘Neo-

The morality of freedom is the morality to be able to freely pursue

vilified for the same reason. In recent times, Jeremy Bentham has
been a noted philosopher of this school of thought. But the freedom

‘harmony and co-incidence of Duty and Self-Interest, Virtue and
Felicity, Prudence and Benevolence are explained and exemplified.’

‘Morality,’ Bentham says, ‘is the art of maximizing happiness: it
gives the code of laws by which that conduct is suggested whose
result will, the whole of human existence being taken into account,
leave the greatest quantity of felicity.’

Bentham tried to measure pleasure—or happiness—and considered
it moral for people to pursue their pleasures freely. For this reason
he has often been ridiculed and not taken seriously. But in his
‘hedonistic calculus’, Bentham maintained that we all measure one
very important characteristic of any pleasure we pursue—and that is
its ‘duration’. We will not pursue vice if left free to do so simply
because the duration of the pleasure is too short: long-term misery is
the inevitable result of a life of vice. The rational seeker of pleasure
will not pursue such a life.

Bentham avers that the calculus of the hedonist, which is what the
moralist seeks, can be ‘reduced to a single inquiry’:

pleasure purchased? What repayment of future pleasure may be

THE ORIGINS OF PAPER MONEY

The inventors of paper money were goldsmiths. If you had a little
store of gold, you kept it with a goldsmith—who would give you a
receipt with your name on it acknowledging his liability. Now, when
you decided to make a purchase, you would go across to the goldsmith,
hand over the receipt and collect your gold—and make your way
through the unsafe streets of your city to the merchant whose goods
you wanted to buy. You would hand over your gold and make off
with your purchase. That merchant would then have to negotiate
those same unsafe city streets himself, with the gold, and deposit it
with a goldsmith—maybe even the same goldsmith—in exchange for
a receipt. It becomes obvious that if you had simply handed your
receipt to the merchant, the entire transaction would have become
much easier. Thus, the invention of paper money. The problem with
the early goldsmith’s ‘notes’—as these receipts were called—was
that they bore a name upon them and were encashable only by the
person named. Once it was realized that there could be ‘bearer’
notes, we had modern paper money. Today’s notes follow the example
of the goldsmith’s note: they have no name on them, but they have
the same promise. Only the goldsmith is no more—and the central
bank governor’s promise is empty.

The fact that this promise is empty brings into question the morality
of laws like FERA—India’s highly repressive Foreign Exchange
Regulation Act. I stress the word ‘morality’. A fundamental basis of
morality is property rights. Unless we can all call certain things

124 / ANTIDOTE—ESSAYS AGAINST THE SOCIALIST INDIAN STATE
‘mine’ and distinguish them from what are ‘not mine’, we become
savages who plunder. We snatch; we do not trade. The morality of
property rights underlines trade—a basic civilizing activity. FERA
involves a violation of property rights—by the central banker. The
asset underlying the paper token is the property of the noteholder.
When the central banker cannot redeem his promise, it is he who
should be in prison: a debtors’ prison. FERA is not a law that can be
morally enforced.

Getting back to the goldsmiths of yore: These goldsmiths were
also moneylenders—always. They used to lend out small amounts of
gold for a fee called interest. With the invention of paper money they
soon discovered that they could lend out bits of paper for a fee. And
this was naturally an attractive prospect. That is, they need not lend
gold; they could simply stock gold and lend paper. But remember,
their paper always had to be convertible. So they could not lend out
much more paper than the gold they had in stock. This put an effective
check on the amount of paper money they could safely issue—and
hence on the amount of profits they could make. So, to increase their
ability to issue notes, goldsmiths began to compete for gold deposits
of the public by sharing the interest they earned from lending money
with those who kept gold with them—and deposit money, the cheque
and fractional reserve banking were born.

We look back to this period and call it ‘free banking’ or ‘free
money’. The state did not control any aspect of the industry. At best
it raised money for its own purposes from these private bankers.
[Many great bankers, including the Medicis of Florence, suffered by
lending excessively to states (monarchs).] It is important to realize
how free banking was essentially stable—there was no chaos. Nor
was there that recurring disease of modern times: inflation. Free
banking was stable because it guarded against the over-issue of
currency by any one bank. Every private bank had to stay afloat on
its own—there being no ‘central bank’ performing ‘lender of last
resort’ functions to bail it out. To stay afloat and avoid bankruptcy,
each private banker had to keep a close watch on his stock of gold
and the amount of notes he issued. If gold stock increased, he would
issue more notes. If they depleted, he would quickly destroy all the
notes that came back to him for redemption—and not re-issue them.
Since every private banker was forced to act in this rational fashion,
the entire system was inherently stable.

QUANTITY THEORY OF MONEY
Suppose the nation was losing export markets and its foreign trade
was running at a deficit, each of these goldsmiths would find his
stock of specie running down (as gold would be going overseas) and
he would bring down his note issue. This would have the effect of
bringing down prices, thereby making the nation more competitive
and restoring its trade. Conversely, if the nation was running a huge
trade surplus and piles of gold were flowing into our goldsmiths’
coffers, they would issue more notes and this would have the effect
of raising prices and thereby, once again, restoring the overall trade
balance. This relationship between money and prices is called ‘The
Quantity Theory of Money.” Irving Fisher is supposed to have
discovered this theory, but the phenomenon has been noted by
’ historians ever since money first made its appearance. When the
Spaniards discovered huge quantities of silver in the Potosi mines of
the New World, prices rose in the whole of Europe.

To understand this simple theory, imagine yourself in an ancient
South Indian town in which cowrie shells constitute money. Now
suppose that, walking along the beach one day, some people found a
huge pile of these little shells washed up by the sea. They would
naturally be overjoyed, and head for the market to buy everything
that money could buy. The shopkeepers in the market would
individually see demand increase—and would raise their prices: we
all know of demand and supply. But in this case what actually happens
is that the supply of cowrie shells has increased and their value has
gone down. Each cowrie buys less than it did before. The price of a
chicken relative to a sack of potatoes may probably remain the same.
That is, if chicken prices increase from 10 cowries to 12 cowries and
potatoes from 5 cowries to 6 cowries it means that a chicken is still
worth two sacks of potatoes—relative prices are unchanged. It is the
price of money that has gone down because its supply has increased.

The Quantity Theory of Money says just that: if you increase the
supply of money, prices will rise. Vice versa for reductions in the
quantity of money. Or to put it another way: increase the supply of
money and the value of money goes down (it buys less); vice versa
for reductions in the quantity of money. Continuous unabated
inflation—a phenomenon of our times—is directly related to the
quantity of money issued. All this money is issued by governments.

STATE AND THE MONETARY SYSTEM

Historically, monarchs coined currency, but this was not token
currency. They were coins in gold and silver of certified purity and
weight. The role of the state was standardization. It earned small
profits in this way, there being a small difference between the value
of the coin and the amount of gold it actually contained. This
commission that the state earned was called ‘seignorage’.

Now there were good kings and bad kings. A good king would
earn his modest seignorage and be proud of the purity of the coins
that carried his face to the distant corners of his realm. A bad king
would scheme ways by which he could increase the base metal content
(say, by inserting more brass in the gold) of his gold coin, or reduce
the weight marginally — so as to be able to issue more coins for the
same amount of gold. These extra coins he could then spend on
wine, women and war. This is called ‘debasement’ of currency. It
naturally caused inflation—as has been explained earlier. Debasement
ruined many an economy.

BANK RUNS UNDER FREE BANKING

Banks face what is called the ‘illiquidity risk’ because they all keep
fractional reserves. This does not imply that the bank is insolvent, it
is just that its assets are tied up and it cannot generate enough liquid
funds if suddenly called upon to cough up a huge amount. Thus, it is
said, a free-banking system will witness many ‘runs’ on banks. As
there will be no central bank as ‘lender of last resort’, there will be
no deposit insurance. This argument is countered by pointing out
that bankers take more uncalled for risks when they know there is a
‘lender of last resort’. This is known as the ‘moral hazard problem’.
When incentives are designed to elicit perverse behaviour, there is a
moral hazard. In this case, the lender of last resort gives bankers the
perverse incentive to take excessive risks. (So when the IMF wants
to be the globe’s lender of last resort, the entire earth’s bankers face
a moral hazard.)

Granted that bankers will avoid unnecessary risks when there is
no lender of last resort; but the question remains as to what a free-
banking system will do to handle runs. Runs can be of two types:
deposit runs and note runs. A deposit run occurs when all the bank’s
depositors rush to the bank to redeem their deposits in notes. Let us
suppose that every customer with money deposited in a particular
bank comes forward to withdraw his entire holding. The customers
want money—notes. But this is not a note run—where all note holders
approach the bank simultaneously to get specie—like gold—for their
notes. This is the critical difference between a deposit run and a note
run. In a deposit run, customers want to convert one kind of bank
liability (deposits) into another (notes). In a note run, they want
assets which lie outside the banking system in exchange for their

notes. A deposit run could become a note run at a later stage. Let us
see how a free-banking regime would handle such crises.

First the deposit run. This is the most common type of run in
banking history. Central banking regimes, faced with a deposit run
on a particular bank (or the entire system), would have to perform
lender of last resort functions. Free banking does better than that.
(Remember the free bank can issue its own notes.) In free banking,
banks are able to create liquidity at willi—and this ability ensures
stability. All that a bank does is convert one type of liability (deposits)
into another (notes).

That is, a bank’s balance sheet shows assets and liabilities. The

all that the bank has to do is issue notes to its customers. In the

process, the bank’s accountants reduce the bank’s liabilities on account

of deposits and increase the bank’s liabilities on account of notes.

THE PITFALLS OF BUREAUCRATIC ORGANIZATION

The philosophy of the market does posit a public administration.
This is now a highly evolved area of research. Free marketeers do
have ways of seeing public goods and services delivered, using
principles of market economics—tike competition. Hence, we do
not just speak of freedom; we also discuss the core issue: public
administration.

So far in India, public administration has been carried out by the
bureaucratic method of organization. The Indian Administrative
Service is at the top of an entire clutch of central government and
state-level organizations. It is a descendant of the Indian Civil Service,
which itself arose from the covenanted service of the East India
Company. The Company’s service had all the characteristics of
bureaucracy: promotion was strictly by seniority; and hierarchy was
paramount. Recruits had to prove intellectual competence; standards
were high. It was also essential that they were ‘gentlemen’; and this
gave Indian bureaucracy its elite position. This position was earned
the hard way, through hard work—which has, unfortunately, now
been lost.

Bureaucracy, if we go by the typology set by Max Weber, has four
essential characteristics, best remembered through the acronym HICE:
Hierarchy; Impersonality; Career; and Expertise. Indian bureaucracy
has lost the social respect it once commanded simply because it has
failed on the count of Expertise. It practiced something called
‘generalism’ with great gusto—which only ensures that politicians
can transfer officials willy-nilly. But experts in homicide cannot be
shifted to traffic management! Thus, in a country where politicians
usually represent illiterates, where knowledge could enter government
only through merit-based bureaucrats, the Government of India has
become a government by ignorance. Proof exists on the streets of
India, where traffic management has never been attempted simply
because the knowledge to do so does not exist with the state. India
Gate is probably the most unsafe roundabout in the world!

Max Weber laid great store by bureaucracy as an organizational
form that could achieve excellent results. But he was not unaware of
its limitations. He warned that bureaucrats could not be relied upon
to provide leadership—which had to be left to charismatic politicians.
The bureaucrat was a kleber,’ he said, using the German word for
‘sticky’ or ‘gluey’. That is, the bureaucrat would stick to his chair,
refusing to take bold decisions. To him the chair was all important.
A politician is more likely to resign on a major point of difference
and make the matter public. This is important for democracy. Thus,
good politicians are essential. Bureaucrats cannot deliver on their
own because they are followers, not leaders.

There have been some prominent critics of bureaucratic
organization, foremost among them the Austrian economist, Ludwig
von Mises. He said that there are two ways of conducting ‘peaceful
co-operation amongst men’. One is bureaucratic management; the
other is profit management. Some things—like police forces, courts
and tax-collecting bureaus—need to be bureaucratic. The rest do
not. It would be better to confine bureaucracies to just these subjects,
and not stretch it to areas where management for profit can deliver
better. The most important point Mises made was that bureaucracies
are graveyards for talented youth, who sacrifice themselves for their
seniors:

Public administration takes a very close look at what is happening
in its sister subject: Management. Change was in the air in the world
of business, and this served to inspire NPM.

Giant corporations were slowly becoming ‘hollow’. Major toy,
athletic footwear and various other kinds of corporations were no
longer vertically integrated. Design and marketing were centralized
in a small office in New York, while manufacturing was being
contracted out to various parties all over the developing world—

do proof-reading and editing at home, leaving labour-intensive
typesetting and printing to contracted parties in Singapore. The
question therefore arose: Like the hollow corporations, can we not
get a hollow state? Just as corporations were contracting out their
work, could not bureaucracies be replaced by public service managers
whose task would be to invite bids, make out contracts, enforce
these contracts, ensure that the service has been delivered according
to the terms of the contract—and that is all. The state should not

There is a certain deficiency in this bureaucratic approach which

He will, therefore, have little time to spend on the ‘output’ of his

It is not very intelligent to spend public money in such a way that
there is no relation between costs and benefits—since the output is
not ‘sold’. Things are much worse when, over and above the fact that
there is no relationship between cost and benefit, the actual
performance of the task is not monitored effectively by the bureau

This bureau does not sell its output—cleanliness. In this method
of bureaucratic delivery, there cannot be any relation derived between
cost and benefits. There is no answer to the question: Is this
expenditure worth it? If there has to be an answer to this question,
there must be some way of monitoring output: to quantify cleanliness.
This cannot happen where the head of the bureau is burdened with
bureau inputs. When he cannot and does not monitor output, the
question ‘Is this worth it?’, is totally unanswerable.

THE NEW PUBLIC MANAGEMENT

Enter New Public Management. It would prescribe ‘contracting out’.
The bureau chief’s work would now consist of identifying the work
to be done; stating how it should be carried out; advertising for bids;
drawing up contracts; and supervising the work to ensure that it is
being performed as per contract. This approach brings in the market.
There would emerge firms who would compete to perform the task,
making them cost-conscious. Not only would expenditure lessen;
service delivery would improve remarkably.

The literature on NPM is vast and varied. There are government
documents—like ‘Government Management’ by the New Zealand
Treasury, the first country to take to NPM. There is also Reinventing
Government by Osborne and Gaebler,> to which Bill Clinton has

Democrat, NPM easily crosses the left-right divide.

Over the years it has become possible to identify the basic thrust
areas of NPM and thereby list its essential principles. According to
one study,° these are:

1. Separating ‘provision’ from ‘production’: This is the logic of
‘contracting out’. It has various advantages, chief among them
being the fact that it separates ‘steerers’ from ‘rowers’.
Politicians and bureaucrats steer, managers manage and row.

2. Serving consumers: The idea is that public services are in
demand. So it is in the interest of the bureau to serve its
customers.

3. Market pricing rather than taxes: This makes bureaus serve
customers better.

4. Clean subsidies: Subsidies, if any, should be clearly worked
out—and should reach targeted groups directly, without
affecting other prices.

5. Extending competition: When work is to be bid for between
competing firms, the most cost-effective outcome is likely to
emerge.

6. Decentralizing provision: This is in line with the principle of
‘subsidiarity’ which says that provisioning should be left to
the lowest rung of government that can effectively look after
it. If a municipality can do it, let it. If not, it goes to the higher
level; and if they cannot handle it, only then does the work
devolve upon the national government. The European Union
recognizes this principle.

front. This applies more to citizens of predatory states: states that
have attempted to plan everything and failed at each task. We live in
uncertainty about the future of the world and its environment. But
one thing at least Indians should know: whatever the problem, we’ll
be better off tackling it if we are free than if we allow our predatory
state to amass powers on the basis of this excuse. We have already
examined the case of Delhi’s air and what ham-handed state action
cannot accomplish. In that case, it was pointed out that car companies
and consumers will bear costs of better equipment, but the air will
not be cleaner because of state failures. On the environmental front,
our state’s actions generally produce rent-seeking opportunities for
bureaucrats, costs on producers and manufacturers, and little benefit.
There is an established school of free-market environmentalism and
a great deal of environmental research using market principles is
going on. In India, Dr Shreekant Gupta of the Delhi School of
Economics is conducting research on the environment, looking for
solutions within the free market paradigm. His views on the work

done by state pollution control boards is most unflattering. The basic
problem is that they impose costs all right, but there are no
corresponding benefits. They are basing their actions on the wrong
paradigm. They are not using incentives and disincentives properly.
EXTRA-REGARDING PRUDENCE
Environmental concern is a form of extra-regarding prudence—and
all humans possess it. (Even leaf-cutting ants possess it!) We are,
therefore, all concerned about the environment, and this has been
used by politicians and bureaucrats the world over to amass powers.
These powers are not the solution to the environmental problem.
The solution is knowledge-based politics of the environment within
civil society. This will build an informed citizenry and take away the
“scare psychosis’. This scare psychosis is extremely harmful because
it prompts ham-handed state action; further, it precludes the possibility
of taking action based on reason.

In the Julian Simon vs. Norman Myers debate, a question was
asked whether the economist (Simon) was utilitarian in a strict sense
while the environmentalist (Myers) displayed a spiritual, aesthetic
ethic. Simon answered as follows:

I do not think 1 am as you describe me. I don’t like to swat flies and
squash spiders. I’d much rather shoo them out of the house. The notion
that one of us has more of a feeling for some aspects of nature or the
environment, which explains what we say... I don’t think that explains
our differences at all.... I don’t think that Mr. Myers and I stand in
different relationships spiritually to nature or to anything else that
accounts for our views. I think what does account for our views is this:
I consistently look at the evidence of the past and I look for the longest
possible data series, and I examine what has happened and J extrapolate
into the future. In contrast, instead of looking at the historical evidence
of the past, Norman (in common with most biologists and people on his
side of the fence) looks at a set of theoretical propositions about
phenomena that ‘must’ be happening based on supposed physical,
chemical, or biological principles. This I believe is the difference. His
is a speculative analysis of what must happen versus my empirical analysis
of what has happened over the long sweep of history. This I believe is
the fundamental difference between us.‘
“Simon, J.L., op. cit., p. 148.

174 / ANTIDOTE—ESSAYS AGAINST THE SOCIALIST INDIAN STATE

This is the basic point. Free-market economists like Simon and
me do care about the environment in much the same manner as
anybody else. Where we differ from the doomsayers is in our analyses.
We look at history and see that we are constantly able to sustain
more life on this planet as well as harness more natural resources.
The prices of these resources are all going down, showing that their
availability has increased over time. The price of human beings—the
average wage rate—on the other hand, has been consistently rising,
showing that, if there is a resource that is short, it is human beings
(despite rising numbers). The doomsayers, on the other hand, have a
theory that predicts doom: this ‘must’ happen. In the 1970s they
predicted an ice age; today the earth is warming. There is need to
show extra-regarding prudence; there is need to look for accurate
information; there is need to process all this information and produce
real knowledge—but there is no need to be alarmed unnecessarily.

The basic historical record shows that human beings create more
than they use. ‘This applies to to all metals, all fuels, all foods, and
all other measurements of human welfare, and it applies to all
countries.’> This is how the market, as an ecosystem especially created
by us, works. When we see poverty and degradation around us, and
filth, it is not the human animal that is responsible for this—this is
not due to his ‘overbreeding’—rather it is due to bad policies and
institutions that take away individual liberty. These prevent us from
generating wealth, from living well, and also from looking after the
world’s natural resources by exercising property rights over them.
The predatory state as planner seeking to industrialize the country
by restricting trade; the same state as plan financier resorting to
inflationary finance; the very same state, as the nation’s biggest
landlord, systematically allowing tragedies of the commons to occur;
and the disregard for property rights (as with rent control)—these .
are far greater threats to the environment than the hole in the ozone
layer, the declining number of tigers, or global warming. It is time
for Indians who care about the environment to ‘get real’ and see the
real threat.
FOR A MORE HOPEFUL OUTLOOK

‘An Optimistic Economist’. Yes, indeed he was optimistic, and so am
| I. I reject the doomsayers. I am often asked at seminars, where I
present these views on population being a cause of prosperity (and
environmental betterment—if economic freedom were to be granted),
| if these are a ‘minority opinion’. They are not. They are the established
view of a school of thought that sees the special attribute of all humans
to ‘truck, barter and exchange’ as the basis for the division of labour
and knowledge and the consequent generation of prosperity through
the market mechanism. Those who look at human beings as a problem
do not notice this attribute. They see the naked, brown bodies of
{ Third World children and advocate massive aid programmes for
‘family planning’. They do not press for free world-trade based on
sound money, instead. And they shudder at free immigration—that is
their love for humanity.
, Similarly, on the environment, they are blind to the working of
the market mechanism as an ecosystem that will allow niches in
{ which the environment will be carefully husbanded. Their belief
that human beings are a problem—and not a resource—prompts them
to look for solutions in the state, rather than in economic freedom,
by which each one of us have incentives to find solutions. Their
ideas are an equivalent to central planning. They advocate an
‘intellectual-moral elite’ or a ‘group of professionals’ with strong
powers to solve environmental problems. They could not be more
‘ wrong. But, what is worse is that their views are dangerous: a ‘techno-
fascistic elite’ will rule if they have their way. They also promote a
hopeless world-view, by which teachers teach children that they are
a problem, and not the future hope of mankind. And everyone sees
the predatory state as the only solution.
As we have seen, there is a role for the state, but that is the
. preservation of property rights and the enforcement of contracts.
Law, order, justice and some public goods. On the environmental
front, too, the state must be ‘hollowed out’ and market principles
brought into play. Today, the environment ministry is running millions
of acres of forests in much the same manner that the predatory state
is running railways, airlines and hotels: running them into the ground.
The people of this country must see this predatory state and the
economic repression it has launched on its people as the main
environmental problem. They must see the children of India as the

resource that will fix it. That will give us the hopeful outlook necessary
to face the challenges of the future head-on.

CONSUMERISM AND HAPPINESS

Environmentalists lambaste free-market economists saying that we
promote ‘consumerism’. J have already said that the cities of the
future are an environmental challenge and that citizens must be aware
of the good or the harm they do the world by what they consume.
However, the point needs to be taken a little further, because sound
economic reasoning does not indicate that consumerism is a means
of maximizing happiness.

Of course, we must consume. In nature, the principle of life is:
Eat without getting eaten—and reproduce. But there is a difference
between consumption for the sake of living and living for the sake of
consumption: and in this context, an economist may have some
pertinent thoughts to offer. By ‘consumerism’ then, I mean living
for the sake of consumption. Like living to eat.

In his writings on the people of underdeveloped countries, Lord
Peter Bauer often remarks that these people are not really ‘poor’;
they are ‘needless’. That is, they manage to satisfy their basic needs
and have no requirements for anything the market has to offer them.
They, therefore, do not ‘work’ to produce goods for the market.
Some call this ‘subsistence agriculture’; Lord Bauer prefers to look
at it as a state of ‘needlessness’. He goes on to prescribe not state
action for ‘development’ but the entry of traders with ‘incentive goods’.
These goods carried by traders tempt needless people into entering
the market economy. Development proceeds. There is a lesson here.

Happiness is needlessness. Psychologists call it ‘homeostasis’. A
psychologist called Henry Murray totted up a list of over 50 ‘human
needs’ and if you were to go through that list, you would realize that
you would be better off without many of them. Having excessive
needs does not make us happy. Each time a need is satisfied a new
one arises and disturbs homeostasis. Markets create and satisfy needs
—that is the purpose—but, for the individual, a headlong dive into
reckless consumerism is not the recipe for happiness. It is a dive
into something that our ancients always spoke of: the maya jaal—
the illusion.

One could perhaps cite philosophers who have made this point,
but I would prefer to quote at some length from Jerome K. Jerome’s
classic, Three Men in a Boat: To Say Nothing of the Dog! The trip is
| about to commence, and our three heroes are talking about what
| they need to take along, when George says: ‘We must not think of
| the things we could do with, but only of the things we can’t do
' without.’ This then prompts the narrator to make the following
observations: ‘

George comes out really quite sensible at times. You'd be surprised. I
| call that downright wisdom, not merely as regards the present case, but
with reference to our trip up the river of life generally. How many
| people, on that voyage, load up the boat till it is in danger of swamping

with a store of foolish things which they think essential to the pleasure
. and the comfort of the trip, but which are really only useless lumber.
| How they pile the poor little craft mast-high with fine clothes and big

houses; with useless servants, and a host of swell friends that do not
care twopence for them, and that they do not care three ha’ pence for;
with expensive entertainments that nobody enjoys, with formalities and
fashions, with pretence and ostentation, and with—oh, heaviest, maddest
lumber of all!—the dread of what will my neighbours think, with luxuries
that only cloy, with pleasures that bore, with empty show that, like the
criminal’s iron crown of yore, makes to bleed and swoon the aching
head that wears it.
| It is lumber, man—all lumber! Throw it overboard. It makes the boat
so heavy to pull, you nearly faint at the oars. It makes it so cumbersome
and dangerous to manage, you never know a moment’s freedom from
anxiety and care, never gain a moment’s rest for dreamy laziness....
Throw the lumber over, man! Let your boat of life be light, packed
with only what you need—a homely home and simple pleasures, one or
two friends, worth the name, someone to love and someone to love you,
\ a cat, a dog, and a pipe or two, enough to eat and enough to wear, and
| a little more than enough to drink; for thirst is a dangerous thing.°
While discussing this passage one day, a friend remarked that Jerome
spoke like a socialist. I don’t agree. This is something that makes
absolute sense to any free-market development economist who
has understood the significance of Lord Bauer’s concept of
‘needlessness’.
‘Jerome, J.K., Penguin, London, 1889, pp. 26-7.

178 / ANTIDOTEs-ESSAYS AGAINST THE SOCIALIST INDIAN STATE

The free market will not promote mindless consumerism and its
concomitant destruction of the environment. What it will promote is
freedom—economic, political and cultural. In freedom, human beings
will find out how to be happy, how to seek happiness, how to be
fulfilled as human beings. In the natural ecosystem of the market,
with freedom, each human being will find the niche in which to
excel and from which to obtain by exchange the products of others.
This will lead to the fullest flowering of the human creative potential.
It will yield prosperity. But prosperous people who have flowered as
human beings will not be mindless consumers. They will seek culture,
art and music. Philosophy will bloom. That is the world to dream of.

... It is true that we are called a democracy, for the administration
is in the hands of the many and not of the few. But while the law
secures equal justice to all alike in their private disputes, the claim _
of excellence is also recognised; and when a citizen is in any way
distinguished, he is preferred to the public service, not as a matter
of privilege, but as the reward of merit. Neither is poverty a bar,
but a man may benefit his country whatever be the obscurity of
his condition. There is no exclusiveness in our public life, and in
our private intercourse we are not suspicious of one another nor angry
with our neighbour if he does what he likes; we do not put on sour
looks at him which, though harmless, are not pleasant. While we are
thus unconstrained in our private intercourse, a spirit of reverence
| pervades our public acts; we are prevented from doing wrong by
1 respect for authority and for the laws, having an especial regard for
| those which are ordained for the protection of the injured as well as
; to those unwritten laws which bring upon the transgresser of them
the reprobation of the general sentiment...We are lovers of the
beautiful, yet simple in our tastes, and we cultivate the mind without
loss of manliness. Wealth we employ, not for talk and ostentation,
but when there is a real use for it. To avow poverty with us is no
disgrace; the true disgrace is in doing nothing to avoid it. An Athenian
citizen does not neglect the state because he takes care of his own
household; and even those of us who are engaged in business have
a very fair idea of politics. We alone regard a man who takes no interest
in public affairs, not as a harmless, but as a useless character; and
if few of us are originators, we are all sound judges of a policy. The
great impediment to action is, in our opinion, not discussion, but
the want of that knowledge which is gained by discussions preparatory
to action. For we have a peculiar power of thinking before we act,
and of acting too, whereas other.men are courageous from ignorance
but hesitate upon reflection...

Introduction
Whe a group of friends met and thought of felicitating
Minoo Masani on his eightieth birthday, there was unanimity
of opinion that the most befitting way to honour him would be
to present him a volume of essays to educate and to reaffirm the
values. that he had cherished all his life. Also, since a whole new
generation is at the helm of affairs, it was agreed that it was only
proper that they should be reminded of the contribution that an
earlier generation had made to national development and freedom.
Some of the ideas propagated by Masani have been more than
vindicated by subsequent global events and they are too well ©
" established to need any further reiteration. Socialism and its varieties -
are no more the shibboleths that they were in earlier decades.
Masani has battled for some values and has affirmed the need
for a pure public life, for freedom and for the right of the lone
individual to assert his point of view. These of course, have a
continuity in the modern Indian tradition of political discourse
and one of the aims of this volume has been to present Masani
as a distinguished heir and an exponent of the Indian Liberal
tradition. Long before the classic assessment of Shonfield’s Modern
Capitalism and John Strachey’s book on the same theme, Masani
had been advocating the important role that it can play in Indian
economic development; in a free and open society the predatory
activities of businessmen can be controlled and capitalism shaped
to keep to its social responsibilities. The importance of a free press,
the right of small groups of citizens to assert themselves, the need
to educate the ‘freedom fighters’ in values have been themes near
his heart. In assembling this book of essays, it has not been possible
to touch upon all the themes that have interested and engaged
' Mr. Masani. People who have been his close associates have
contributed to this book. The essays in this volume are addressed
to the general public, especially to the young men and women
who will play a vital role in a crucial period of our development.
To include in a book of this kind all the varied topics which

INTRODUCTION» Vii
interested Masani would have made it encyclopaedic in its range
apart from making it unmanageable.

Minoo Masani in many respects represents a vanishing species
of public men and it is not unlikely that the next generation
_ will see almost none of his type. He should be basically regarded
| as one of the remaining liberal intellectuals who dominated the
earlier era of modern Indian politics. The earlier school of liberalism
of the pre-Gandhian era was trained in politics by personal precept,
example and interactions. The relationship between Ranade,
G. V. Joshi and Gokhale is well-known; similar personal links
were not uncommon. Gandhi almost missed being a member of
the Servants of India Society; also, Pherozeshah, Wacha, Gokhale,
Krishnaswami lyer, V. S. Srinivasa Sastri were all tied by personal
, friendships. However, the generation of Masani had little of any
direct contact with the earlier generation of liberals. In fact, they
were intellectually in opposition to that school, and worshipped
at new shrines. °
Barring Gandhi, Masani seems to have been influenced by no
elders of the national movement. Of course, his father was an
important public figure in civic politics and his contributions to

i public life as well as to university administration were not negligible.
Though perhaps Masani never met Gokhale, there are attitudinal

and intellectual similarities between the two and dissimilarities
between J. P. and him, — J. P. with whom he was so close personally
and whose causes he championed with ardour. Very much like

- Gokhale trudging the dusty plains and hills of the Bombay Presidency

raising funds for his institutions, Masani too in later decades was

to wander through the distances of India mobilizing cadres and

loyal partymen for his Congress Socialist Party. This was his Bharat

darshan. This gave Masani an intimacy about the real conditions of

the country which may not be immediately apparent to the observer.

In another respect too, Masani recalls the old Liberals. Basically

an intellectual, he from his salad days has continually attempted

to build institutions—it is quite likely that this belief in the
importance of building institutions and extending civil ideals and
civic education was perhaps the influence of his days in the London

School of Economics when participation in Workers’ Education

Viii Freedom and Dissent _

and similar activities were part of the obligation of academic
intellectuals. It is here that the similarities with the older liberals
is striking and he is so different from Jayaprakash. J..P. was basically °
a populist and one who was no builder of institutions like the
older liberals. Masani experimented in the organizing of a political
party and finding the limited use of this, tried to supplement
this with the creation of voluntary organizations. Some of these
were of course not destined to last long. Had he been born half
a century earlier, he would have built up educational institutions
and social reforms leagues. Like intellectuals in India in the nineteenth
century, he had to do several things simultaneously.

Gandhi and following him Jayaprakash, being basically populist
romantics, believed that nationalist politics would continually give
tise to’a race of public servants like themselves—visionaries, fired
by a’sense of enthusiasm for a public cause, unselfish, committed

. to cleansing public life and dedicating themselves to improving
the country and its politics. But the liberals were generally more
realistic and were not fired by any similar enthusiasms. While they

were themselves impeccable in their honesty, they had very little

of any illusions and stressed time and again the need for instilling

civic values and the. responsibility that came to them naturally.

The Liberal tradition had always emphasized the urgency of
fully utilizing the existing political institutions and through creative
use of these, extending benefits for the government, recruiting

- new participants to the political process, educating them in new
values and making civic politics a co-operative endeavour. They were
tireless in working in committees, local governments, co-operatives,

. legislatures etc. Masani too was to have a brief period of experience
in local government as well as in many others and he excelled
in several of them. His tenure in parliament was not only a bright
period in his political career, but will also remain an important
chapter in the history of India’s parliament. He brought to bear
the same passion to public affairs that Gokhale did in an earlier
decade but free from the restraints which Gokhale had to labour—
for he was an equal to the highest political officer in a free
republic.

INTRODUCTION . ix
While the thirties and the forties saw him active in founding
and strengthening a socialist party, the winning of independence
"and the consolidation of the forces of nationalism compelled him
, to stress the older values that the liberals had emphasised, and he
began floating a number of organisations, the most significant of these
being the Leslie Sawhny Programme’, the Democratic Research
Service, the Adult Education Institute, the Indian Liberal Group
etc. Masani’s own experience had indicated the fatal attractions of
- communism and how easily it could become an extension of Soviet
political designs. The Democratic Research Service was created
mainly to educate Indians on the wiles of communist treachery. The
Leslie Sawhny Programme was basically an updating of the dream
of the Liberals to prepare an aware and alert citizenry which would
be conscious of its rights, demand these and organize itself for
asserting its civic rights. It is interesting to note that Masani and
other public figures in the fifties began to reassert the very same
| values of liberal pluralism which de Tocqueville pointed out as
| informing the American democracy more than a century ago.

The running of institutions, the floating of voluntary organisations
and the criticism of the powers that be are the essence of an open
polity—the ideal of which was expressed by Pericles in his famous
oration more than two thousand years ago. It is this speech that
prefaces this festschrift.

In the long history of India, the values of an open polity, that
of discussing politics in public, putting forward alternatives to the
government, relentlessly criticising the government for its limitations
and yet co-operating with it when found necessary were all practised

; by the Liberals from the last decades of the last century. During
the nationalist movement, it was inevitable that some of these should
be under a cloud. The opportunity for resuming these presented
itself after independence, but the natural cupidity of the ordinary
politicians, the passion for office laid waste the hope for freedom
and for other civic values. It has been men in the opposition, men
as different as Kripalani, J. P., Rajaji, Masani, Nath Pai and S. M. Joshi
* At the time of writing the good work of the LSP has earned it an award from the
Indian Merchants Chamber.

x ° Freedom and Dissent
and others who had kept the spirit alive and helped preserve the
timbre of public life in the country. .

It was during the Emergency that they had to face the greatest
challenge. With leaders like J. P. and others imprisoned, it fell
to people like Masani, N. G. Goray and others to fight the battle
but through acceptable means. The decision to keep the magazine
‘Freedom First going and challenging the censor in courts of law
and exposing the Emgergency was the contribution of Masani
and it should not be lightly brushed aside. Equally important was _
the support that he gave J. P. and to sustain his spirit when they
were sinking low because of continuous deterioration of the health
of the Lokanayak.

’ While those who are politically aware do know of Masani and
his contributions, there is another Masani for many others; who
know him as the author of Owr India and other books that they
read at school either in English or in translations. New consciousness

and a new awareness were created in tens of thousands of school
children who were educated for the first time in civic values but
in so disarmingly an engaging manner. This brought some of the
creative latent talents in him; for he has remained basically an
educationist in the best sense of the term. His capacity for conveying
complex ideas in a simple manner is enviable. Alone of our political
leaders Masani is able to empathize with generations far younger
to him. It is this rare quality that he shares with Rajaji that makes
him have a wide rapport across different generations.

What is common to the Liberals, Gandhi and Masani, is the
stress they lay on raising the tone of public life. All of them have
emphasized the need to spiritualize politics and this can be done
only in the full glare of public gaze. Closed politics or court
politics as it is in India is basically the politics of kickbacks and
concessions privately arrived at. Masani, both in the inner councils
of the Congress Socialist party and later in the Swatantra has
refused consistently to come to terms with what he regarded as
evil or compromising with first principles. This stress on open
politics, stresses other values which are central to Masani—the
freedom to opt out, to choose and to stand by one’s convictions;
ultimately the values of individuality as understood and regarded

INTRODUCTION xi
by J. S. Mill as the priceless possession of man. It is this that
makes for man to be a moral person and for a society to be one
based on free association and which ultimately maximises choice.

Masani’s public life has been spent far more in the ranks of
the Opposition than in the government. This was the lot of the
Liberals in modern India and in a sense this is something that
ought to be praised and commemorated. “In whose service is
perfect Freedom” is more a religious sentiment and it does not
smack of worldly wisdom; but often (and naturally so) it remains
at the verbal level than in action. The liberals believed in a secular
version of this and gave their best to the community which they
loved so much and to which they gave willingly. What sustains
people of the calibre of Masani is the sense of optimism which
makes them champion at an age when others would rest on their
laurels. One cannot better recapitulate this than in the words of
Robert Browning: oO

Then, welcome each rebuff
That turns earth’s smoothness rough,
Each sting that bids nor sit nor stand but go!
Be our joys three-parts pain!
Strive, and hold cheap the strain;
Learn, nor account-the pang; dare, never grudge the throe
Grow old along with me!
The best is yet to be
The last of life, for which the first was made:
Our times are in His band
Who saith, “A whole I planned,
Youth shows but half; trust God; see all, nor be afraid!
R. SRINIVASAN
