_ Minoo Masani As I Know Him
J.R. D. Tata
ntil Minoo Masani joined Tatas in 1941, I knew him
U only by name and reputation as a young controversial
socialist politician who, starting as a militant advocate of
Marxism, had gradually turned into an equally militant
opponent, while claiming throughout to be a firm Gandhian
and democrat. This baffled or infuriated many, including his
political comrades and peers of various parties and hues,
: who, not unnaturally, considered him either as a dangerous
revolutionary or a turncoat or opportunist whose debating
brilliance, integrity and organising talents were, however,
never doubted.
I was fascinated by these conflicting aspects of his
personality and political philosophy, which my politically
untutored mind interpreted as those of a born rebel who, .
while he saw in the Russian Revolution the dawn of redemption.
from the gross injustices and shameless colonialism of
nineteenth century capitalism, was too intelligent to swallow,
| wholesale, Marxist dialectics. Yet, like many other dreamers
* of the time including Jawaharlal Nehru, he believed that,
somehow, freedom could be made to co-exist with Marxism.
- Considering Minoo’s early exposure to the Marxist fervour of
England’s youth after World War I, then to the turmoil and
throes of the freedom struggle and, last but far from least,
to the glaring economic inequalities prevailing in India, he
seemed predestined to be the stormy petrel of Indian politics
that he duly became.
Increasingly disillusioned though I myself grew to be with
Indian politics where, apart from slavish acceptance of a
| misconceived socialism, the acquisition and retention of power

2 * Freedom and Dissent
seemed to be the main motivator of Indian politicians, Minoo
was one of the few I continued to admire and respect despite
my disagreement with most of his political credo. I understood
his denunciation of the Marxism which he had so fervently
advocated earlier, and I admired the courage and honesty he
displayed in admitting he had been wrong. I therefore had
no hesitation, despite the doubts expressed by some of my
colleagues and friends, in welcoming him into Tatas in 1941
when he retired from the political field. In those sixteen
years that Minoo spent with us, my regard and affection
for him grew. As I came into closer contact with him and
listened to him and read his writings, 1 became increasingly
surprised that a man of his intelligence, character and un-
compromising integrity had been denied inclusion in the top
leadership of the country. .
In Tatas, Minoo played a variety of roles, always with
- competence and despatch, demonstrating a remarkable adapt-
ability to ideas, tasks and problems wholly different to those
he previously had to deal with. Although I was, therefore, .
happy to have him in the Tata team, I was delighted when
the Prime Minister appointed him India’s Ambassador to .
Brazil in 1948 as I hoped, in the national interest, that
it would lead, on his return, to more important assignments,
possibly within the Government itself. But that was not
to be, presumably because his strongly independent character
and the mistrust his radical change of political ideology
had made him unacceptable to the Congress Party. Minoo
would indeed have proved a difficult colleague in a
Government and party so heavily infiltrated by Marxist
fellow-members. .

So Minoo came back’ to Tatas where; in charge of the
Group’s Public Relations Department, he filled increasingly
valuable roles as an adviser on management, on human
relations in industry, on personnel and labour problems, for
which his earlier experience in the trade union field made
him particularly helpful. In fact, I found his views and advice
to the Firm so useful to me that I got him to join my personal

J. R. D. TATA . 3
"secretariat as ‘chef de cabinet’ where I could take full advantage
of his practical and insatiably active mind, his wide-ranging
| experience of men and affairs, his sense of history, his
authorship and his mastery of English. I could not have made
a better choice.

Although our minds often operated on similar, if not.
common, wavelengths, we both were somewhat impatient by
nature, and I sometimes baulked at the speed at which he
wished me to take decisions which I usually did in the end,
but only after pondering, perhaps beyond need, over possible

, implications or ramifications. Like all of us who, today, have
. the privilege of being able to look upon others from the lofty
| heights of advancing age, Minoo has mellowed and lost his

earlier passion for immediate action.

We found no difficulty, however, in agreeing with each

; other on two matters. One, the need for industrialists to adhere
strictly to their social responsibilities as trustees of shareholders,
consumers, workers and society, all of which Jamsetji Tata
himself had made a part of the Firm’s philosophy from the
start. The other, in regard to the need to develop a real

partnership, based on mutual trust, between management and
labour. In the first matter, Minoo was largely responsible for
inducing me to get a paragraph included in most of the Tata
companies’ Articles of Association, declaring their mindfulness
of their social and moral responsibilities. In the other, he

. played an important role in the development of a highly
successful system of joint consultation in Tata Steel, which
itself has been largely responsible for the unique labour
relations prevalent at Jamshedpur for the past forty years or
more.

One of the most striking traits of Minoo’s character is his

‘ deep understanding of human relations, somewhat unexpected

| - in an ‘ex’ fiery political activist. All in all, Minoo Masani
| was, and still is, a remarkable human being whose talents and
character, sadly for India, failed to be recognised and used as

/ they could have been to the country’s great benefit.

The Maverick Crusader
S. V. Raju
In his preface to the first volume of his autobiography,
Minoo Masani writes :
Swimming against the tide became so much of a habit,
almost a part of my nature. I wonder whether in later life,
particularly in my political activities and attitudes, the
patterns of my habit asserted themselves.
And aptly he titled the second volume of his memoirs Against
the Tide. :

In a twenty-five year association with him, first as Executive
Secretary of the Swatantra Party of which he was General
Secretary and later President; thereafter as an associate in
his Management Consultancy business, and for the last five
as a friend participating in a number of voluntary public
activities, 1 can say with conviction that Masani is never
happier than when he is swimming against the current.
In fact among his favourite quotes is this one.from James

) Russell Lowell :
They are slaves who dare not be
In the right.with two or three
As General Secretary of the Swatantra Party, when con- |
fronted with the need to take hard decisions he would often .
say that his job was to be effective and accomplish the task
and not seek popularity.

In the political game in India success is measured in terms
of office achieved. If this be the yardstick then Masani like
his friend Jayaprakash Narayan, has been a failure. But

| how does one measure a man’s achievement if he deliberately

6 Freedom and Dissent.
chooses. to reject opportunities if acceptance means
compromising with his beliefs? A clue is provided in his report
of Sri Prakasa’s encounter with Nehru who used strong
language to pull up Sri Prakasa for daring to suggest the
partition of Kashmir. Sri Prakasa who was then Indian High
Commissioner in Pakistan, lumped the scolding and continued
in office rather than annoy Nehru. Comments Masani: “Here
was an example of one of India’s biggest tragedies — the
inability to stand up to someone in authority.”
.. Immediately after India’s independence, Masani was indeed
‘very much a part of the then Congress establishment and
close to Jawaharlal Nehru. Despite emerging differences with
Nehru in economic and foreign policy matters, the latter —
recommended Masani as an expert on the UN Sub-Commission
for the Prevention of Discrimination and the Protection of
Minorities. When Masani crossed swords with the Soviet
" -Union’s representatives questioning their claims of having
satisfactorily settled the minorities problem in the USSR,
Nehru was far from pleased. When despite India’s objections
Masani was elected Chairman of the Sub-Commission, Nehru
vetoed the election. However, as a Congress Member in India’s
provisional parliament Masani being a thorn in Nehru’s flesh
-was sought to be removed by persuading Masani to go to
Brazil as India’s ambassador. Masani accepted a one-year
assignment and at the end of it declined an extension or a
posting to some other Latin American country. The rejection
did not increase his popularity with Nehru whose need was
for pliant men. Sri Prakasa, a fine gentleman though he was,
was rewarded with a Cabinet Ministership and later the
Governership of Madras; Masani’s refusal to toe the line
resulted in his drawing away from Nehru and with it his
association with Nehru’s Congress.

It is easy to be in the opposition if the individual concerned
sees little prospect of power. But to be near it and yet reject
it if it meant compromising with one’s principles speaks for
courage and integrity of a high order. And these qualities
Masani has in abundance.

S. V. RAJU . 7
Masani was a founder-member of the Congress Socialist
Party conceived in late 1933 in Nasik Jail in the company
-of Jayaprakash Narayan, Yusuf Meherally and others. Six
years later in 1939 he resigned from the CSP. His campaign
to get communists expelled from the CSP met with much
opposition. But Masani was vindicated. In his Memories of
Yusuf Meberally, Bertram Wolfe reported :
The Congress Socialist Party of India was taken in by
the fair words of friendship and not only accepted the
| Communists into its ranks but helped the Communist Party
to enter into the Indian National Congress. The Indian
Communists were under secret instructions to penetrate
and try to capture the Congress Socialist Party and above
all to discredit and destroy Mahatma Gandhi. Though the
Indian Socialists, Meherally among them, were as candid
and unsuspecting as the socialists of other lands, yet they
proved to possess an anti-toxin which saved them from
: destruction.
The only person, according to Meherally, who sounded
- a note of warning that the Communists were not morally

Minoo Masani also felt exactly around this time that not

In this area Minoo Masani was the first to propound the

theory of ‘mixed economy’. In his path-breaking booklet

“A Plea for a Mixed Economy”, Masani argued as early as

1947 that what emergent, new India needed was to find a

new path for its own economy, and in so doing both the

public sector and the private sector had to work in harmony,

instead of each claiming superiority over the other. The old

This little booklet had obviously an enormous impact on
Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, who presented to the country its
first “Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948”. This Resolution

the various sectors of the economy and that both the public
and private sectors had to grow jointly; secondly, it added that

which could not be achieved by ‘the mixed economy’; only in

_ the latter case, there would be more production, and perhaps
| more productivity. A far better solution in the spirit of the
‘mixed economy’ would be to allow the public sector also
grow simultaneously with the private sector.

The Concept of Liberalism and
its Relevance for India
S. P. Aiyar
Origins and Outlook
A ny one who sets out to prove the relevance of liberalism for
England or the United States or for any of the established
democracies of the Western World would appear to his
contemporaries as a curious and interesting crank. In these
countries the social and political philosophy of liberalism is
now part of the institutional framework and constitutes the
ethos in which government functions. On the other hand in
large parts of Asia and Africa liberalism is often regarded
as an out-moded philosophy with little or no relevance to the
problems of economic development. In Communist countries,
of course, liberalism is hardly spoken of, being synonymous
with bourgeois subversion. The relevance of liberalism arises
precisely in those historical situations where the rights of men
- are suppressed or in countries that live under the menacing
threat of tyranny in one form or another.
In the history of ideas, liberalism has presented two faces..
It has been a philosophy of revolt as well as an affirmation
of human freedom. As a philosophy it has dominated the
intellectual life of Europe since the beginning of the Refor-
mation and has sought to liberate men from medieval con-
ceptions of authority. In its origins— and indeed, throughout
its history—liberalism has sought to encourage individual
initiative as the motor-force of all progress. It began in a mood ”
of revolt in an era when Europe was poised for great changes.
It revolted against State-dominated feudal interests but it also
represented the outlook of the commercial and other new

74 “7 Freedom and Dissent
classes which were emerging during the end of the Middle
Ages. Liberalism set the ambit of political authority and sought _
| to confine the functions of government within the framework
of a legal system emphasizing the freedom of new economic
interests. In his Rise of European Liberalism Harold Laski
attempted to provide an economic interpretation of this
movement of thought. He attempted to show that liberalism
was merely an aspect of European history in a period of which,
it was, to quote Ruggiero, “a by-product of the effort of the
middle class to win its place in the sun.” It was Laski’s intention
to prove that liberalism had lost its relevance but it has
outlived him and the passing phase of European history when
he flirted with the prevailing currents of thought. Laski’s
Marxist interpretation had many valuable insights but it did
not prove the irrelevance of liberalism. On the other hand,
it merely served to underline the contribution liberalism had
made. It had freed men from the numerous restrictions which
~ had been imposed on trade and commerce and helped the
growth of the industrial society in a formative period.
Liberalism gave a new lease of life to the activities of men in
all spheres and helped the growth of science. In the first flush ~
of enthusiasm created by the growth of the physical sciences
and the grand idea of Progress, liberalism attempted to pattern
its world view on that of physics by trying to explain society
as a system governed by its own laws. The social order became
part of the “natural order” and any interference with the
social system was believed to be detrimental to its smooth
functioning.

I have already stated that liberalism was a revolt against the
restrictions and privileges of feudalism. It placed the individual
at the centre of its philosophy and emphasized his ability to
reason out social arrangements and sort things out for himself.
It stressed his right to trade and enter into contracts, his
freedom to bargain and the freedom of enterprise. Above all,
it postulated private property as one of the conditions of social
progress. It was, therefore, the function of government to
guarantee the peaceful employment of property and provide

| S. P. AIYAR . 75
the external conditions of law and order.

Liberalism was a revolt not merely against feudal interests
but also against the dogma and authority of the Church. It
rejected the medieval claim that “Truth” was revealed. It went
back to the Greek idea that Truth had to be discovered through
the methods of science. Since truth had to be discovered, it
became necessary to protest against institutions and individuals
claiming possession of final truths. In the process, liberalism
asserted the right of free men to express opinions and assert
their civil and political rights. The heart of the matter was the
liberation of individuals and society from irrational restraints.
In its revolt against the authority of the Church, it emphasized
the demarcation of the spheres of Church and State. Thus

the history of liberalism in Europe is coterminus with the
process of secularization and the growth of a modern rational
bureaucracy.

Before we leave behind us this brief account of the intel-
lectual origins of liberalism in Europe it is necessary to
mention that liberalism was primarily a social and political
philosophy and acquired its economic content later. The great

exponents of liberalism were philosophers and not business
men and even a casual look into any history of liberalism
would show that they were often as critical of business interests
as they were of the Church or the State.
Liberalism is not an Ideology
Liberalism is a philosophy and not an ideology; it provides
the broadest framework for the progress of individuals and
societies. This is why most of us get stumped when confronted
by a question requiring us to give a short definition of
liberalism. It has been a movement of ideas emphasizing
freedom and growth; the variety and complexity of society. ,
It postulates the diversity of human interests and the creativity
of individuals. When classical writers on liberalism talked of
“Minimum government” they did not ask for the total with-
drawal of the State, giving free rein to individuals. Politics

76 Freedom and Dissent —
is but a small part of social life, occupying a corner of the
average man’s universe of interests. In its many spheres he
desires to be left alone. Even in the sphere of the economic
~ and the political he stands to gain only in arrangements which
make possible the free play of competing forces. Liberals have
been opposed to monopoly in every form and in every sphere.
It was the Church in the sixteenth century; it is the State
in the twentieth. Liberals want government to enter wherever
it can ptomote social progress through the freedom and
creativity of individuals but never to smother and snuff them
out.

Liberalism made a distinction between Society and State,
regarding the latter as primarily a regulatory mechanism,
taking over only those activities which individuals cannot and
which are directly in the larger interests of society. Liberalism
was never a negative philosophy —a positive element of State

activity was always present in the classical exposition of
liberalism. This is why liberalism has found little difficulty
in adapting itself to the expanding activities of the State under
the growth of science and technology. What liberalism has
retained in the course of its development, however, is a
suspicion and fear of the concentration of power in the State,
to balance which, it has sought the strengthening of other
competing social forces. Liberalism has no dogmatic creed,
no ideological strait-jacket. It claims to have no body of
solutions — unlike Marxism —for all countries irrespective of
their history, culture and development. The spirit of liberalism
lies in finding solutions appropriate to given situations but
only those compatible with freedom.
Liberalism in India
It is. against this background of European intellectual develop-
ment that Indian liberalism has to be viewed. It was a product
of the Western impact on the Indian mind and contributed to
India’s constitutional and political development. So profound,
indeed, has been this influence that the history of Indian

S. P. ATYAR . 77
nationalism and constitutional development, more or less,
coincides with that of liberalism until World War I. The
Gandhi period of Indian politics which followed cast a veil
over the real achievements of the outstanding liberal leaders of
the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and it is but appropriate
that we now seek to lift it. ,

No one, except purblind Marxist intellectuals, will deny
the contribution British rule made to the process of moderni-
zation of India; Westernization became the vehicle of moderni-
zation although it is perfectly valid to say that the two processes
are not identical. Ram Mohun Roy, with whom the history of
Indian liberalism begins, was quick in perceiving the signi-
ficance of the great changes on which India was poised in the

; first quarter of the nineteenth century. He was, to quote his
biographer Sophia Collet, the “bridge over which India passed
from her unmeasured past into her incalculable future” and
“in him, the New England became acquainted with the New
India.” His mastery over English, Bengali, Sanskrit, Persian:
and Arabic and his interest in comparative religions gave him
an unrivalled position in understanding the historical forces
which were shaping India in his time. Roy’s concern for social
reform and the uplift of women, for education as a means of
, Social transformation, for the freedom of the press— not to
speak of his passion for liberty—were inherited by the great
liberals of India. Some of them’ were in government service,
others in important political positions but they were never
the flatterers or sycophants that they have sometimes been
made out to be by those ignorant of modern Indian history.
The liberals were the most incisive critics of British rule.
One has only to recall the great volume of critical thought
based on study and reflection which the literature of Indian
. liberalism has produced. Men like Dadabhai Naoroji, Mahadeo
Govind Ranade, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Dinshaw Eduljee ’
Wacha and Pherozeshah Mehta were no captious and irrespon-
sible critics. One finds in their writings a power and intensity
which has, perhaps, never been excelled in the Gandhian
era. What gave urgency to their thought and commanded the

attention of the rulers was their anxiety always to be fair in
criticism and the integrity with which their arguments were
documented. It has been the lot of Indian liberals—then as
now to be cast in the role of an opposition, with little or
no chance of getting into power and they saw themselves as
the creators of public opinion.

For instance a recurring idea in Gokhale’s writing is that
leaders of public life must reconcile themselves by serving their

Superficially viewed, we have the political counterpart of the _
Karmayogin, indifferent alike to failure and success. But a

of a political leader is very different. Since public life is a
matter of slow growth, even a failure may be deemed a success,
if it contributes in the long run to the political education of
the people. A classic expression of this aspect of Gokhale’s

nothing better than the mere ploughing of the sands of the

Westernized Elites?
It has often been said that the liberals constituted an elite—a
description which they would hardly have objected to. They
constituted an elite, in the true sociological sense, and were
alive to their social responsibilities. But to imply that they

. were not interested in the welfare of the masses, is both wrong
and unfair. A few of them were aristocrats with only tenuous
contact with the masses but they were not the outstanding
leaders of the movement. To judge Indian liberalism through —
its lesser lights is like passing an indictment on Mahatma —
Gandhi through the performance of those who have crucified
his ideals. :

Nor were Indian liberals imitative, blindly accepting the
principles of Western liberalism. Western concepts were
tested, adapted and even rejected. Let me cite but one example.
Indian liberals like Roy, Ranade and Gokhale never accepted
the negative role of the State—the passing idiom of nine-
teenth century England.

In his Essays on Indian Economics Ranade pointed out that
the reaction to the meddlesomeness of mercantilism had been
carried to the other extreme. But there was a reaction to
the /aissez-faire system. Ranade said “speaking roughly, the

province of state interference and control is practically being
extended so as to restore the good points of the mercantile
system without its absurdities. The State is now more and
more recognised as a national organ for taking care of national
needs in all matters in which individual and co-operative efforts
are not likely to be so effective and economic as national
effort. This is a correct view to take for the true functions
of a state. To relegate them to the simple duty of maintaining

80 * Freedom and Dissent

peace and order is really to deprive the Community of many of
the advantages of the Social Union. Education, both Liberal
and Technical, Post and Telegraphs, Railway and Canal Com-
munications, the pioneering of new enterprize, the insurance of
risky undertakings, all these functions are usefully discharged
by the State. The question is one of time, fitness, and
expediency, not one of liberty and rights.” I must add that it
was not Ranade’s intention that liberty could be sacrificed in
the pursuit of economic development. The whole temper of his
work was to strike a balance between progress and freedom.
Like all liberals, he derived the rational temper from Western
thought. They approached the institutions of traditional Hindu
society with a rational outlook and sought to reform them
through an appeal to reason. Liberals in the West, as mentioned
earlier, saw the danger to personal freedom from concentration
of power in the State. Indian liberals, on the other hand, saw
. the individual cribbed, cabined and confined by ancient super-
stitions and irrational practices. They took a deep and abiding
interest in questions of social reform and did not hesitate in
using the power of the State—even that of a foreign govern-

ment—for purposes of social reform.

Four Aspects of Indian Liberalism
In my Liberalism and the Modernization of India (Twelfth
Annual Lecture at the Harold Laski Institute, 1966) I have
discussed four major aspects of the outlook of the Indian
liberals. Firstly, they perceived the “total” character of the
modernization process and the inter-dependence of economic
development ‘and political stability. They saw how closely
related were the processes of social and political development
and stressed the need to maintain continuity in the cultural
traditions of the people. Consider, for instance, Roy’s interest
. in India’s religious history, Ranade’s theism and his exposition
of the relevance of the teachings of the saints of Maharashtra,
Sastri’s interest in the Ramayana and Rajagopalachari’s love
of the Kural. Liberalisin has sometimes been described as

S. P. AIYAR . 81
conservatism — so.it is, in the best sense of the word for it
seeks to conserve everything that is good in the past.

Secondly, Indian liberals have always entertained a certain
apprehension of unenlightened revolt of the masses and sensed
the dangers of mass movements. Liberals, at all times, have
cautioned against rousing the people through an exploitation
of their emotions: Shivaji and Ganpati festivals at the time of
Tilak, non-cooperation movements under Gandhi and the
populist gimmicks of politicians which have become endemic
in Indian. public life today. The liberal apprehensions of the
orgies into which uncontrolled movements often degenerate
have now been amply supported by studies in crowd psychology. —
Sir P. S, Sivaswamy Aiyar pointed out that one of the great

; difficulties in non-cooperation and non-violence movements
is to maintain their essential non-violent character and this
_line of thinking can be found also in the speeches and writings
of Gokhale and of Srinivasa Sastri. .

Thirdly, they saw the danger of helpless dependence on
foreign assistance. They welcomed the import of Western
skills and knowledge but they warned against unimaginative
dependence on foreign aid and foreign experts. What is
important is to develop the initiative of the people and promote
the skills necessary for development. Consider Gokhale’s
warning in this direction, echoed after many decades by
Rajagopalachari in the pages of Swarajya and Sivaswamy

_ Aiyar’s plea for technical and professional education.

Finally, all the liberals have shared a common concern for
the expansion of education and opening up opportunities for
woman — without watering down standards. Theirs was no
sentimental flirtation with the Goddess of Learning. They
examined the educational needs of the country; they saw the

‘ weakness of a purely “Arts” education compelling people to
take government jobs and making them more dependant than .
ever on the foreign government. This is one of the reasons
why Sivaswamy Aiyar had emphasized the importance - of
education in commerce and mechanical engineering. More
than any other liberal, with the exception of Gokhale, it was

Sivaswamy Aiyar who gave his utmost to the problems of
Indian education. As early as 1919 he drew attention to the
problem of popularizing Western knowledge and encouraging
the translation of standard works into Indian languages. But
he gave a timely and early warning against the tendency of
coining equivalent words in the vernacular in the pursuit of a
false patriotism. Some of them saw the political implications of
thoughtless educational expansion resulting in the swelling of
the ranks of the educated unemployed. A certain “man-power
approach”—as ugly expression this!—was implicit in their
thinking, and made explicit at times as in the writings of
Dadabhar Naoroji.

. Thus the contribution of the Indian liberals was not only
outstanding but far removed from what one might conclude
from the superficial and uncharitable remarks of Jawaharlal
Nehru in his Autobiography.

The Relevance of Liberalism

In India, as all over Asia, the path to economic development
is generally believed to be socialism and there is a widespread
belief that liberalism is an outmoded doctrine of nineteenth-
century England. Most people regard it as an apology for
capitalism unrestrained by the State. Capitalism in India is a
dirty word; so are “business”, “businessmen” and “profits”.

_ In the context of the massive poverty of the country and its
ever-expanding population and gross inequalities, these words
naturally evoke the image of a few profiting through-unscru-
pulous ways. Despite the assumptions and strategies of Indian
planning seeking to give both the private entrepreneur and
the State responsibilities in economic development, politicians
and socialist-minded intellectuals have talked as though private
enterprise exists only at the mercy of government. Socialism,
has been an attractive siren song for many centuries; it has
appealed to the masses as the only way to material prosperity
and a just, egalitarian society. Its many shades of meaning
range over the entire ideological spectrum; it covers everything

; S. P. ATYAR 8 83

from regulated private enterprise to State-regimented
economics; it includes utopianism of many varieties—of
Gandhi, Vinoba, Jayaprakash Narain et a/l—and much
romantic sentimentalism.

: It is difficult, even futile, to examine here the reasons for
the popularity of this ill-defined concept in India. Let it be
granted straightway that its emphasis on egalitarianism and
equitable distribution is both correct and laudable; that it
springs from a concern for social justice on the part of most

' people, except those who aspire to profit from their admission
into the ruling class. More than this cannot be ‘said for

socialism. But at the heart of the Asian Drama lies the great
debate between socialism and liberalism, between those who

advocate the expansion of the State in every sphere of economic
activity and those who wish to broaden the entrepreneurial
base. Socialist-minded economists and political scientists have
argued the irrelevance of liberalism on the ground that
its validity is tied up with the notion of the free market
mechanism —a figment of the nineteenth century economic
imagination. They further assert that free enterprise and
liberalism have worked in the countries of Western Europe
through a fortuitous combination of circumstances; therefore,
they will not work in the peculiar circumstances of India. .
The notion of the free market was merely a model and no one
| has ever pretended that existing markets can ever approximate

, to it. This is why liberalism has always recognized the need
for regulation.

The exponents of classical liberalism were fully aware. of
the imperfections of human nature and their deleterious effects
on the economy. Adam Smith, for instance, spoke of the

, “sneaking arts of underlying businessmen” and further

observed! “People of the same trade seldom meet together,

| even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends

in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance .
to raise prices.”

( In the history of liberalism, there has been a significant
distinction between intervention and interference, between

controls and regulations which sustain and strengthen
competition and those that hamper and destroy it. It is hardly
necessary for me to add that those who speak of the “Permit-
License-Quota Raj” do not advocate the dismantling of all
governmental restraints. Such a step would lead not to
competition but to the law of the jungle—the very thing
which liberals have been anxious to avoid) Likewise, liberals
recognise that the State has-a crucial role to play in the.
economic development of Asian countries.
Pragmatism of the Liberals
Liberalism never supplied any formula for the scope of State
activities; these would be determined by the particular circum-
" stances of the country and even within each country, the extent
of State participation would change from time to time. At
_ a week-long seminar held in Poona under the auspices of the
Friedrich-Naumann Stiftung and the Indian Group of ‘the
Liberal International in January 1968 the point was emphasized
by many participants. The points made then are still relevant
after twenty years. Thus V. K. Narasimhan rightly argued
that the “mixed economy” should not be regarded as something
determined once and for all. It is necessary, he urged, to have
a dynamic view of the mixed economy in which the proportion
of the “mix” would be determined from time to time, not
on the basis of some abstract principle but in the light of
knowledge and experience. This is the crux of the liberal
position and the main point of departure from.that of socialism.
Throughout its history, liberals have always insisted that
political and economic problems should not be approached
from an ideological point of view. Ideology, by its very nature,
runs counter to science and rationality; it is impatient of reality
as the history of Marxism has demonstrated over and over
again. In the long run, facts are stubborn things and reality
will assert itself: Lysenkos and Michurins must own up their |
ideological charlatanry and socialist countries are compelled
to accept, albeit reluctantly, the logic of the market mechanism

S. P. AIYAR . 85
and even provide for the profit principle!

, The massive poverty and gross inequalities of India do not
prove the irrelevance of liberalism but its contrary. Precisely
because the entrepreneurial base is narrow does it need to be

_ broadened so that the fruits of technological development can
-be increased and distributed. Production and distribution are
but aspects of industrial production — private enterprise and
State regulation have both important roles to play in the
process. Nowhere have the great liberal writers asserted that
production alone matters and that distribution will take care
of itself. Peter Drucker is right when he speaks of the inter-

dependence of modern economies leading to the “symbiosis”

of organizations; it is equally true that the lines dividing

a “private” and “public” tend to get functionally blurred. But
it is not true to say that the lines need not be drawn or that

they are irrelevant. Liberalism has stood for releasing the
creative energies of people, treating the State and its agencies
as means for social progress and not as ends in themselves.
Paradoxically, both Marxian socialism and liberalism have been

~ concerned with the problems of production and distribution;

but while Marxism has emphasized these in purely economic

terms, liberalism has sought to place them in the larger
perspective of human freedom. I have mentioned earlier that
liberalism has been primarily a political philosophy of freedom
and it seems odd that one should want to prove the “relevance”

; of freedom for India. The possibilities of freedom in under-
developed countries are tied up with the problems of production.

| Students of revolution from Aristotle to Hannah Arendt and
Crane Brinton have pointed out that the most crucial periods
of history are those which promise signs of improvement
and it is not difficult to see that India is now passing through
a period of great ferment.

In conclusion I wish to argue that to speak of relevance of ©
liberalism to the Indian situation is an understatement. It is ©
more than that for it provides not only the philosophy of our

Constitution but also a framework for the future development
| of the culturally diversified society of India. Ironically the

.

policies of the Indian government for three decades and a half
have served to underline some of the lasting lessons of
liberalism. The expanding power of the state in all the key
areas of human activity, the growth of Indian bureaucracy,
the control of not merely the economy but also of the mass
media, the clumsy and costly system of regulation and control
have all conspired to smother initiative. It is no wonder that
creative individuals have either suffered frustration or have
become sycophants of the powers that be. Several who have
had the opportunity to go to foreign universities have been
reluctant to come back to the country. The philosophers of
Liberalism have always warned against the dangers of Etatisme.
Thus John Stuart Mill in his classic work On Liberty said:
“A government cannot have too-:much of the kind of activity
which does not impede, but aids and stimulates, individual
exertion and development. The mischief begins when, instead
of calling forth the activity and powers of individuals and
bodies, it substitutes its own activity for theirs; when, instead
of informing, advising, and upon occasion, denouncing, it
makes them work in fetters, or bids them stand aside and does
their work instead of them. The worth of a State, in the long
run, is the worth of the individuals composing it; and a State
which postpones the interests of their mental expansion and
elevation, to a little more of administrative skill, or of that
semblance of it which practice gives, in the details of business;
a State which dwarfs its men in order that they may be more
docile instruments in its hands even for beneficial purposes —
will find that with small men no great thing can really be
accomplished; and that the perfection of machinery to which
it has sacrificed everything, will in the end avail it nothing,
for want of the vital power which, in order that the machine
might work more smoothly, it has preferred to banish.”

The near “one party system” which has long dominated the
Indian political scene has given rise to a host of social
problems and heightened intolerance of criticism. The threats
to individual freedom are ever present making it necessary
for freedom loving individuals to organise for civil liberties

and constantly explore new channels for the expression of
critical thought. In the long perspective of Indian history and
tradition concern for the individual and his rights has been
conspicuous by its absence. India can progress on the lines
indicated in the Constitution only through a break with the
dead past.

There are three senses in which we can use the term

Indian Liberalism :

(a) A broad sense of making the country modern, on
western lines in contrast to the traditional social norms
and order. This is historically the oldest and names
such as those of Vidyasagar, Agarkar and Ranade are .
associated with it. It did not press for an uncritical
adoption of western norms but advocated absorption
of western critical standards, rethinking on social
matters and a gradual change of Indian social structure.

; While the Liberals worked hard in trying to bring
about a transformation, they were labouring in
an environment where attempts at changing coagulated

| customs was not even conceivable. But in debating about

| these, they created a climate of opinion where change
could be contemplated as a theoretical possibility.
Indian society, particularly Hindu Society was gradually ”
changing but it was due more to economic, and
sociological factors than to conscious adopting of new

| values. One cannot categorically state that as social

philosophers they were successful in transforming

But one could claim that the Liberals made the proposi-

as basically a political approach. This had distinguished
adherents and in a sense was extremely successful in
that, that it not only gained a following but was able
to strike roots into the intellectual consciousness of
the country. It was by and large derivative, deriving
its inspiration from the doctrine and the political
practices of the British. Its leading figures were
Gladstone, Bright and John Stuart Mill. Those among
Indians who were intellectually gifted attempted to
grapple with the writings of Bentham and Mill and
other leaders of liberal thought.
However, such people with these rare skills were a
minute group. A larger number had to nibble at more
tender pastures. Vast cohorts of western educated
Indians indirectly imbibed liberal principles, though
initially they had no clear conscious desire to be
educated in these values. Many of them took to the
law and drew their principles mainly from their legal
. practice and whatever social and political philosophy
they learnt came from their study of law and juris-
prudence. Since the law in which they cut their teeth
was mainly the Common Law of Britain, it was
inevitable that the philosophy of Common Law as it -
had developed till their times should have become
part of their intellectual baggage.
Secularism, individual rights, legal channels for the
redress of grievances, limited government, separation

of the executive from the judiciary, all these constituted

these political principles were part of modern India’s

(c) In a third sense, the Liberal Federation of India,

Were they Anglophiles?

It has been criticised that they had been exclusively

7 moulded by British influence and practice; this of course
is a true charge but Britain transformed itself in half a
century and it was the only model of economic and political
| development then available to them. The way of progress

such as Germany and the U.S. had followed. They advocated
similar policies for India. Individual initiative had played —
an important part; business and industrial enterprise did
have an equally distinct role to play; political parties were
founded, so were self-help associations, co-operative ventures,
libraries, and financial institutions. These things transformed

service and dedication advocated by Samuel Smiles is now
generally sneered at. But whole generations were trained on
his books both in the English speaking world and in India.

Smiles put forward the gospel of Manchesterism and
the leading figures of these were Cobden, Bright and the

faire and reform. The high moral tone of politics that
Bright and Gladstone advocated and which later Morely was

Condemning the liberal methods as inadequate and

Also, their admiration for the British Liberal Party

liberals in British politics was not due to any especial

in its formation. A year after the founding of the

Irish question. In developing their political principles
exclusively from the British political party, the liberals
inadequately realized the historical peculiarities of
British political life and principles and the impossibility.
of their replication elsewhere. .

Even if one were to concede to the criticism of the

The Record of the Liberals
The Liberals came into their own in the 1890s; this was the
period of their glory. The best among them occupied important
public positions and continued to do so during the next three
decades. Since they were mainly taught to look up to the
British it was but natural for them to believe that similar
developments in India would be in order. They supported
a government that would economise, support and promote
Indian industries, (here of course they departed from Free
Trade), Indianize the services, gradually extend the repre-
sentative element, promote primary education etc. They had
the example of Japan and they argued that if Japan could
modernize herself so rapidly, so could India. Industrialization,
representative government by stages, gradualism were their
ideals. They were not fully aware of the shortcomings of
an industrial civilization. -
With their predominantly legal background, their exclusive
exposure to British political institutions, and their urban and
| upper caste filiations they tended to see certain aspects of
politics and ignore others. The native traditions and social
| order were regarded as basically backward and a drag upon

the west as would be possible in this country. They were
concerned with questions such as ensuring the foundations
of a liberal democratic order, with the issue of Dominion

of the cry of Swaraj, the civil service question, the communal
issue, local self-government, primary education, reduction in
military expenditure etc. These were issues that particularly
suited the liberal mind and approach. They could be debated
upon, issues clarified, social implications unravelled, and
some sort of acceptable solution hammered out.

They were committed to work with the government
wherever possible. They realized the limitations of such a

: compromise and this: very often reduced them to ridicule in
the public eye. For instance Gokhale with considerable search

of heart agreed to the Press Bill (1909). The intense debate
that took place within the inner councils of the liberal elite,
the moral dilemma in which both he and others were placed
were not known to the public. Opposing the bill would have
led to the resignation of Lord Sinha, the first Indian member
in the Council and to the jubilation of Tories and the diehards
in the British bureaucracy and to halt the tardy pace of reform.
Assenting to it would have meant betraying the cause of
nationalism. Gokhale did not want to throw a spanner in the
wheels of reform. He was misunderstood then and it is only
now that we have the full details and are in a position to judge
the event with the full background. But to his contemporaries,
he was a betrayer. Similarly, on the extension of the communal
franchise, the liberals almost persuaded Lord Morley to a
secular alternative principle. The Vicerov was more persuasive
and the Secretary of State gave in despite his reservations.
The Liberals were again to be twitted by the Extremists.

As the decades passed by, the liberals mattered as individuals
but the group as a whole could do little in Indian politics’
Its annual meetings conducted in an esoteric language were
barely of any appeal, for there was little of sloganeering and
the bandying of phrases. They had no charismatic leaders.

Success and Failure
Though they had concern for the masses and the downtrodden,
their approach was basically one that was elitist and paternal
not in the sense of condescension but in the sense of noblesse
. oblige. Ranade and no less than Sivaswami Aiyer knew of their
responsibilities to the masses. But their methods were out of
tune with the developments that were taking place in the
country. B. C. Pal, and Tilak had indicated the enormous
potential that could be mobilized in this country and which
once aroused would shake the edifice of the government and
the administration.
The methods used by Gandhi and his capacity to mobilize
the masses, his absolute control over his followers made

liberals of an open polity, reasonable compromises, and
dialogues with other parties in search of an acceptable solution.
But he tried to foist populist politics on liberal methods and
founded his brand of politics which only he could manage
because of his personality, moral earnestness and tremendous
seriousness. Only a saint in politics could do this—but alas
Indian politics had not many of that vintage.

By the late thirties the liberals in a general sense had
succeeded in converting the whole nation to the value of an
open polity and a limited government. They remained valuable
links between the government and the Congress and tried to

work out the compromises as best as they could. Electorally
with no base to stand upon, they had to be acceptable to
the government, to the Congress and other interests. Sheer
character, hard work, intellection of a high order, a sense of
visible altruism were all the assets they had and they were

‘ indeed valuable assets. They had no ideology that would have
been acceptable to the masses — it was too open-ended to make
sense to a people restless for instant solutions.
Economic and Political Policies
It should be remembered that Indian Liberalism was primarily
a social and a political movement and its economic dimensions
were derived from the earlier liberal school of Adam Smith
rather than of Herbert Spencer. Adam Smith had advocated
State activities in those areas of the economy where the
individual would not act on his own. Following him, J. S. Mill
was to give an impressive list of economic activities to be
fostered by the state : roads, docks, harbours, canals, irrigation,
hospitals, schools and colleges. Ranade propagated state inter- ,
ference in the economy for promotion of economic goods and
production. He contrasted the administration of the Dutch
in Java against the inactivities of the Indian government in
the economic sphere. While in the field of political economy,

the liberals led by Ranade expected active state promotion,
in the field of social reform too they advocated that the state
step in and regulate social customs and legislate on many
social evils. Indian liberals were not Social Darwinists.

The programme of Ranade and Gokhale remained the core
of the liberal’s economic ideology. Beyond this they were not
able to innovate. With the political problems nearly within
reach of solution, for it was only a matter of time, one would
have expected that they would come to grips with economic
developments and with Western intellectual movements that
were shaking Europe and which soon were to have wider

ramifications. But having come of intellectual age in an
earlier decade they were not willing to re-examine the
foundations of their economic ideas and were not willing

to risk revolutionary ideas. Not only in India, but in other

parts of Asia as well the liberals were no great enthusiasts

' or champions of either revolutionary or Marxist ideas. Most
found the broad confines of their ideology ample enough for

. them to roam about. They failed precisely in an hour when
their contribution could have been most valuable. For as

Sastri had mentioned they did not have to chase votes and

had nothing to lose by pursuing ideas to their logical end.

At this stage it may be necessary to contrast the political
and economic principles of Western Europe when the liberals
adopted European principles. By the last few decades of the
last century their political principles had been vindicated
by European and American practice. The philosophy had
effectively controlled government, made responsible govern-
ment practicable and helped in the realisation of individual
rights. It was easy to see the utility of the philosophy and
adopt it. The only alternative to this was either anarchy or
irresponsible government.

The twentieth century economic counterpart to this was
socialism. The theory was attractive and the moralist
humanism that informed it was doubtless a strong magnet.

There were two economic alternatives—one fuzzy and
unclear but highly acceptable and the other with. extensive

These were the Congress versions of economic development

now, till the first decade of the century, none of these varieties
of social, economic and political alternatives was available
for consideration for the national reconstruction of a country.
The Congress congeries of ideologies dominated by the
populism of Gandhi would brook little of any questioning.
Rural economic issues were regarded as basically solvable by
constructive work, promotion of khadi, prohibition and the
practising of contentment. The Mahatma believed that all
the differences and conflicts between the capitalists, and
labour, zamindar and tenants could be harmoniously resolved
by love, peace and ahimsa. The Congress would take care of
all of them. Ipse dixit—and could anyone question it? It
should be remembered that the supporters of the Congress
from the rural areas would not have tolerated any interference
into the rural status quo. Temperamentally, the Congress
did not want to rock the boat.

in Public Life
R. M. Lala

F or thirty years Jayaprakash Narayan pursued the road to
Marxism. In 1934 along with Minoo Masani and some

other idealists, he launched the Congress Socialist Party. J.P.

and his young colleagues spent hours discussing with Gandhiji

; questions on Marxism and religion, on ends and means —all
against the back-drop of the freedom struggle. “One day,” said

He did—four years after the Mahatma’s death. Gandhiji
was not the only one to be interested. Minoo Masani had
already changed his views on Marxism. In the 1940s when
J.P. was in prison, Masani sent him books like Arthur
Koestler’s ‘Darkness at Noon’. Still J.P. held on to his views.
It was only in the early 1950s that J.P. began to waver. He
had just concluded his three week fast in Pune, in 1952,
when he bade good-bye to Marxism.

_ _ In an article he wrote at Masani’s invitation in Freedom
First, J.P. said that for years he had worshipped at the shrine
of the goddess of dialectical materialism but he had come to
realize that “materialism of any sort robs man of the means
to be truly human. In a material civilisation man has no
rational incentive to be good.”

“In days gone by”, said J.P. “men tried to be good, impelled
by some higher moral force in which they believed; and
goodness means such things as truthfulness, honesty, kindness,
chastity, unselfishness. Men felt that it was the highest moral
duty to try to be good. Society provided every individual
with the motive to be good; it was the command of religion,
of God; it was necessary for one’s highest growth, for self-

realization; it brought peace and supreme happiness; it brought

“In present society, with the hold of religion gone, faith
in God shaken, moral values discarded as dead-weights of the

men’s hearts, are there any incentives to goodness left?
Indeed, has the question any relevance at all to present facts,

, problems and ideals of human society?
“I hold emphatically that no other question is more relevant
to us today.”

“The individual asks today why should he be good. There is
no God, no soul, no morality, no life hereafter, no cycle of

fame, power and position?

In words that ring so similar to Gandhi’s, Lord Acton said

The role of the Judiciary
The Founding Fathers laid great store by the judiciary. They
realised that without an effective and independent enforcement
machinery fundamental rights would be no better than mere
maxims of political morality. They did not accept the position
that the legislature and the executive can be trusted to observe
the limitations placed upon them. Mr. Ananthasayanam
Ayyangar warned that the “executive which comes into being
for the time being is apt to abuse its powers, and therefore
the Supreme Court must be there, strong and untrammelled |
by the day-to-day passions which may bring a set of people .
into power and also throw them out in a very short time.”
Kazi Syed Karimuddin bluntly said: “We cannot entrust the
interpretation of these clauses in the fundamental rights to
the vagaries of legislatures.”

practice of requiring indigent persons to furnish bail or to
provide sureties with monetary obligations which would be
plainly beyond their capacity. The Court observed :

Poor men—Indians are, in‘: monetary terms, indigents—

young persons, infirm individuals and women are weak

categories and courts should be liberal in releasing them
on their own recognisances—put whatever reasonable
- conditions you may.
The question of free legal aid has been discussed and
debated in the country for years. Till now, there is no central
. legislation embodying a comprehensive scheme for legal aid.
The Supreme Court took the lead in the case of Madhav
Hoskot. In this landmark decision the Court held that free
legal services to the poor and needy are an essential element
of any reasonable, fair and just procedure and ruled that where
the prisoner is disabled from engaging a lawyer on grounds
such as indigence or incommunicado situation the Court shall,
if the circumstances of the case, the gravity of the sentence
_and the ends of justice so require, assign competent counsel
for the prisoner’s defence and pay the assigned counsel such
sum as the court may equitably fix, provided the party does
not object to that lawyer.

Article 21 has come to the much-needed succour of
numerous undertrials languishing in Indian jails waiting for
their cases to be heard and disposed of. The Supreme Court
in an epochal judgement held that “speedy trial, and by speedy
trial we mean reasonably expeditious trial, is an integral and
essential part of the fundamental right to life and liberty
enshrined in Article 21.” This and subsequent judgements
of the Supreme Court have secured freedom for numerous
under-trial prisoners.

SOLI J. SORABJEE * 129
Affirmative remedies
One of the greatest contributions of the Supreme Court has
been the easy access to justice it has provided by revolutionising
the concept of /ocus standi and developing affirmative
remedies. The court has repeatedly ruled that where judicial
redress is sought of a legal injury or a legal wrong suffered
by a person or a class of persons, who by reason, by poverty,
disability or their socially or economically disadvantaged
position are unable to approach the Court, any member of the
public, acting bona fide and not for oblique considerations,
can maintain an action for judicial redress. This has been
done even by addressing a letter drawing the Court’s attention
to such legal injury and the Court has taken action upon it.

Of late, the Court has concerned itself with the Bhagalpur
blindings, the evils of traffic in human beings, bonded
labourers, and deaths in so-called ‘encounters’ with the police.
In cases concerning bonded labour, it has appointed advocates
as commissioners to visit certain quarries and report to the
court whether labourers were working there willingly or were
in a state of involuntary servitude. It has also issued directions
to the authorities to take positive measures for rehabilitation
of the labourers freed from their bondage.

More important, the Supreme Court by its rulings has
secured the implementation of welfare legislation for the
benefit of employees in respect of their wages and living

conditions. Thanks to these liberal pronouncements, vast
sections of our people are able to avail themselves of their
basic human rights despite their poverty and ignorance.

There are indignant critics who charge that the Supreme
Court is acting as a super legislature and is dabbling in
matters outside its proper sphere. These critics forget that —
it-is the proverbial tardiness of legislatures and the inertia,
almost bordering on callousness, of the executive branch
which provide a proper occasion for judicial activism. When
a public-spirited person or a bona fide organisation brings to
the notice of the Supreme Court derelictions of constitutional

130 , Freedom and Dissent

obligations by public authorities, the Court cannot refuse to
act. Unlike an administrative bureaucracy or a legislature,
the judiciary can neither prevaricate nor procrastinate. It
must respond if fundamental rights are to be living realities
for the downtrodden and the oppressed.

It is not sufficiently realised that, in all these public
interest cases, the question is of the enforcement of a particular
fundamental right or the other. The Court’s recent role in
this field indicates its commitment to ‘Taking Rights Seriously’,
or as Prof. Upendra Bakshi has aptly said ‘The Court is taking
suffering seriously.’ -

Ultimately it is by that yard stick that one can answer the
question whether the Supreme Court of India is the sentinel
on the gui vive for the bulk of its citizens.

Opposition as a Luxury —the
Theoretical Challenge
Padma Srinivasan
Economic development, the most important consideration
T he leaders of the new states tell us that the most urgent
problems facing human societies today are those of
7 economic development. They say that the pressing tasks of
development will be hampered by multiple points of view
from those who disagree. Unlike the developed countries,
dissent and opposition are luxuries we cannot afford. Their
argument often stretches on from the position : ‘Opposition?
Not now’, to a further one: ‘Opposition? Never.’
What is the nature of this challenge? How serious is it?
Is it a new one or has something like it been made before
in history? Is there any validity in the claims made? How do
we meet the challenge? I am raising these questions here not
because I have any satisfactory answers to them but because
their challenge to all of us is alarming. It becomes all the more
so when we think how easily the unwary can be convinced by
them—for isn’t economic development more important than
all other considerations? Of course it is! And, as I hope to
show in this paper, this is precisely why starry-eyed idealists
are fighting for basic freedoms. Material ends and creature
comforts can only be attained in an atmosphere of freedom
for the human spirit. The dichotomy between the material
and the spiritual is a false one.
Ubiquity of Opposition
Opposition has been occurring in all societies and at all times.

148 > Freedom and Dissent
Throughout history it has almost always been discouraged and
suppressed. This universal animosity towards Opposition has
rarely been accompanied by any conscious theorizing. Rather,
the citadels of orthodoxy appear to have been maintained
by constantly encouraging conformity in the young during
their most impressionable years. Mankind seems to have been
enamoured of the notion of unanimity. The maintenance of
widespread consensus and ‘Good Governme.it’ were the ideals.
Every effort was made to bring the errant and the eccentric
back to the fold. In the Middle Ages, consensus and unanimity
‘were the highest ideal to be attained. Even in Britain, in the
17th and 18th centuries, the idea of a group or class opposing
the Government was unthinkable. It was thought that Parlia-
ment as a whole may criticise and watch the executive;
but opposition could be justified only in exceptional cases
when the government was bad. The general opinion was that
Parliament must be freed from the bane of parties.

A little pondering and we, today, can plainly understand
that no government receives indefinitely the total support
of the people over whom it asserts its jurisdiction. And yet
the people of yore thought that unanimity was the ideal to be
striven for. The general trend was towards conformity. Dissent
and opposition were banal: they were among those things
that are ‘just not done’. Such being the trend there was no
organized body of theory concerning the concept, and hence,
no theoretical offensive against it. Indeed, opposition itself did
Not, until recent times, gain any elaborate conceptualization.

The theory of Opposition has arisen out of a progressive
understanding of the dynamics and behaviours within demo-
cratic political systems. Since these political systems also
happen to be Western the theoretical offensive is coloured
by an anti-Western or anti-imperialistic stance. The most
powerful arguments in this theoretical assault on Opposition
comes from African leaders and thinkers. Thus, though
opposition, as a fact of social life, is old, its theory is young.
The challenge from Africa is especially serious because it
undermines the very basis of Opposition as a concept. —

, PADMA SRINIVASAN ~ 149
In order to meet the challenge with any degree of success

it behoves us to examine the phenomenon of Opposition both |
as fact and as theory. If we know what it is and why it arises
at all, it might be easier for us to answer its opponents.

| Opposition has occurred, as we have noted, at all times,
in all climes and in every conceivable human community.
Even India’s noble myth of the Lord Rama’s perfect state

| tells us of at least one significant case of dissent. The incidence
of Opposition is so ubiquitous that we, today think of it as
one of the givens of man’s life as a social animal. When
people say: ‘Opposition is a luxury’ or ask: ‘Is Opposition
necessary?’ I am reminded of Thurber’s query: ‘Is sex
necessary?’ Anthropologists have studied the different ways

in which ethnic groups strive to cope with tensions and
dissent and maintain the level of consensus necessary for
co-operative life. Some human groups are more individualistic
than others; i.e. there are different degrees of consensus
among them. But no anthropologist has yet discovered a
community that is wholly and continually consensual.
Opposition in a Small Tribal Society
Let us now examine a little more closely the way dissent
and opposition occur in any situation. Let us think of a small
group of persons. Several of them agree upon a course of
concerted action and want to go ahead. But a few persons
do not agree—they either want deferred action, or no action
or a modified type of action. Now, these few have had occasion
to disagree because the others have taken the initiative.
If there has been no thesis in the first place, there would have
been no antithesis. An observable feature of the phenomenon
of Opposition is that antithesis follows on the heels of thesis.
But for the thesis, the antithesis would not have come into |
being. So, antithesis is the other, complementary half; it is
the portion that completes the globe of truth. No person or
group, however learned or aged or wise, can be in possession
of the whole truth. But there can be an appoximation to the

150 , Freedom and Dissent
truth if the dissenting opinions are painstakingly considered
and woven into the texture of the decision.

This is how decisions have been taken for centuries in
Africa. Such decision-making is still a way of life for the
millions of Africans who live in villages. Let us look at a
real life situation to get the feel of the process. My example
comes from the Sonjo people of Tanganyika among whom the
anthropologist, Robert Gray, lived and worked. The Sonjo
live in semi-arid country and need to practise irrigation.
There are six villages, each of which has its own irrigation
system under the control of a council of elders in which all
members have equal authority. This council constitutes the
-formal government of the village. It was at one of these —the
village of Kheri—that Gray made a detailed study of the
methods of irrigation. There are several categories of lands
which are irrigated and cultivated in different ways. One type

of land called isireni is less productive than other types,
and so it is only planted in years when water is plentiful.
In dry years the limited water is applied to the more productive
. lands. While Gray was there, a decision had to be made
whether or not to plant the ésireni fields. The seventeen elders
of the village retired to their meeting place to ponder this
question in private. After two whole days of discussion they
had not yet reached a decision because of the disagreement
among themselves. It was only on the third day that they were
able to announce their decision that the isireni fields should
be planted. This incident, which took place in a small village
in Tanganyika in the late 50s, shows us the need for weaving
the opinions of all into the fabric of consensus. This is no
easy task. In this process there is no suppression of dissent.
The decision arrived at may not necessarily be the right one;
it may only be partially so. Every problem is complex and many-
sided — whether it is ésireni fields or fiscal policy, international
trade, or educational strategies. Nobody really knows what is

the right strategy for development.

The interplay of both thesis and antithesis is necessary
for taking decisions which are going to affect all the people.

The challenge to Opposition is serious precisely because it is
a theoretical one. For, political theory is fundamental to
Man’s life as a social being. Security for an absolutist ruler
_ can become double sure only when the myth of Dissent is
hanged along with the dissenter. The assault is being made on

(a) Stability and (b) Economic Development.

vigorous discussion about the compatibility of the Westminster

Socialist Antipluralism
Closely linked to the fatal attraction of unanimity is the
antipluralism of those African States that profess socialism.
European socialism recognizes the existence of pluralism in
the society by regretting the clashes between classes. But
African socialists go one better; they deny that there can

ever be such clashes between Africans, given their different
historical background. African idealogues like Sekou Toure
and Nkrumah have been right in asserting that there are no

of classes is taken to imply also the absence of important

An interesting consequence of the myth of unanimity and

its impact upon the concept of political neutrality, which
embraces both the civil service and the military. The concept

thousands, beyond the pale of politics. This implies, among
other things, that they are not to criticize the Government.
Within the pale of politics, an ordinary citizen may criticize
the Government without committing treason and, thus,
continue to be loyal to the State. Thus, the State/Government

blurred for the bureaucrat and for the soldier; they cannot
criticize the Government without commiting treason. Thus,
the State and the Government merge for the two services.
The compulsive principle here is that they shall serve the
lawfully elected representatives of the body politic without

which has at least two political parties. But in the single- |
party states of Africa the principle of neutrality, at least that
of the Civil Service, was done away with. In these states, the
sole party was identical with the entire nation. Its highest chief

Stability, Economic Development and Unitarism
The second assault on Opposition must be considered in two
stages:

(a) that of Stability, and

(b) that of Economic Development.

(a) Africa’s leaders have made the bid for absolute power on
the need for stability in the new state. They have urged that
the greatest danger to stability could come from the diversities
of tribal groups. Given the heterogeneity of most of the new
states of Africa, the question of federalism assumes especial
importance. Authoritarian forces, under the leadership of
Obote in Uganda and Kenyatta in Kenya, were able to establish

; their rule only after dismantling federal structures. Structurally
federalism is more conducive to democracy than unitarism
because of its greater institutional complexities. The linkage
between federalism and democracy becomes stronger in the
African context when one considers the presence of two factors:

(i) the ethnic diversity of the population; and

(ii) the fact that most of the tribes have had cultures that

are hospitable to democracy.

The first factor indicates the affinity between the structures
of society and that of federalism. The second factor gives the
linkage between political cultures and democracy. Hence, we

. see that African states have structural and cultural linkages
with federalistic democracy. Like India, a quasi-federal pattern
which has room for both a constitutional opposition and
bicameralism is ideal for new states because these, along with
a relatively strong centre, would make for political stability.
Stability is also consequent upon the wider participation
afforded by the several parties and parliamentary institutions
of the federal set-up. ;

As a power structure the federal pattern involves
decentralization. The opposite of this is the unitary pattern
which involves centralization. But in the African context it
was not merely a perference for one power structure to another.

Populism in Indian Politics
: Adi H. Doctor
The Nature of Populist Politics
T he word populism can be used in three distinct senses.
As a movement; as a term to describe a community
viz. a populist community; and as a term to describe the nature
; and style of politics viz. populistic politics. This paper is
primarily concerned with the last mentioned usage of the term.
K. Ishwaran in his recent book, A Populist Community and
| Modernization in India, uses the term to refer to a peasant
| community that elects to preserve its local identity, essentially
the core-culture.! Such a society may change or modernize
but it follows the “populistic pattern of modernization”, that
is, it accepts change only at the periphery; the core culture
stays intact. Ishwaran mentions its other characteristics to be,
| plural, emphasising localism and having no ideology.
| At a conference held at the London School of Economics
arid Political Science, 19-21, May 1967, “To Define Populism”,
the term was largely understood to stand for a movement
| which had the following characteristics:

It glorifies people and is often inconsistent with the realities
of politics; it generally advances the claims of lower classes
and is peasantist in character. As Isaiah Berlin noted, it believes
in some kind of integral society having its roots in the past,
either imaginary or real, bound by a sense of fraternity and
by a certain kind of social equality (generally held more dear
than liberty) and is opposed to what it calls the western
competitive atomised society. It is generally apolitical and

| does not put much faith in political institutions though it may
| use them for its ends. The state is not its ideal.

182 - Freedom and Dissent

Its aim is the human individual or society and it talks more
in terms of moral regeneration than laws.? —

Finally the term is used to refer to a kind of politics, a use
we are concerned with in this paper. Elaborating the nature of
populist politics, J. D. Sethi observes: “It is inherent in
populist politics that all parties, whether of the Right or Left,
apply techniques of street politics in which masses are brought
in on one excuse or another in support of one demand or
another”.? Populist politics in this sense, tend to be extra-
constitutional politics. Now, it is not anyone’s argument
that a society should and can function hundred per cent
constitutional. But for any society that wants to function
effectively it is necessary that it strike a balance between
‘constitutional and extra-constitutional politics. For instance,
No society can afford to have frequent resort to populist politics
to change constitutional governments by agitational or extra-
constitutional means. Populist politics in resorting to extra

legal mass agitation techniques, may use the language of
socialism, communism, freedom, fascism, regionalism or
communalism. In this sense populist politics can be right wing
or left wing or be based on narrow regional or communal
_ chauvinism. Its one essential characteristic is its seeking to
bypass institutions and make direct appeals to the people. In
a populist model, social and economic conflicts are not analysed
in terms of class conflicts but as a perpetual struggle between
_ the people and vested interests, in which the people are
portrayed as not only having the right to rule but also as being
wise and virtuous.
The Origins of Populism in India
Populism in independent India became a strident force between
1967 and 1971, though its origins can be traced to earlier
times. In the late fifties, and thereafter, for instance,
Prime Minister Nehru gave and propagated the slogan of a
“Socialist Pattern of Society”, but during all that time the
country actually pursued a capitalist path of growth. During

ADI DOCTOR . 183
the period from 1956 when Panditji first gave the slogan in
1964 (when he died), the growth rate of Indian big business
was one of the fastest. The populist streak in Prime Minister
| Nehru’s stance resulted in rousing expectations of a new
| socialist era with the masses and compelled the successor prime-
: minister also to resort to populist slogans. Thus Mrs. Gandhi
| had the slogan of “Garibi Hatao”. But just as Panditji could
| not but let big business grow (if development was to take place
in India), similarly Mrs. Gandhi could not overnight adopt
drastic distributive measures without first having achieved

| growth.
Even then so long as the Congress party could resolve its
internal differences within the party organization it was not
required to adopt populist politics on a large scale. But this
became impossible in 1967 and thereafter when an inner party
struggle for leadership began between the two groups that
| popularly came to be known as “Indicate” led by Mrs. Gandhi
and “Syndicate” led by S. Nijalingappa, Sanjiva Reddy, Morarji
Desai and others. At this stage, one of the factions tried to
bring in the masses in support of its claim, thus giving rise
to populist politics. Between 1969-1971 Mrs. Gandhi’s group
adopted populist policies which sought to mobilize Harijans and
weaker sections; small farmers and the rural proletariat; urban
lower middle classes and industrial working class and resorted
to such measures as bank nationalization and abolition of privy
purses in a renewed bid to win a mass base. By the 1970s, Sethi
opines, the Indian political system changed from democracy to
pervasive populism.‘ This does not imply that Congress is or
was the lone populist party. In the middle 1970s the opposition
resorted, under the banner of J.P., to a purely populist
movement to oust certain state and central governments. After
the defeat of Mrs. Gandhi’s government, during the short
phase of coalition (Janata Party) rule at the centre, certain
central ministers, like George Fernandes and Charan Singh
did not hesitate to take issues to the people in order to settle
intra-governmental disputes, nor hesitate to make use of such
_ inherent conflicts as between management and labour, big and

|
