small industry, city and rural hinterland to promote their
factional interests.

-Manifestations of Populism in Our Economic Policies
The bane of our economic development is that it is ridden with
populist poison. Our planning objectives and Strategies have
been distorted by pressures of all kinds, some genuine, many
pseudo-radical, exerted by parliament, political parties and
various intellectual and economic interests. Thanks: to these
pressures the government came to accept and mouth various
social welfare theories which won mass or popular acclaim but
- _ did not square with the economic realities of growth. When
our politicians state that the goal of economic growth with
social justice is within the reach of Indian planning they are

not being fully honest.

Take, for instance, the various economic goals and
objectives as listed in the previous Five Year plans. These
included innumerable contradictory goals, but the planners
gave the impression that all were possible to achieve
simultaneously. Thus the plans sought (a) removal of poverty
and achievement of a larger growth rate, (b) economic self-
reliance, (c) prevention of concentration of economic
power, (d) consolidation of the democratic political order,
(e) reduction of disparities of income and wealth, (f) balanced
regional development, (g) creation of massive employment,
(h) realization of a socialist pattern of society. These objectives
are not only conflicting but not even capable of simultaneous
attainment since all of them compete for the same scarce
resources. A non-populist approach to politics and development
required that the government and the Commission enlighten
the people about the technical feasibility of the different
objectives. For instance, in the short-run it may not be possible
to attain self-sufficiency and at the same time prevent the
concentration of wealth. Similarly it is not economically easy
to reconcile growth with the goal of reduction of income and
wealth disparities. Economists tell us that economic realism

ADI DOCTOR 185
requires us to distinguish between inequalities which flow
from development and may even be necessary and those which
are not necessary and may arise from such property relations
as help the rentier class. To disallow such inequalities as
flow from development will amount to penalising innovating
entrepreneurs. This is.not to say that economic growth must
take place unaccompanied by social justice; what is being
stressed is that there can be no social justice without growth.
What our failure to adopt economic realism and take refuge
in populist politics has done, is that it has given us a low rate
of growth which has made it difficult for us to have any
meaningful programme of distributive justice. To give an

"example, take the textile policy of our government. The textile
mills were forced to produce standard cloth; but the goods
produced could not be lifted by the states because there was
not enough money with the poor to buy it.

Several populist ideas especially in the realm of economics
have become so deeply entrenched today that it may not be
difficult to rid the body politic of them as for instance the
idea that social justice demands the payment of a bonus even
to those who work for a losing concern and even if the money,
in the final reckoning, comes from the public exchequer; or,
that it is immoral to link new wage scales with productivity;
or the idea that if something is wrong with an industry,
nationalization will cure all the evils, or that controls are
necessary in the public interest and against business monopoly,
whereas the reality is that they are welcomed by the bureau-
cracy because it helps them increase their power vis-a-vis
politicians. Big business does not really mind these controls
Since it will enable businessmen to sort out problems with
politicians and administrators through graft and bribery rather
than on merits.
The brief Janata interlude was not very different from the
earlier Congress regimes. Under the influence of its leading

party became anti-industry and populist. George Fernandes
wanted nationalization of big industrial plants like Hindalco

The reasons why we have called these stances of the Janata

P. T. Bauer and B. S. Yamey

Purpose and Methods of Aid
R elief of acute need and misery in poor countries has been
the declared purpose of foreign aid—that is, official
. transfers from richer to poorer countries, as distinct from
, military assistance, commercial investment, or the efforts
of voluntary agencies—since President Harry Truman
launched the Point Four program in January 1949, well over
a generation and hundreds of billions of dollars ago. This
objective has always been the aim of the many genuinely com-
passionate supporters of foreign aid. Yet foreign aid goes to
governments, not to the poor. To support rulers on the basis
of the poverty of their subjects effectively rewards the policies
| that cause impoverishment. We have not emphasized this criti-
cal consideration sufficiently in our previous writings on

foreign aid.*

Since in those writings we have considered at length the
numerous other arguments which have been advanced for

Aid advocates have usually envisaged two different routes or

be termed the direct method, is the relief of acute poverty
through transfers of money to governments of the poorest

| development; in the last decade or so, the emphasis has shifted
to the direct method.
These two methods are often intertwined in aid discussions.
_ They do, however, differ radically in their criteria of allocation
and in their expected results, much as scholarships, grants, or

What happens to Aid?
The money sent via the direct method does not go to the
pitiable figures whose photographs we see in the campaigns
of the aid lobbies. It goes to their governments — that is, their
rulers. All too often it is these very rulers who are responsible
for the gruesome conditions depicted in aid publicity. Foreign
aid enables them to go on pursuing policies harmful or even
utterly destructive to the population at large. A depressing yet

many of these governments neglect such elementary

| Aid can relieve immediate shortages. It thereby conceals

| respectability on the rulers. In these ways, aid keeps

damaging policies. The famine in Ethiopia is only a recent

antecedents and analogies elsewhere in Asia and Africa — for
instance in Vietnam, Tanzania, Uganda, Zaire, and Ghana,
among others.
To support rulers on the basis of the poverty of their
| subjects not only enables the rulers to pursue extremely
damaging and even inhuman policies; it positively rewards
them for doing so. Thus, per-capita incomes are reduced if a
government restricts, persecutes, or expels its most productive
people, often but not only ethnic minorities — Asians and
Europeans in East Africa or Chinese in South east Asia; or if a

and Africa where there is no machinery whatever for state
relief of poverty. Indeed, state help to the poorest usually _
does not accord either with local mores or with the political

there are ethnic, cultural, and tribal diversities. Is an Arab-

-among blacks in the southern Sudan, hundreds of miles away,
with whom most of the time it is in open armed conflict? Can

include brand-new capitals built from scratch at the cost of

: Aid and Development
Can official aid, then, help relieve poverty and acute need:
_ indirectly, by promoting development through augmenting the
supply of investible funds? The answer is no. Official aid
cannot contribute substantially to Third World development,
and is indeed quite likely to retard it.
To begin with, the volume of investible funds is not critical
. for economic development. If it were, millions of very poor
people — individuals, families, groups, and whole societies —
could not have risen from poverty to riches in a few years or |
decades, as immigrant communities in South-east Asia and
. North America, among others, have done. And governments
__ and enterprises which can use capital productively and conduct
. their finances responsibly can borrow at home or abroad, even
if they are poor.
Thus, even in very poor countries Western trading firms in
the past habitually provided substantial financing to trust-
worthy local firms and individuals. And governments of poor
countries have often borrowed commercially for infrastructure
or other purposes. Therefore, the most that aid can do for
development is to reduce the cost of borrowing investible

development. Incidentally, this applies also to technical

often done in the past, for instance by the Japanese in the
late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Against the benefits of the reduced cost of investible funds
must be set major adverse repercussions affecting the basic
personal, cultural, and political determinants of development.

politicization of life, with its adverse or even disastrous
consequences for economic activity), official aid also often
encourages imprudent financial policies and discourages, for
instance, the building-up of reserves. All too often balance-
of-payments deficits are not unwelcome because they can serve

as a useful argument for requesting external assistance and

| In sum, at best foreign aid can do little to relieve Third

Suggested by the proponents of aid — in various publications,
we simply list some of them here,

First, it is official aid that has created the Third World as

a collectivity which, as such, is hardly a friend of the West.

Aid therefore underlies the North-South conflict. Further,

because, unlike Soviet-bloc aid, Western aid routinely goes to

governments at loggerheads (even at war) with each other, it

Second, by promoting and reinforcing the politicization .
of life, aid not only damages the welfare of Third World
peoples in the ways described above; it also harms the political
interests of the West.
Third, the advocacy of aid has spawned a plethora of writings
hostile to the West and its economic arrangements.
Fourth, powerful strands in this advocacy envisage aid as
a first step in a world-wide income redistribution among
countries, again to the detriment of the West and its economic
arrangements.
It does not follow from our argument that the West cannot
do anything to improve the lot of the peoples of the Third
World. Indeed, the countries of the. West already offer both
huge markets and vast sources of supply not only to one
another but also to the Third World. The removal or reduc-

the benefits of international commerce. Moreover, the
condition of the poorest in the Third World could be alleviated
| by the operation of non-politicized charities, which could be
expanded with judicious official encouragement and support.
We recognize, in conclusion, that a demonstration that aid
cannot achieve its proclaimed purposes—even if such a
demonstration were seen to be valid — is not likely to change
the operation of foreign aid or reduce its volume. This is so
because of the powerful emotional, political, commercial, and
institutional interests behind it. These forces are unlikely to
be deflected or attenuated by analysis, evidence, and argument,
whatever their cogency. And so the damage will go on.

| Consumer Rightsor Obligations
| T here is a character in one of Moliere’s plays who is
| surprised when told that he has been speaking prose all
| his life. Most people are surprised to learn that all, irrespective
po of any difference based on sex, caste, creed, religion, ideology
or what-have-you, are basically consumers; further, the end

Moreover, many day-to-day troubles and problems can be
solved only if people realise their importance as consumers
and fight for their rights and fulfil their responsibilities as
| consumers, | | ;
Basically, consumers have four rights :

(1) Adequate and correct information on the product

or service offered to them.

(2) Reasonable quality of goods or services.
(3) Reasonable price.

(4) In the event of any dispute, regarding the purchase,
. a fair interpretation of the law or rule governing
the sale.
Because most consumers are not aware of these rights, they
suffer in their day-to-day life. They get meagre or misleading

information from the suppliers; exorbitant prices are charged

| for goods and services; quality is either absent, or poor; when
| people find that they have got a raw deal, the table is turned
| against them that they have been at fault and nothing can
\ be done about the complaint.

214 Freedom and Dissent

These four rights carry with them some corresponding

responsibilities also.

Unlike other movements which place stress only on rights,

the consumer movement is based on rights balanced by

‘responsibilities. These responsibilities are:

(1) The consumer: should not make wild allegations or
general complaints. Complaints should be specific,
and wherever possible supported by bills and other
documentary evidence. ,

(2) Before making a complaint, the consumer should try

to understand the viewpoint of the seller.

(3) In some situations, the consumer has to cooperate

, with the seller of goods or services. For instance,
standing in a queue for a bus is in the general interest.

(4) Consumer rights should be asserted, but never by
means which hurt the legitimate interest of others.

For instance, satyagraha, rasta roko (halting traffic
on roads), morchas (processions) which disrupt traffic
etc., are undesirable methods of asserting one’s rights.
The general public which has nothing to do with a

. specific complaint, is hurt by these methods of
expressing one’s displeasure.

_ (5) Consumer complaints should be normally against a
system, and not against individuals. It is customary
to attack the head of an organisation or specific
individuals, while the real culprit is the system which
works against consumer interests.

The Movement Abroad

The consumer movement has progressed phenomenally in

countries like U.S.A. and the United Kingdom. Ralph Nader’s

heroic fight against the corporate giant General Motors, and
subsequent emergence of Nader Raiders dramatised the growth

of this movement into adulthood in U.S.A. In the U.K.,

WHICH magazine has become a byword for consumer

M. R. PAI . 215
alertness because of its scientific analysis of various products
and services.

Today, the consumer movement is not confined to liberal
democracies of the West where people enjoying political
democracy realise that it is not complete without economic
democracy. While the former consists in the periodic casting
.of the vote for electing representative governments, the latter
involves daily ballotting im the form of making a choice between
different goods and services, and competing brands of goods
or services. Millions of such decisions by people as consumers
give a democratic direction to the economy. What makes
political democracy meaningful is also the element of
consumers’ choice and the freedom to choose.

Where there is a Command Economy, with centralised
comprehensive planning as in communist countries, one would
not naturally expect a consumer movement. But even in such
countries, the consumer movement is emerging as a force
to reckon with. The governments of such countries have to
heed the voice of the consumers and try to placate them. When
the consumer is suppressed, riots overtake such totalitarian
political systems. In other words, consumerism is emerging
as the answer to political totalitarianism in some countries.
These countries are faced with a dilemma: If consumer
assertiveness is respected, the day is not far off when the
freedom to choose in the economic sphere will extend to
freedom to choose in the political sphere. Thus both the
Command Economy and totalitarian rule will face a challenge

| from people.

The Movement Begins in India
The emergence of consumer movement in India, which enjoys
political democracy but suffers from an attempt at centralised
comprehensive planning, is a recent one.

The consumer is slowly waking up in India. For years, a
closed market created by a dispensation of governmental
controls left little choice to the Indian consumer. The

216 > Freedom and Dissent
consumer had to stomach whatever was available, irrespective
of quality, and at the dictated price. The rapid increase in
the number of consumers in some sectors of the economy
has suddenly projected the problem of efficient service at
a reasonable price. Banking is one instance. The national
. objective is to convert class banking into mass banking, and
rightly so. In earlier days, the manual system of operations,
from maintenance of ledgers to clearance of cheques, was
able to cope with the limited banking business confined to
the elite. With expansion of the banking industry, territorially
and in terms of new clientele, the old system was unable to
cope with the load of work. It has virtually broken down. The
new system of electronic banking has not yet been introduced.
' The result is near chaos in the banking industry, with con-
sequential inefficiency and frauds. Belatedly, computerisation
and modern management practices are sought to be applied
to banking.
Whether it is banking or travel by air/railways/bus, or
telephones, or civic services, or supply of consumer goods,
: the conversion of a class into a mass economy is the big
"problem facing India today. The emergence of consumer
consciousness, with expectations of a better life, has shown
up the inadequacies of the present economic policies all
the more.
The consumer movement has started in India, but it has
not yet arrived.

INTRODUCTION
. belief was fostered after independence by
Ae political elements in the country that
Industrialists, Businessmen and Traders were
mainly confined to making money by whatever means,
that they would make every attempt to avoid paying
taxes and would have no hesitation even in exploiting
the consumer. Heavy taxes were imposed on
businessmen and complicated laws were introduced
to make their life increasingly difficult.

To correct this wrong impression, the business
community sought, through their representative
mercantile and trade bodies and chambers to educate
and inform public opinion on the ethics and role of
business and the benefits of a free market economy.
Also involved in this task were institutions such as

2 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life

the Forum of Free Enterprise, Committee for Fair Trade

Practices, Mumbai Grahak Panchayat and the Bank

Depositors Association, etc. started on the initiative

of public spirited citizens mainly to educate the general
. public but also the businessmen, the industrialists and

the traders on their duties.

One such organisation founded by Minoo Masani
over thirty years ago was the Freedom First
Foundation. This Foundation organised in Mumbai in
April 1984 a seminar attended by over 60 persons
comprising a representative cross section of society,
on the role of business community in public life. The
participants were a veritable who’s who from the world
of commerce and industry, the professionals including
lawyers, medical practitioners, chartered accountants
and chairmen and managing directors of well known
enterprises. The well known luminary N. A. Palkhivala
delivered the inaugural address. He made some very
pertinent remarks largely on the role of businessmen
and their obligations. —

“As I see it”, said Palkhivala “there are distinct
obligations which business owes to society.

* The first is the obligation towards Nature —
preserving the environment, preventing pollution,
preserving ecology in its true sense.

* The second is the obligation you owe to the
community around your factory or your workshop.

* The third is the obligation to take part in public
life, which is perhaps the one obligation which is
least observed”.

3
Introduction / 3
While all the obligations are as relevant today as
they were when he delivered the address, the two that
are of immediate relevance to the contents of this
volume are his observations on the second and third
“obligations”.

Explaining the second obligation Palkhivala said
“You can be engaged in commerce without having a
commercialised outlook. You can contribute not only
to the gross national product, but, as I am fond of
saying, to gross national happiness... As a professional,
you can cultivate your mind not merely with a view
to offering it for sale as a commodity in the market
place but with a view to enriching yourself and society
around. The gift is the gift of knowledge and I think
that those who are engaged in educating the people
are perhaps doing a more signal service than anyone
else.

“We have all heard of the ‘unacceptable face of
capitalism’. But it is equally true that it has an attractive
face, if only one can have a look at that face”.

Regarding the third “Obligation to Take Part in
Public Life”, he said: “This is the one obligation where
we are perhaps more in default than in any other way.
I have never accepted the theory that it is the business
of the businessman only to do business. It is his duty,
first and foremost, to be a good citizen and to do his
duty by the nation. In this country, as you are all aware,
politicians dominate businessmen and businessmen
run after politicians (unlike in Japan where it is the
politicians who run after businessmen) making you
realise there is something wrong with our values and
in our system. Those business houses which believe

4 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
they have no duty to perform, there is no public life
in which they have to be interested are, to my mind,
committing a grave error. Whatever may be your
thinking it is right that your thoughts be propagated,
. be promulgated, be disseminated as widely as possible.
If today businessmen have a chance of surviving it can
only be if they are interested in selling their ideas as
much as, I repeat, the importance of selling their goods.
I put great emphasis on a seminar like this because it
shows you the importance of selling your ideas as
much as, I repeat, the importance of selling your goods.
This is very, very, important. I do not think this country
would have come to this abysmal sorry pass if even
one-tenth of our businessmen had done their duty.”

I was present at this seminar and hearing his
speech reminded me of the role played by numerous
patriotic businessmen and industrialists who at great
risk to themselves and their enterprises not only
participated in our country’s freedom struggle but who
funded the freedom movement. Names that come to
mind are G. D. Birla, Jamnalal Bajaj and Ambalal
Sarabhai among many others.

I had the privilege of knowing G. K. Sundaram
of the Lakshmi Mills textile family who participated
in the freedom struggle. As a young man he joined
the Vedaranyam Satyagraha led by C. Rajagopalachari,
or Rajaji as he was nationally known - the southern
version of Gandhiji’s Dandi March or Salt Satyagraha.
Sundaram played a key role in the work of the
Swatantra Party in Tamil Nadu. There were many
others in business and industry, known and unknown,
who participated, funded and gave their all to free

Introduction / 5
the country from British Rule.

Yet, after freedom, and after the passing away
of Gandhiji and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, the attitude
of the party that led the freedom struggle changed and
as mentioned at the start of this introduction
businessmen, industrialists and traders were viewed
with mistrust. The Second Five Year Plan launched in
1957 marked the beginning of Statism with the launch
of the socialistic pattern of society. The permit licence
quota Raj sowed the seeds of corruption.

Rajaji and Minoo Masani were the first to publicly
denounce Nehruvian Socialism, encourage
businessmen and industrialists to shed their fear of
the government in power and seek to change the
system by involving themselves in the electoral process
and make their voice heard in Parliament. They
founded the Swatantra Party in 1959 and welcomed
them to join the Party for this purpose.

In the general elections of 1967, for the first time
a number of young businessmen contested as
candidates of the Swatantra Party and nine of them
including D N Patodia were elected to the Lok Sabha.

The socialistic pattern of society leading to the
State occupying the ‘Commanding heights of the
Economy’ led to the permit licence quota raj and which
in turn, engendered corruption and wrong doing on
a massive scale sparing no section of society. It also
led to the emergence of what Masani described as
socialist India’s ‘New Class’ comprising cliques of
corrupt politicians, corrupt bureaucrats and corrupt
businessmen.‘

6 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
Politics and politicians lost their credibility and
despite being regarded with disdain by the common
people at large, they were tolerated as a necessary evil.
Yet there were those in industry, commerce and trade,
. who tried hard to be honest and introduced reforms
within their ranks, as already mentioned, through
organisations like the Forum of Free Enterprise,
Committee for Fair Trade Practices, the Federation of
Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI)
and the Indian Merchants’ Chamber among others.

It was the Swatantra Party that brought D. N.

Patodia and this writer together over forty years ago
in 1967. I first met him at a meeting of the Party’s
parliamentary group in New Delhi. He was then a 40
year-old newly elected MP from Rajasthan. I was a
34 year-old executive secretary of the Central Office
of the Party in Mumbai representing the Swatantra
Party’s organisational wing.

We met in Mumbai a few years ago when he was
in the city on a personal visit. He had virtually retired
from active public life. We got talking, as old friends
do when they meet after a lapse of time, recalling the
past, of things pleasant and some not so pleasant. The
conversation veered to our work in the field of politics
and the NGOs with which we were connected. I asked
him what he had done with the huge amount of papers
and documents he had gathered over the years and
shouldn’t he be writing his memoirs. He had not only
been a member of parliament but had headed a
number of organisations chief among them being the
Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce &
Industry (FICCI) of which he was the President in 1985.

Introduction / 7
I was always fascinated by the spectrum of
Patodia’s pursuits, his constant desire to stay well-
informed about men and matters, his reading interests
covering a wide canvas and an eagerness to know
more.
He replied that he had indeed preserved many
documents, papers and photographs over the years.
But he was clear that he was not interested in writing
his memoirs. “Let my work speak for me” he said.
Failing to persuade him, I offered to write a book based
on his writings and speeches if he would place them
at my disposal. He welcomed the idea but asked for
time to think it over. I was therefore delighted when,
a few months later, he got back to me and said that
he would be glad to place at my disposal his papers
but reiterated that he was not interested if it was going
to be a biography. I assured him it would not be so
but if I was to write the book it would be around his
persona and his public life because he was a first-
person witness and on occasions even a partner in
activities that influenced events. Also, that he should
briefly put down his reminiscences of issues and events
as perceived by him during his active years in public
life. He agreed though rather reluctantly. He was being
true to form, for generally, when I had occasions to
interact with him I found him knowledgeable and
sincere but reticent to talk about himself and preferring
to shun the limelight.

Thus it is that this book begins with his
reminiscences, a little bit about his family and his
business and how he got into politics. He also writes
about his maiden speech in Parliament on the very

8 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life

first day of the first session of the 4th Lok Sabha
recording his protest over the imposition of President's
Rule in Rajasthan, the very state that returned him to
Parliament.

His recollections about his four years in
Parliament are warm and not only does he have a good
word even about those who belonged to other
opposition parties in the House including communist
members but also those in the treasury benches be it
Indira Gandhi, Y. B. Chavan or Asoka Mehta. This was
in keeping with the culture of the Swatantra Party to
which he belonged. Rajaji, Ranga and Masani kept
reminding their colleagues that the Party did not
believe in opposition for opposition’s sake, that
personal criticism and name-calling should be avoided;
each issue should be judged on its merit; and above
all due respect should be extended to the Parliament,
the Speaker and his rulings.

Patodia sent me his speeches and interventions
in his four years in parliament and the many meetings,
seminars, symposiums and workshops he attended
including papers he presented on a wide range of
subjects in his public activities. Many of them are as
relevant today as they were when he made his
presentations and explain why the situation is what
it is today; the Kashmir question which has become
such a complicated problem or the spread of the
Naxalite /Maoist movement. The material he sent me
is a perceptive record of much historical and educative
value. This explains why this narrative covers a wide
canvas on various aspects of India’s political economy
between the sixties and the early years of this century.

Introduction / 9

Patodia, as already mentioned earlier, entered
electoral politics in 1967. In retrospect he couldn’t have
timed his entry at a more opportune time. Political
pundits have generally regarded the outcome of the
1967 general elections as the first game changer, a
watershed for Indian democracy. There were other
turning points, or ‘tipping points’ in the decades that
followed but 1967 heralded the fact that India was
changing.

When one looks back at events as recorded by
Patodia when they actually happened, one could say
that political commentators who interpreted the results
of the 1967 elections as a game changer were not far
wrong. 1967 did trigger a churning of Indian
democracy — a churning, with all its highs and lows,
that went on for the next three decades before settling
down to what we are witnessing today - the emergence
of democratic coalition politics.

Again, as already mentioned earlier, after August
15, 1947 with the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi
on January 30, 1948 and the passing away of Sardar
Vallabhbhai Patel of a heart attack two years later on
December 15, 1950, Indian polity came to be dominated

by and large, made good use of the system and voted
for change when he or she felt such change was

not have any effective representation in Parliament and
their case largely went by default.

policies, India stayed behind languishing in poverty.

Integration of India after Independence

hen, on 15 August 1947 India became an

as Head of State and its own Constitution. The new

° The story of the integration of Princely States and

volumes.' V. P. Menon who started in 1914 as an
assistant in the Home Department of the Government
of India was Cabinet Secretary in 1945. When the
Ministry of States was created by the Interim
Government of India in July 1947, Menon worked in

Thanks to the genius of Sardar Patel ably assisted

of the 554 princely states were politically integrated
into the Indian Union. The Constitution of India came
into force on 26 January 1950, making India a Sovereign
Democratic Republic.

In 1956, Parliament enacted the States
Reorganization Act. This Act abandoned the British
system of provinces and princely states and replaced
them by new states and union territories largely based
on ethnicity (particularly in the case of the North east)
and language. This led to fierce agitation over the
demand for a separate State of Maharashtra with

Bombay city as its capital. The agitation was successful
and Bombay State was divided into the linguistic States
of Gujarat and Maharashtra in May 1960.

In the years between 1960 and 2014 the
reorganization of States continued mostly for
administrative convenience and a few based on
language and ethnicity. These were the states of
Nagaland, Punjab and Haryana (with Chandigarh as
the shared capital, though the city itself was declared
Union Territory), Himachal Pradesh, Manipur,
Meghalaya, Tripura, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh,
Mizoram, Goa, Chhattisgarh (created out of eastern

recently as June 3, 2014, Telangana (carved out of

Imposition of President’s Rule

D.N. Patodia was among the 44 members of the
Swatantra Party elected to the fourth Lok Sabha in the
1967 General elections from the Jalore-Sirohi
parliamentary constituency in Rajasthan. Not only was
the Swatantra Party the second largest party in the Lok
Sabha (even if the difference between its numbers and
that of the Indian National Congress was huge), it was
also the second largest party in the Rajasthan State
Assembly with 48 members in a house of 184.The
Congress with 84 members was 9 short of an overall
majority. It was then that the central government, in
its anxiety to ensure that the Congress Party was able
to form the government, played for time. The Governor
of Rajasthan prevaricated and President’s Rule was
imposed by the blatant misuse of Article 356 of the
Constitution.#

To protest against the ruling party’s action, a
motion of No Confidence against the Central
government was moved in the Lok Sabha in March
1967. Patodia was nominated by his Party to speak in
support of the motion. It happened on the very first
day of his parliamentary career — his maiden speech.

Tracing the events that led to the Swatantra Party

Inter-State Relations in a Federal Polity : Rajasthan / 51
in Parliament moving the motion of No Confidence,
Patodia pointed out that “initially, the Assembly was
expected to be convened around 22 March. But on
persistent demand from the Opposition, the Governor
agreed that the Assembly would be convened on 14th
March. Even after having had so much time at his
disposal, Shri Sukhadia (the leader of the Congress
Party in the State Assembly) realized that he did not
have a majority, and that he was not in a position to
form the Government. The only other constitutional
alternative the Governor had, under those
circumstances, was to invite the Leader of the
Opposition to form the Government; and only
thereafter, if the Opposition failed to produce a
majority, to consider any other alternative step.
“Instead”, said Patodia, “the Governor chose, possibly
in consultation with the Chief Minister, to take the
advice of the Home Ministry to find out by what
method and in what manner, somehow or other, an
Opposition government could be prevented from being
formed and some more time could be given to Shri
Sukhadia to maneuver and manage the numbers”. It
was in such circumstances that the President’s Rule

Article 370

Article 370 of the Indian Constitution giving
special status to Kashmir (including their own
constitution) was preventing the emotional integration
of the Kashmiris with the rest of India. For instance,
this provision prevented Indians from other parts of
the country expanding their commercial and industrial
activities in the state. This essentially political provision
actually retarded progress in the state and led to further
frustration among the Kashmiris.

Patodia’s report concluded that the incident of
the missing Hindu Pundit Girl was an administrative
Police matter for investigation to be decided by the
Magistrate. On account of bad administrative handling,
the matter was unnecessarily permitted to assume a
communal colour. The behaviour of the Police was far
from satisfactory and it resorted to avoidable,
unnecessary excesses both in dealing with the minority
and majority communities. It was a serious mistake
on the part of the State Government to have permitted
a Football Tournament. A weak administrative
command was responsible for Police forces from two
different States to be carried away by communal
feelings.

In their reactions both the State Government and

guided by vested interests, and be dragged in opposite
directions on different occasions influenced by different
political pulls. Pro-Pakistani and anti-national elements
were permitted to raise their heads to such an extent
that it went out of control. There was no serious
attempt to check these growing elements.

His report concluded “A long term solution of
the delicate problem of Kashmir lies eventually in
permitting and encouraging maximum possible
mobility and interflow of the Kashmiri community
with the rest of the country. Any provision like Article
370 of the Constitution which prevents free mobility
and interflow must be scrapped and all such
administrative measures that are needed for
encouraging free mobility should be encouraged. A
discrimination of this type between two citizens of the
same country belonging to two different provinces is
most unfortunate and undemocratic. The people of
Kashmir must develop a sense of belonging and as a
partner in the bigger family of Indians.”

The situation was still very much India’s internal
matter — a domestic quarrel that could have been
settled over a period of time despite Pakistani
meddling to aggravate tensions between the two
communities. Indian public opinion was of the view
that the Central government’s inept policies and not
allowing free and fair elections, had turned Kashmir
into a happy hunting ground for terrorism particularly
after the 1971 war that led to the dismembering of East
Pakistan.

TIBET
A FRIENDLY NEIGHBOUR
BETRAYED
ibet, often referred to as the Roof of the World,
is a vast country over two thirds the size of
India. It is a land rich in minerals and in the
variety of its flora and fauna. It is not entirely arid and
barren as it is generally believed, but is rich in forests,
pasture lands and fertile valleys. It is also the source
of the Brahmaputra and Indus rivers. Tibet borders
India, Nepal and Burma to the south; the Xinjiang
Uyghur Autonomous Region of China (formerly the
Republic of East Turkestan) to the north and China
to the east.
The Tibetan people are a distinct race with their
own spoken and written language, their own culture,
traditions, food and dress. Five hundred years before

78 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
the birth of the Buddha the Tibetans practiced the Bon
religion. Buddhism came to Tibet when Guru
_Padmasambhava founded the first Monastery and
established the supremacy of Buddhism and converted
° the indigenous deities.

The Mongols invaded Tibet around 1350 A.D and
Kublai Khan was converted to Buddhism. A close
spiritual relationship developed between Tibet and
Mongolia. In 1642 the fifth Dalai Lama became the ruler
of all Tibet and demanded from the Ming Emperor
of China recognition of his sovereignty. This was given.
In 1904 a British Expeditionary Force to counter
Russian influence in central Asia entered Lhasa and
a treaty was signed between Tibet and Great Britain.
China did not object to this treaty between two
sovereign nations. In 1909 the Chinese invaded Tibet
and the thirteenth Dalai Lama fled to British India and
sought British help. Civil unrest in China helped the
Dalai Lama return to Tibet a few years later. He passed
away in 1933.

Forty years later in September 1949 the Chinese
invaded Tibet once again. For the next ten years the
fourteenth Dalai Lama sought to negotiate with
Communist China. His attempts to reach an
understanding failed and when the Chinese Army
occupied Lhasa the fourteenth Dalai Lama escaped on
March 17 1959 and sought political asylum in India.
He was followed by an unprecedented exodus of
Tibetans into exile. Never before in their long history
had so many Tibetans been forced to leave their
homeland under such difficult circumstances. There
are now more than one hundred thousand Tibetan

Tibet — A Friendly Neighbour Betrayed / 79
refugees all over the world.'

It is important to understand that throughout
China’s history impossible claims have always been
made by the Head of that State that its outlying border
territories were provinces of China. The gifts sent to
the Emperor of China by neighbouring countries were
regarded as tributes from subordinate States to the
all-powerful Son of Heaven. A powerful China always
took an aggressive stand against the weaker border

areas.

“This is wholly understandable, for the highly
developed ancient Chinese civilization had a profound
influence on the outlying territories, the most important
of such impacts being on Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

“The pronouncements of Mao Tse Tung have been
in keeping with this tradition. In his book Chinese

| Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party, he
writes: ‘In defeating China in war the Imperialist States

have taken away many Chinese dependent states and

a part of her territories. Japan took away Korea, Taiwan

and Ryuku islands, the Pescadores, and Port Arthur;

England seized Burma, Bhutan, Nepal and Hong Kong;
France occupied Annam and even an insignificant

country like Portugal took away Macao.’ These words

written in 1939 have an ominous significance today.”

Legends would have it that “2500 years ago a

person belonging to the Kingdom of Kaushal (in
northern U.P.) went from India and established the
Kingdom of Tibet and from that day the historical and
traditional ties between Tibet and India continued in

addition to the religious, cultural and philosophical

“In this tragedy the attitude of India is shameful.
We were instrumental and a party to the domination

“By admitting Chinese suzerainty over Tibet we

have surrendered the sovereignty not only of Tibet but
have committed a big blunder from our own defence

ground of China from which they could have attacked

“Shri Lal Bahadur Shastri, our late Prime Minister,
had admitted it in the course of one of his speeches

“Various treaties on Tibet were entered into

and Britain. Until 1954 when a treaty was signed with

never questioned. The Chinese presence in Tibet can
be described as some sort of a privileged person,

| enjoying certain rights without in anyway affecting
the autonomous status of Tibet, and without affecting
the rights of the Tibetan people.”

Tibet, till the Chinese annexation, was a free
nation can be proved by two or three events. “In 1876,
ignoring Chinese displeasure, the Tibetans did not

: permit the British Mission to visit Tibet. Again, during
World War II, Tibet did not allow war materials to be
transported to China via Tibet. These two illustrations

Even in the 1951 treaty between India and China, the

“But there was one safeguard put into the treaty

“The Chinese never honoured this agreement.

There is no reason why in spite of all that has

China is today a very powerful nation politically

world under communist rule. It did succeed in

Though allied with the USA and Western Europe
in the Second World War, the defeat of Hitler’s Nazi
Germany also signaled the end of the alliance and the
emergence of the Cold War (which erupted into a hot
war as in Korea and Vietnam) between the Soviet
Union and its allies, on the one side and, the United
States of America and Western Europe, on the other.

As a colony of the British Empire, Indian soldiers
were part of the British Army and, at least, until 1947
on the side of the USA and its allies in the Cold War.

After 1947, India proclaimed it would be neutral
in the Cold War and took the initiative along with
newly independent countries in Asia, Africa and South
America in forming a worldwide movement called the
“Non-Aligned Movement” or NAM.

The Non-Aligned Movement was formed to be
neutral in the Cold War. Reports are that NAM was
generously funded by the Soviet Union. With the

collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold
War, NAM has been struggling to find relevance and
is today only a shadow of its old self. As recently as
August 2012 NAM held its 16th world summit in
Teheran. It, however, continues to lead a tenuous
existence (a number of members have left NAM). It
is also generally referred to as an organisation of Third
World countries (largely comprising under-developed,
or developing countries). A third category that has
gained currency in recent years is the ‘Emerging
Nations’. India, for instance, is now considered an
Emerging Nation.
India’s policy of non-alignment or neutrality was

he story of the Indian Economy is a story of

not have been missed but were missed because

us by while our leadership, after the passing away
of Mahatma Gandhi and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, was
swearing by what came to be notoriously known as
the Socialist Pattern of Society — also called Nehruvian
Socialism. Between 1957 and mid-1980s, this was the
policy that kept India from growing.

In 1988, Patodia, wrote a seminal article on what
was happening in the world outside and the crucial
need for India not to miss the bus.i The following
write-up is based on this article.

Agriculture

The potential for agricultural development is
immense in our country. Against the world average
of 10.4%, more than 50% of land in India is suitable
for agriculture. India is among the few countries where
crops can be grown almost round the year. Yet, only
31% of our total cropped area is irrigated and our yield
continues to be lower than the world average.

Our self-sufficiency in foodgrains is a myth as
it totally ignores the very low level of nutrition value
available to the people. Inhabited by 14% of the world’s
population, India produces only 8% of the world’s
foodgrains. Going by the average need of calories for
our people, we will have to produce 75% more
foodgrains to be fully self-sufficient.

The importance of agriculture in economic
development has been amply demonstrated by many
other countries. The USA produces huge surpluses of
foodgrains exporting 40% of its product. Agriculture
is the most important economic factor in the European
Economic Community better known as the EEC. The
development of Canada and Australia has centred
round agriculture.

There is no reason why India should not be

the Gosplan as the Soviet called it. It considerably
influenced the nature and scope of the Planning
Commission.
Sardar Patel was not a socialist. He was inclined

towards free enterprise, private ownership of land or

therefore, closer to Gandhiji’s philosophy of Gram
Swaraj.

° Gandhiji was assassinated on January 30, 1948
and the Sardar died three years later on December 15,
1950 — the two who could have changed the direction
of India’s Economic Policy. But that was not to be.

The National Planning Commission, reporting
directly to the Prime Minister of India who was also
its Chairman, was established on 15 March 1950, with
Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru as the Chairman. The
Planning Commission is neither a creation of the
Constitution of India nor an institution created by an
act of Parliament, hence not answerable to parliament
but an arm of the Union Government.

The First Five-year Plan was launched in 1951.
This Plan was formulated when Sardar Patel was still
alive. Not surprisingly, it emphasised the development
of the agricultural sector.

With both Gandhiji and Sardar Patel out of the
way, Nehru went full steam ahead with what came
to be known as Nehruvian Socialism. The Second Five
Year Plan (1956-61) turned away from agriculture, and
firmly established the concept of the State controlling
the ‘Commanding Heights of the Economy’, the
emphasis shifted more towards heavy industries, and
a strategy that came to be known as ‘Planning by
Physical Targets’. The Third Five Year Plan (1961-66)
was a continuation of the Second Plan. It suffered a
break in 1965 because of the Indo-Pakistan conflict.

The Indian Economy : The Planning Commission / 115
Two successive years of drought, devaluation of the
currency, a general rise in prices and erosion of
resources disrupted the planning process leading to
a period described as a ‘Plan Holiday’ between 1966
and 1969, and replacing the Third Five Year Plan with
three Annual Plans. The Fourth Five Year Plan came
into being in 1969:

The experience of fifteen years of Planning, the
disastrous results of the Third Five Year Plan and the
relative awareness and admission of several lapses by
government spokesmen clearly indicated the need for
a new approach. The hope was that Government
would adopt a more realistic, practical and meaningful
approach so that future Plans were growth-oriented
and based on an assessment of resources available for
its implementation. Three years of ‘Plan Holiday’, a
logical consequence of the difficult period of stress and
strain through which the economy had to survive, had
further strengthened this hope.

In 1965, a year before the Plan Holiday, Minoo
Masani addressing a meeting in Bombay spoke on why
the Five Year Plan had failed to achieve its ambitious
targets. He attributed this to what he described as the
“four fallacies indulged in by the Government of India
and the Planning Commission and which contributed
to slowing down the rate of growth in industrial and
agricultural production.”

“The rate of our progress”, said Masani, “has in
fact been in inverse ratio to the size of our Five Year

inherent and inevitable and that a big Plan must mean
slow progress because of the diversion of scarce

“The reason why resources that are drawn within

these Plans are likely to yield lower returns than if they
. had been left free in the pockets of the people is that
we have been indulging in four fallacies:

“The first of these is that we as a nation spend
money which we may not possess. This results in
inflation, rising prices and all its social implications.

“The second fallacy is that not agriculture but
the manufacture of steel and machinery is India’s basic
industry, which takes priority over the consumer’s

“The third fallacy is that government should
produce more and the people less. Hence, while these

“The fourth fallacy is that the National Planning

right to dictate what shall and shall not be produced

with the ‘indicative’ planning of France and Britain.
It has also created a veritable jungle of controls, licences
and permits which kill incentive and breed corruption.”

During those years, while other countries
including India’s neighbours registered impressive
growth, the Indian economy continued to suffer. And,
it was only around 1984-85, after a realization of its
poor economic growth that the government finally
decided to act. Several reform measures were
introduced under which 25 industries were de-licensed,
the application of MRTP Act was made less stringent,
taxes were reduced and foreign investments were
liberalized.

_ In the new economic environment the business
community extended full support and cooperation. The
results were promising as reflected in significant
growth in investment and production, larger
opportunities of employment, better flow of foreign
investment and higher collection of taxes. With such
a major transformation of the Indian economy it
became imperative for FICCI to reorient its approach
to deal with the changing economic horizons. After
detailed deliberations Patodia initiated much needed
reforms in the working of the FICCI Secretariat to
ensure proper coordination with the Government in
the shaping of various economic policies including
international treaties.

To encourage free and frank deliberations
between Government and the Business Community,
on the recommendation of Patodia, a small informal

The Indian Economy : FICCI - Serving Trade and Industry / 157
forum calling itself the ‘Wednesday Group’ was set
up. This initiative proved to be very effective. The
Group used to meet once a month to deliberate on a
specific economic subject to which, apart from business
leaders, ministers and secretaries connected with the
subject were also invited. The discussions were free
and frank and helped the government representatives
better understand the business point of view.

At the political level until the late 1960s and early
1970s the governments at the centre and in the states
were almost totally controlled by the Congress Party.
Other political groups, considerably smaller in size,
did not have much influence in the shaping of
economic policies. The picture started changing from

| 1967 onwards bringing new political parties into the
mainstream leading to a gradual change over to a more
federal polity. In line with the changing political

| contour, FICCI too extended its operations so as to
remain in contact with all political parties represented
in the Parliament many of which were influential in
their own states.

Under the new economic dispensation emerging
in India and considering the rapidly increasing
economic activities around the world, the growing
involvement of government agencies, international
treaties and increasing complexities, it became
imperative that FICCI as the apex body of trade and
industry and the government should, to the extent
possible, present a common and joint approach at
international forums. To achieve this objective, Patodia

presented FICCI’s case ably with the then Prime
Minister Rajiv Gandhi and Finance Minister V. P. Singh

158 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
suggesting that during the Prime Minister’s visits
abroad, wherever possible, he should address joint
meetings of business leaders from that country and
India. After considerable persuasion, the Prime
Minister agreed to meet and address joint meetings
. of the Indo-French Joint Business Council in Paris on
6th June 1985 and the Business Cooperation Committee
of India and Japan in Tokyo on 28th November 1985.

1985 was observed as the ‘India Festival Year’ in
France and our Prime Minister was invited on the
occasion as a Chief Guest by the French President.
While addressing a joint meeting of French and Indian
business leaders in Paris, Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi
praised the progress made in high technology areas

by France and invited French cooperation in various
fields particularly in aeronautics and oil exploration.

In Tokyo, applauding the long standing
cooperation between the two countries, the Prime
Minister complimented Japan for extending support
for the promotion of industry in India. He also outlined
various economic measures, spoke of the new
economic climate in India and invited Japanese
business to be the partners in India’s economic growth.
In particular, he invited Japanese business to help
increase exports from India.

FICCL, in its efforts over the years, achieved
successful results in establishing close economic
cooperation with several other countries and by the
year 1985 it had already signed Joint Business Council
Agreements with 31 nations. Also during his tenure
as FICCI’s President, Patodia led Indian delegations

| The Indian Economy : FICCI - Serving Trade and Industry / 159
| to several counties, and also played host to several

delegations visiting India including Her Majesty Queen
. Beatrix of the Netherlands, H.E. Miguel d le Madrid,
| President of Mexico, H.E. Dr. Kamal El-Ganzouri,
| Deputy Prime Minister of Egypt, Sir Sridath Ramphal,

Secretary General of the Commonwealth of Nations,
i among others.

During his term of office, Patodia was invited to
speak by several leading institutions and organisations
including the Planning Commission; the Federation
of Indo-German Societies in India; the Indian Institute
of Foreign Trade; Forum of Financial Writers; the

| TISCO Management at Jamshedpur; the National
| Defence College New Delhi; the United Writers
Association, Chennai; and by the New Delhi Traders
Association on the occasion of their Golden Jubilee
. Celebrations.

When Patodia took over as President in 1985,
trade was already an integral part of FICCI’s activities.
Patodia sharpened FICCI’s focus. He accepted an
invitation to address the Golden Jubilee Celebrations
of the New Delhi Traders Association on 25 May 1985.

| In his address he recalled the qualities and integrity
of the country’s trading community and the respect
they enjoyed in society. He also took the opportunity
to highlight the immense contribution made by traders
in the different fields of economic activity. Describing
the hardships and discriminations suffered by the
trading community due to very complex laws and high
rates of taxation, Patodia called upon the Government
| to bring about reforms and to remove the hardships
| suffered by the community. For an abridged version

160 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
of this lecture, please read Appendix ‘A’.
Delivering the Frank Moraes Memorial Lecture
on 3 May 1985, Patodia referred to the First Industrial
Revolution in the 18th century in Great Britain when
. the use of steam and coal signaled a major
breakthrough in building a modern society. The Second
Industrial Revolution took place around 1880 in
Germany which recognized the role of electricity as
the prime mover. This was followed by the Third
Industrial Revolution in the realm of information and
communications leading to far reaching and fascinating
developments and demolishing old concepts. For an
abridged version of this lecture please read Appendix
‘B’.

Patodia delivered the Raja Ramdeo Anandilal
Podar 15th Memorial Lecture in Jaipur, Rajasthan on
22 February 1986 on “Opportunities and Challenges
for Business in India”. For an abridged version of this
lecture please read Appendix ’C’.

FICCI hosted a meeting of the Indo-US Joint
Business Council in New Delhi on 12th March 1986.
It was a very useful meeting in which several Indian
ministers participated. Various difficulties and
opportunities in doing business in both the countries
were discussed in detail. The delegation also took time
to call on Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and exchanged
views with him on economic issues of mutual interest
between the two countries.

Towards the end of Patodia’s term of office, FICCI
organized a major event - The All India Businessmen’s
Convention on 12th March 1986 addressed by Prime

Minister Rajiv Gandhi. Finance Minister V. P. Singh
and Industry Minister N. D. Tiwari also participated.
It was a significant event which had the advantage
of ministers and senior representatives of the
government and leading businessmen from across the
country taking part. In his welcome address, Patodia
made a pointed reference to the fact that the Indian
economy was moving away from a rigid and regulated
framework to a new liberal regime based on
competition and efficiency. He complimented the Prime
Minister for his vision and the broad initiatives taken
by him. He highlighted the positive results achieved
by way of higher investment, larger employment and
increased production. While presenting a blueprint for
growth he pleaded for the introduction of more policy
initiatives needed to achieve the desired goal.

In his response, the Prime Minister made a
pointed reference to the contribution made by industry
and trade in the economic development of the country
and called upon the Indian society to change its
attitude towards growth. He laid stress on better
cooperation between the government and business and
assured the business community of extended

cooperation in the task of nation-building.

Finally, at the end of his term as President of
FICCI, the Annual General Meeting of FICCI was
inaugurated by the Finance Minister V. P. Singh on
22nd March 1986. It was an important event in which
large numbers of business representatives from all over
the country participated. In his welcome address as
President, Patodia, while complimenting the
government on initiating major reforms in liberalization

162 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
of the economy, laid stress on the areas which still
needed immediate action. He particularly expressed
his concern with the high cost economy and adverse
impact of different taxes on production/distribution
. costs. Stressing the need for improving the balance of
trade and the growing importance of agriculture,
Patodia recommended specific measures for the
government. He assured the Finance Minister of the
total support of the business community in
contributing to the country’s economic growth.

The Finance Minister in his address was generous
in his compliments to FICCI for its significant
contribution and advice on various economic matters
and specifically complimented President Patodia for
his full cooperation. Taking up various points raised
by the business community, the Finance Minister
frankly explained the government's point of view and
his limitations. He also laid stress on the growth of
the small scale sector; the need for stability; creating

more opportunities for employment and on inviting .

business cooperation in rural development activities. .

THE HousINGc PROBLEM

! Travelling extensively in his own constituency in

the Jalore-Sirohi district of Rajasthan, then the

second largest constituency in the country very
sparsely populated, with wide stretch of sand and
dunes. Patodia almost always came across people
living in pathetic conditions in the district without even
the semblance of roads having village tracks in most
of the areas, the vast stretch of land without a drop
of drinking water for miles together and without any
respectable house roof for shelter; and travelling
around the country he further observed that in many
of the rural areas of India the conditions are not very
different particularly in respect of housing and roads
and realized that the pressing problems of rural India

164 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
after food are housing, roads and drinking water.
Connected with these pressing needs, Patodia
constantly raised questions in Parliament and
participated in debates on these very subjects apart
. from making repeated representations to the State
Government. After long drawn efforts, the State
Government finally agreed to some of the suggestions
made by Patodia for providing drinking water.

Deeply conscious of the pressing problem of
housing in the country, Patodia conducted a detailed
survey, prepared a report, discussed and distributed
the report amongst members of the Parliament and |
the members of the Rajasthan State Assembly. The
report was widely appreciated as a useful document
on the subject.

Even today, almost 50 years after the reporti was
prepared, the problem of adequate housing in the
country continues to haunt us.

“Housing, like food, clothing and drinking water,
is a basic necessity of life. It has so far (1969) been
amongst the most neglected sectors of the economic .
development of India. The planners who were
entrusted with the task of building a welfare society,
where basic necessities of life would have priority over
all other forms of development, have miserably failed
to touch even the fringe of the problem.

Magnitude of the Problem

“In order to give importance to the subject a

separate Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty

Alleviation was created in the Central Government as
early as May 1952.

“Acute shortage of housing both in the Rural and
Urban areas persists, and even whatever is available
is of very sub-standard variety. Most of the houses in
rural areas are kutcha in the form of thatched mud
huts without any strong foundation and not entirely
safe. Some figures were compiled by the Government
in 1961 regarding housing requirements in the country:

“At an estimated rise of 10 million in population
every year and 5 persons on an average constituting
one household, as many as 2 million new houses are
required to be constructed annually to meet the
demand of the rising population alone. Actual progress
during the Third Five Year Plan had been much slower
and as against 10 million houses needed for increased
population alone, only 4 million houses (including
those in the Private Sector) were expected to be
constructed out of which possibly only 3 million could
finally be built, leaving a staggering backlog. In
addition, another 18 lakh houses were estimated to

adding further to the backlog.
“By another assessment made by the Government |

was estimated to be 741 lakhs comprising:

Investment & Achievement so far
“During the First Five Year Plan about 700,000
houses were estimated to have been constructed under
. various Public Housing Schemes. During the second
Five Year Plan nearly 500,000 houses were constructed.
“A study of various schemes and projects taken
up by the Ministry of Housing reveal how ineffective
the schemes were to tackle this basic problem. A good
part of the finance was wasted on making plans,
drawing schemes, holding conferences, employing
large secretariats and passing high sounding
resolutions, and yet achieving hardly anything
worthwhile.
Bold approach needed
“The problem of housing is more acute in rural
areas where 80% of the country’s population live and
therefore, the Rural Housing Programme will have to
be taken up on a much wider scale. Only 3% of the
rural population lives in pucca houses and the shortage
of houses in rural areas which was estimated at 627

Seminal Essays : The Housing Problem / 167
lakhs in April 1966 has already crossed the mark of
700 lakhs by now. The problem of Urban Housing is
also very acute. The gradual shift of population from
Rural to Urban areas will further add to the problem.

“With such a colossal problem to be tackled, an
amount of nearly Rs.500 crores which was earmarked
in the 4th Five Year Plan proved to be hopelessly
inadequate and insignificant. At this rate the progress
in the construction of new houses will not be able to
keep pace with even the rise in population and the
situation will continue getting worse. Anything short
of constructing 50 lakh houses a year will not be able
to bring this problem anywhere near to solution. If such
a programme is considered too ambitious it may start
with a programme to build 10 lakh houses in the first
year and raising it to 50 lakh houses in the final year.

“It is only by implementing the programme on
such a scale that the effect of the rise in population
can be neutralized.
Opportune Time
“The present time seems to be the most
opportune for taking up the project of this magnitude.
@ Under present conditions when a large number of
industries are facing the problem of under-
utilization of installed capacities and rising
unemployment, a bold programme for house
building will generate economic activities on a big
scale providing additional employment to the
. millions apart from making a good use of wide scale
unutilized capacities of different industries. In
addition, it will also generate huge additional

168 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
demand for all varieties of goods and services
releasing the forces of economic revival.

@ It will provide direct employment to 150 lakh
people for every 10 lakh houses constructed per

. year. Indirect employment will be much larger.

@ Once economic activities start multiplying, much
of the resources needed in the initial stage to finance
this project will be easily generated through larger
collections of taxes and greater revenues from
Railways, Road Transport, Electricity, etc.

@ A programme of such magnitude will also provide
an excellent opportunity to mobilize these
additional resources scattered around rural areas.

@ The implementation of such a programme will have
to be a collective effort of the Government, both
Central and states and various other public bodies
along with the private sector. A separate
autonomous independent and integrated body
should be set up and may be named as
‘NATIONAL HOUSING AUTHORITY’ or any
other suitable name.

@ It will plan and process all the programmes and
schemes along with financial layouts, with the
Central and state governments and other relevant
bodies and will carry out their implementation.

@ The Central Body should be able to obtain financing
in the form of 90% of the cost as loan from the
commercial banks which, in turn, can be refinanced
upto 80% by the Reserve Bank. Government or the
Reserve Bank should advance to the commercial
banks upto 80% of the cost of construction and land,

the balance 10% to be provided by the commercial
banks themselves. The total amount should be
insured.”

Author’s Note: National Plan for Housing

After presenting his research paper on housing,
Patodia continued to raise the issue in the House from
time to time. In this context, on 18th August 1969 in
reply to a question raised by Patodia, the Minister for
Health and Family Planning and Works and Urban
Development confirmed the facts given by Patodia,
namely that against a demand of 102.4 million dwelling
units in the country pucca units available were only
18.7 million.

The Minister also drew attention to a Conference
of Ministers of Housing, Urban Development and Town
Planning held in Bangalore, in June 1969, which
recommended the constitution of a Central Housing
Authority to raise funds both from within and outside
the country and operate it in the nature of a revolving
fund and that for this purpose, a corpus of Rs.200
crores should be built up out of Governmental
allocations, private savings and contributions from
international agencies.

A year later, in reply to another question on the
subject, the Minister stated:

(a) According to the progress reports received so far
from the state governments, construction of 77,213
houses had been sanctioned in rural areas and
5,57,514 houses in urban areas, under the various
Social Housing Schemes of this Department, since
their inception upto 30 June, 1970. Of this, 47,658

170 / How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life
houses had been completed in rural areas and
425,214 houses in urban areas.

(b) A sum of Rs.193.27 crores had been provided in
the plans of the States and Union Territories for

. Social Housing and Urban Development Schemes

during the Fourth Five Year Plan. According to the
estimates of the Working Group on Housing for the
Fourth Five Year Plan (1969-74), India’s housing
shortage was about 837 lakhs units at the
commencement of the Fourth Five Year Plan. The
respective urban and rural housing shortages
amounted to 119 lakhs units and 718 lakhs units,
on the basis that every household should have a
reasonably permanent dwelling of its own.

Postscript

The Government policy of housing has been
passive throughout the 50 years since Independence.

As briefly stated below programmes for house
building have been discussed and finalized repeatedly
at various stages.

In 1960, the National Building Construction
Corporation (NBCC) was incorporated as a Public
Sector Undertaking. In 1969, the National Co-operative
Housing Federation of India was set up. In 1970,
HUDCO was set up as a fully owned Government
Company. In 1976, a National Institute of Urban Affairs
was set up. In 1985, a National Capital Region Planning
Board was constituted. In 1996, the National Slum
Development Programme (NSDP) was launched. In
1997, the Union Cabinet approved the Swarna Jayanti
Shahari Rojgar Yojana. A new Housing and Habitat

Seminal Essays : The Housing Problem / 171
Policy 1998 was approved and placed before
Parliament on 29 July, 1998. Its objective was to create
surpluses in housing stock and facilitate construction
of 2 million additional dwelling units each year in
pursuance of the National Agenda for Governance.

Under the new economic reforms, a scheme of
Infrastructure Development in mega cities i.e. Mumbai,
Chennai, Calcutta, Hyderabad and Bangalore was in
operation from 1993-94.

The Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act
came into force in 1976 to provide equitable distribution
of land in order to subserve the common good. The
Urban Land (C&R) Repeal Bill, 1998 was introduced
on 11 June 1998.

Different Schemes for Housing Development

The Urban Mapping Scheme was taken up as a
pilot project during the Eighth Five Year Plan for
covering 50 towns from different states. The executive
Agency for the project the National Remote Sensing
Agency (NRSA) had completed aerial photography of
all the towns and they have furnished photographs
and aerial maps for all the towns except three towns.
Low-Cost Sanitation for Liberation of Scavengers

This is a centrally sponsored scheme which is
under the Ministry of Urban Development since 1989-
90.

The Scheme of Integrated Development of Small
and Medium Towns (IDSMT) aims at the development
of selected regional growth centers with infrastructure

and service facilities. From the inception of the scheme

till 31 March 1999, central assistance amounting to only

Rs.345.30 crore was released.

Ninth Plan and Housing

The Ninth Plan laid greater stress on households |
at the lower end and identified priority groups for
support, such as, for example, people below poverty
line, SC/ST, disabled, etc.

India has made a commitment to reach a
sustainability level of rural and urban housing for the |
poor and the Ninth Plan provided the support of
composite credit instruments, modify land use pattern
and city master plans and strengthen the linkages
between the farm and the non-farm sectors in the rural
and semi-urban areas.#

|

Yet, inspite of repeated promises and a host of
programmes emerging from time to time, the problem
continues to remain grave, perhaps has worsened than |
what it was 40 years ago. |

# — Sourced from Wikipedia : Article 356 gave wide powers to the central

government to assert its authority over a state if civil unrest occurred
and the state government did not have the means to end the unrest.
This is one of the Articles that gave the Indian Constitution some
amount of unitary character. Though the purpose of this Article
is to give more powers to central government to preserve the unity
and integrity of the nation, it has often been misused by the ruling
parties at the center. It has been used as a pretext to dissolve state
governments ruled by political opponents. Thus, it is seen by many
as a threat to the federal system. Since the adoption of the Indian
Constitution in 1950, the central government has used this Article
several times to dissolve elected state governments and impose
President’s Rule.
For instance, the Article was used in UP in 1968. Earlier it has also
been used in the state of Patiala and East Punjab States Union
(PEPSU) and then during Vimochana samaram to dismiss the
democratically elected Communist state government of Kerala on
31 July 1959. In the 1970s and 1980s it almost became common
practice for the central government to dismiss state governments
led by opposition parties. The Indira Gandhi regime and post-
emergency Janata Party were noted for this practice. Indira Gandhi's
government between 1966 and 1977 is known to have imposed
President’s Rule in 39 states. Similarly the Janata Party is known
to have imposed President’s Rule in 9 states which were ruled by

It was only after the landmark judgement in 1994 in the S. R. Bommai
v/s. Union of India case that the misuse of Article 356 was curtailed.
In the Bommai case, the Supreme Court established strict guidelines
for imposing President’s Rule. Subsequent pronouncements by the
Supreme Court in Jharkhand and other states have further watered
down the scope for misuse of Article 356. Hence, since the early
2000, the number of cases of imposition of President’s Rule has come
down drastically.
Article 356 has always been the focal point of a wider debate on
the federal structure of government in Indian polity. The Sarkaria
Commission on central-state relations has recommended that Article
