Nearly for two and a half decades, Professor B. R. Shenoy
dominated the discussion on Indian Economic Policy and Planning.
Through the vast number of articles he contributed to profess-
ional and popular journafs, he attained a world-wide recognition
as a powerful dissenter to what Professor Bauer has called ‘“‘the
spurious consensus of development economics”’.

He was born on 3rd June 1905 at Bellicoth, a small village
near the beautiful city of Mangalore situated on the South-coast
of India. In his school, he was considered to be rather shy but
bright and strong-willed boy possessing an unusual degree of
self-control and discipline. In 1920, he passed his high school
examination, with excellent grades. In those days, a career in the
Indian Civil Service was regarded as something which all the
bright young students would eventually strive for. Obviously his
parents also wanted him to go in for this career. However, the
young Shenoy could not keep himself away from the freedom
movement which was then in its full-swing. He left his studies,
plunged in the movement actively and courted imprisonment in

1923. He was placed in the Nagpur Central Jail, where, by a
happy coincidence, Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya-one of the
principal architects of Modern Indian Renaissance and Nationalism-
was also lodged. As Panditji was in weak health, young Shenoy

Ui] |
gladly took upon himself the task of helping and assisting Panditji
in his daily chores. Impressed by his sharp intellect, patrio-
tism, and religious upbringing, Panditji took him under his |
wings, and persuaded him to join the Benaras Hindu University
as a student. His close association with Panditji at a very young
age of his life left a permanent and lasting impression on Profe-
ssor Shenoy’s personality. Some of the distinct qualities of his
character-his life-long intefest in philosophy and religion, his
leonine spirit, his unfaltering courage in defending the intellectual
positions, his vedantic mind-had led him to espouse-for which .
his contemporaries subsequently came to respect him-can be
traced back to his early association with Pandit Malaviyaji. He
completed his studies at the Benaras Hindu University in 1929,
passing his M. A. Examination with first rank in the first division.
His teacher Professor Gurumukh Nihal Singh, who had been §
taking keen interest in his career suggested him to join thé
London School of Economics (LSE) for further studies, and §
gladly made necessary arrangements for his stay at U.K. He left §
India in the same year and registered himself as an M.Sc. student
at LSE. The academic atmosphere of LSE in those days was §&
charged with intense intellectual activity and excitement. Prof. §
Hayek had just arrived at the LSE and was presenting the ff
Austrian Theory of Capital and business cycles to the English §&
speaking world for the first time. Simultaneously, an acute con- &
troversy and debate had started around Keynes’s “Treatise on &
Money”. This was both a challenge and a promise for Prof. F
Shenoy. As a student at B.H.U. he had already developed a ¥
strong fascination for pure theory and had acquired a good deal
of intellectual capacity for abstract analysis, and theorising. 7
Consequently, instead of working on some applied problem—which \
was the usual practice for most of the Indian scholars and stu- o
dents of that petiod-he chose to concentrate on the study of ||
monetary and capital theory. He deeply immersed himself in the . a)
study of these subjécts and published his first paper, “An Equa- | |
tion for the Price-Level of New Investment Goods”, in Quarterly
Journal of Economics (1931). The paper arose out of his dissatis- | |
faction with Keynes’s treatment of the price-level of new investment —_ |
goods in the ‘Fundamental Equations” of Treatise. In Professor | |
Shenoy’s view Keynes’s discussion merely showed uni: what j

i
. [ iii]
. e
conditions the Banking system may prevent a fall in the price—
level of investment goods, but it did not tackle the more funda-
mental issue of how the price-level of new investment goods
itself gets determined. Adhering to the terminological and
definitional frame of the Treatise, he supplemented its system of
Fundamental Equations by an additional equation, and attempted
to show how the system can yield a determinate solution for
the price-level of new investment goods. Subsequently, he published
another paper ‘‘Interdependence of Price Levels,” again in
Quarterly Journal of Economics (1933), wherein he presented
further important results appertaining to this issue.

These two papers were received as important contributions
to the field and established him as a promising young monetary
economist within the profession. To the best of our knowledge,
he was the first Indian economist, whose theoretical papers were
published in a world-class Journal.

During the same period, Prof. Shenoy also acquired consider-
able interest in the wider problems of social philosophy and
methodology. In this connection, his ideas came to be strongly
influenced by Hayekian liberalism and throughout the rest of his
life, as an economist as well as a social philsopher and critic,
he remained a fiercely uncompromising liberal.

After receiving his M. Sc. degree in 1932 from the University
of London, Prof. Shenoy came back to India and for sometime
worked asa Lecturer in Wadia College (Pune) and Gujarat College
(Ahmedabad). In 1936, he again left India and joined the Uni-
veristy of Ceylonas a Lecturer in Economics. His stay in Ceylon _
turned out to be important for him from the professional as
well as from the personal point of view. For it was in Ceylon
that his marriage took place with Ansuya Kamath, who proved
to be an inexhaustible source of inspiration, support and counsel
for him throughout his life. On the professional plane also, it
was in Ceylon that he got his first direct experience of working
in Government and Public bodies. He was appointed as a
Member, Board of Comissioners of Currency, in 1940 and also
occupied the position of economic adviser to the Department of
Commerce and Industry of the Ceylonese Government. His active
association with the Board of Currency and Department of

. [iv] .
Commerce, enabled him to acquire a considerable knowledge of
financial and industrial practices and institutions. The practical
experiences he thus acquired sharpened his understanding of
economic phenomena and led him to view theoretical analysis in a
more meaningful perspective. This is reflected in his first technical

‘monograph - “Ceylon Currency and Banking” — published in
1941. Various subsequent reviews of the book regarded it as
an exemplary piece of applied work for its fine blending of
institutional details and theoretical analysis.

In 1942, Prof. Shenoy came back to India to become the
Principal of L. D. Arts College (Ahmedabad) which at that time
was considered to be one of the prestigious colleges of the cou-
ntry- The College was founded by the Ahmedabad Education
Society with nationalist spirit and zeal and had an enviable record |
of having some eminent scholars of the country on its staff list.
He stayed with the L. D. Arts College for three years and be-
fore he left it to join the Reserve Bank of India in 1945, he
published in a small book form, a critique of the celebrated
“Bombay Plan’’.

From 1945 to 1953 ~a period of almost a decade — he
remained with the Reserve Bank of India; and held various
important positions in the Bank. He was the Director of Rural
Economics and Director of Monetary Research from 1945 to
1946. For one year (1949-50), he acted as a nominated member
of the Board of Directors of the Bombay Bullion Exchange. In
1948, he become the Far Eastern Representative of the Interna-
tional Monetary Fund and subsequently for two years (1951-53),
he acted as an alternate Executive Director of the International
Monetary Fund and the World Bank. ’

In terms of intellectual and professional accomplishments,
the ten years that he spent with the Reserve Bank of India can
be regarded as a very fruitful period of his life. Going by the
usual hierarchical rules of the R.B.I. he was not very far away
from the Governorship of the Bank. On the other hand, besides
a number of technical articles and notes in the R.B.I. Bulletins,
he had published in 1948 one of his widely acclaimed books,
“The Sterling Assets of the Reserve Bank of India’’, which he

. a
{v]
had completed before he joined the Reserve Bank of India.*
Moreover, he pursued his interests in capital theory and contri-
buted two important papers related with the analysis of saving
/ and capital in a monetary economy. In these papers, he gave a °
| lucid and authoritative exposition of Austrian theory of capital
and discussed some important related issues.**
| In 1954, he left the Reserve Bank of India and joined the
Gujarat University, to become the first Director of its newly
established School of Social Sciences. Although he was holding
a position of substantial status at the R.B.I. he accepted the
University invitation because of the attraction for greater acade-
mic freedom which the university position promised, and also
| because of his love for teaching.

The time of his joining the Gujarat University marked the
beginning of his life as a lone advocate of liberal economic order
and a critic of Indian Planning. By training and by conviction he
was an economist of the liberal tradition and quite naturally he
found himself in a major disagreement with ‘“mainstream’’ view
of development planning. He was seriously apprehensive of the
development strategy adopted in the Second Plan. He considered
that the strategy in its heavy reliance on deficit financing for
meeting the resource requirements of the:contemplated ambitious
investment programmes was permanently committing the country
to a regime of inflation and controls. In his view, a genuine and
long-term committment to the policy of maintaining monetary
and price-stability was essential part of a truly growth-oriented
strategy. Furthermore, Indian planning in its emphasis on the
development of highly capital-intensive goods industries, was
imposing on the economy a programme of large-scale transfer
of resources from agriculture and other sectors to low-return

ing reigned—there the ordinary man was in political fetters,

of much hope for the future or of any conception of controll-~
ing his own destiny. The state might prosper and accomplish.

The importance of ideas and the intellectual climate was

There is a remarkable parallel between Japan at the time
of the Meiji restoration and India at the achievement of
independence eight decades later in 1948. In both cases, a major
political change and upheaval broke “‘the cake of custom” and
permitted.a drastic alteration in economic arrangements and in
the rigid class relations among men. In both cases, the political
change placed in power a group of able and patriotic men who
were determined to convert prior economic stagnation into
rapid economic progress-though for somewhat different objectives.
In both cases, these events occurred in countries with ancient
cultures and a high artistic and literary civilization. In both
cases, the countries were technologically far behind the leading
economic powers of the time. Both had an opportunity to
make major economic gains by adopting and adapting techniques
developed at great cost in the West, without the need to create
them anew. ‘

There were also, of course, differences—mostly favoring India.
India’s physical resources are distinctly superior to Japan’s,

except only for the sea round Japan, with its easy transportition
and potential supply of food. Japan had been almost completely

did it ever try to control the total amount or direction of

_ investment or the structure of output. It sold off most of its
pilot plants to private firms within a few years. The state
maintained a large interest only in ship—building and iron and

Steel industries that it deemed necessary to build military power.

It retained even these industries only because they were not
attractive to private enterprise and required heavy government
subsidies. These subsidies were a drain on Japanese resources.

They impeded rather than stimulated Japanese economic
progress. Finally, by international treaty, Japan was prohibited
during the first three decades after the Meiji restoration from
imposing tariffs higher than 5 per cent. This restriction was an
unmitigated boon to Japan, though it was resented at the time.

India has followed a very different policy. Its leaders,
schooled in the doctrines of Fabian socialism and central plann-
ing, have regarded capitalism as synonymous with imperialism,
to be avoided at all costs. They took Russia as their model and
embarked on a series of five-year plans setting forth detailed
programs of investment allocated between government and
private firms, and among industries. Certain areas of produc-
tion are reserved to government. Tariffs, quotas, and subsidies
to exports are widely used to shape foreign trade. When
exchange difficulties arose, detailed and extensive exchange control
was imposed. The Indian government controls wages and prices,
prohibits private enterprises from building factories or making
other investments without government permits, and levies taxes
that are highly graduated on paper though largely evaded in

i practice. .

Reliance on the market in Japan released hidden and unsus-
pected resources of energy and ingenuity, prevented vested
interests from impeding change, and forced development to

| conform to the harsh test’ of efficiency. Reliance on governmental
| controls in India frustrates initiative, or diverts it into wasteful

j channels, protects vested interests from the forces of change,
and substitutes bureaucratic approval for market efficiency as
the criterion of survival.

The difference in policies is a remarkable tribute to the
force of ideas and the importance of the intellectual climate of
opinion. The men who took charge of Japan in 1867 were

dedicated to strengthening the power and glory of their country.
They attached no special value to individual freedom or political
. liberty; on the contrary, they believed in aristocracy and
political control by an elite. Then men who took charge of India
in 1948 had very different ideas. They were ardently devoted to
, ‘ political freedom, personal liberty, and democracy. Their aim
. was not national power and glory but improvement in the eco-
nomic condition of the masses. Yet the Japanese leaders adopted
a liberal economic policy that produced a major widening of
opportunities for the masses and a great gain in their personal
liberty while the Indian leaders adopted a collectivist economic
policy that hamstrung their people with restrictions, undermined
the large measure of individual freedom and political liberty

built up by the British, and led to the recent dictatorship.

The difference in policies followed reflects faithfully the
intellectual climate of the two eras. In the mid-nineteenth
century, liberalism was the dominant view. It was simply taken
for granted that a modern economy should be conducted by
free trade and private enterprise. It probably never occurred to
the Japanese leaders to follow any other course. In the mid-
twentieth century, collectivism was the dominant view. It was
simply taken for granced that a modern economy should be

' .conducted by centralized planning and five-year plans. It pro-
bably never occurred to the Indian leaders to follow any other
course.

Ideas can for a time lead a life of their own, independent
of reality. But sooner or later, they meet the test of evidence.
The fate of mankind hinges on this test coming soon. If the
collectivist ideas so sharply in conflict with the facts con-
tinue in the ascendancy, they will doom mankind toa renewed
era of tyranny and misery. The brief periods of freedom and
affluence will be overwhelmed.

THE OUTLOOK FOR WORLD INFLATION
Henry Hazlitt

This essay in honor of the late Professor Shenoy is being
written in September 1978. My choice of topic may seem a
strange one. It may be reasonably safe, the reader may concede,
to discuss the outlook for inflation in, say, a monthly maga-
zine, but in a book may it not be very quickly outdated—
perhaps even by the time the book appears in print ?

I hasten to assure the reader that though some of my fore-
casts may take a short-term view, and though most of my
specific illustrations are based on what has happened or is
likely to happen in the United States, I have attempted through-
out to look at the problem from a worldwide perspective,
and to look especially at the kind of political forces which,
always and everywhere, tend to bring about an inflation or
continue one.

. It is amazing how many Americans still talk as if their
_ inflation hed developed comparatively recently, in the last few
years, and as if it were a problem largely confined to their
own country. The truthis that the American inflation is already

very old, and that inflation is now worldwide.

For the first time in the history of the world, practically
every country is on a paper money basis. And practically every

a

-country is inflating. It is instructive to recall how this has:
-come about. — :
For a full explanation, we must go back at least 64 years
‘to the outbreak of World War I in 1914. The first thing that
“happened, almost on the day the war broke out, was that the
‘belligerents suspended the convertibility of their currencies
<into gold.
It is important to.remember why they did this. They did
‘not do it because they suddenly discovered that gold was out
 rof date, that is why a “barbarous relic”, that a paper standard
-was altogether more modern, efficient, and scientific. They did
“it, on the contrary, because gold had suddenly become in their
‘  .eyes too valuable. It was a precious war resource. The bellige-
“rent governments knew they would need it to buy arms and
“good from neutrals abroad, and that gold was the only currency
‘other countries would readily accept. They found this out very
“quickly. England, for example, declared war on Germany on
.August 4. A run developed on the Bank of England. The gold
“reserve, which had been 38.6 million in July, was pulled down
‘within a few days to 26 million. Convertibiliry was suspended on
-August 5. In addition, export controls were imposed on gold.
When the First World War ended, some of the belligerents
-went back to the gold standard. England again is the outstand-
-ing example of the problems of doing this and of the mistakes
‘that were made. Resumption of gold payments was under-
‘taken — at the pre-war rate for the pound — in 1925. But two
‘greatly changed circumstances were overlooked. First, there
“had been an enormous expansion meanwhile in the issuance of
‘British currency and credit — that is, in the amount of paper .
“promises that people might want to convert into gold. And
:second, as a résult of that, prices had risen substantially. If ,
“in 1925 the currency had been made convertible only at a corres-
‘pondingly higher “price” for gold. the resumption of gold
“payments might have worked. But the resumption at the old
‘rate made gold too much of a bargain, and forced a contraction
-of British credit and a fall in prices.
In September, 1931, England went off the gold standard
«once again. The U. S. likewise abandoned the gold standard,

?
at its old rate of $20.67 an ounce, in 1933. Unfortunately, . it
was not the war and post-war inflations in both countries that
‘ were blamed for this result, or the ill-advised. retention of the-
old gold-conversion rates, but the gold standard - itself.

When the Second World War broke out, in September:
1939, many of the world’s currencies were again thrown into.
chaos, and for substantially the same reasons as in World
War I. But this time, before the war had even ended in May,
1945, the representatives of some 43 nations were invited by”
the United States to a conference at Bretton Woods, New
Hampshire, to try to set up a new international currency system.

What they set up, under the leadership of Lord Keynes of”
England and Harry Dexter White of the United States, was a com-- _
promise designed to please the advocates of paper money,

flexibility”, and ‘national independence” of currencies, but at.
the same time to reassure conservatives that these currencies
would retain a “link”? to gold. The supposed great merit of
the new system was that the monetary role of gold — the:
“tyranny” of gold — would be drastically reduced.

Only one currency, the U.S. dollar, would have to be
convertible into gold —and even then no longer at the demand
of anybody who held dollars, but only at the request of”
foreign central banks. All the other currencies were to be kept
convertible merely into the dollar. With the dollar anchored
to gold, and all the other currencies tied to the dollar, stabi--
lity was to be assured, and the need for gold reserves to be-
minimized.

The system seemed to relieve every other countfy but the-
United States: from strict monetary discipline. If any country
got into trouble, it was assured almost automatic loans and
credit to bail it our. The agreement also provided that any-
nation could at any time devalue its currency by upto 10 per
cent, and explicitly stipulated that “the Fund shall raise no-
objection.’? The real but unstated and unacknowledged purpose -
of the Bretton Woods Agreements, as the present writer~-
pointed out at the time (in The American Scholar, Winter-

1944-45) was “to make resort to inflation easy, smooth, and.
above all respectable.”

. As early as 1949 the system started to break dowzn. The-

were devalued by similar percentages within the following week.
The Swiss franc incidentally, was one of these. In succeeding:
years there were literally hundreds of devaluations of currencies .
in the Fund.

What had been overlooked from the beginning was:
the enormous increase in the burden and_ responsibility that:
‘the Bretton Woods arrangements put upon the United States..
For the other countries could hold dollar reserves on the-
assumption that this was just as good as holding gold. But:

- their currency stability was, in fact, made dependent on the:
soundness of the dollar.

Yet successive U.S. governments remained completely-
oblivious of the gravity of the responsibility we had assumed. .
Our officials kept undermining the dollar — by foreign aid, huge -
domestic spending, chronic and mounting budget deficits, and‘
by pushing down domestic interest rates and increasing the:
money supply. By 1968 we had practically ceased keeping the: ‘
dollar convertible into gold, even for central banks. And on:

Our repudiation of our solemn commitment was followed’
by mounting inflation, . devaluations, and monetary demorali-
zation everywhere. There seemed no Jonger any point in maine-
taining fixed exchange rates. There was not even any agreement.
on what they could be fixed to.

Now let’s go back a little and look at the long and dismal:
record of international inflation. I am going to begin, arbitrarily, .
not with 1914, but thirty two years ago, with 1946. That is-_
in one respect a good year to start with, for the International
Monetary Fund had been set up on paper, as we have seen, in.

1944, but it was not till 1946 that it opened for business. We-
can trace the international record very well, because the Citi--
bank of New York has kept tabs on it in its monthly letter -
over these thirty-two years.

From 1956 to 1966 the annual rate of depreciation in 45

We come now to the five-year period from 1965 to 1970.
“The median rate of depreciation of 50 currencies during this
‘period was 4.3 per cent a year. In the five-year period from

1970 to 1975, however, the median annual rate of depreciation
-for the 50 currencies was 9.4 per cent.

The Chilean and Argentine pesos, incidentally, each lost

«Chilean peso suffered an average depreciation during the five

The U.S. dollar depreciated an average of 4.1 per cent a

-.a@ year in 1970 to 1975 period. The current rate of depre-
ciation is 11.4 per cent a year. From 1940 to the present, the
- dollar has lost 78 per cent of its purchasing power. Put another
way, compared with 1940 the dollar is worth only 22 cents.

So that’s the past record. Now let’s see how and why this
-inflation has been going on, nationally and internationally. I
“have already brought this story up from the outbreak of World

War I in 1914 to the American abandonment of gold conver-
-tibility of the dollar in August 15, 1971. This, as I have pointed
- out, not only set an example in itself demoralizing, but it left
-no fixed standard for other currencies to hook themselves on to.

. (I should like to point out here that the Special Drawing
* Rights—SDRs—issued by the International Monetary Fund, had
-never been directly convertible into gold, and they were quickly

But the American desertion of gold convertibility in 1971'
was, of course, merely an additional cause of a worldwide:
inflation that had been going on ever since the outbreak of:
World War II. That inflation started when the governments:
directly involved had to increase their budget expenditures at
almost any cost in order to prosecute the war. But when the war
was over, they did not prudently return to their previous level!
of expenditures. They had also enormously increased their tax:
revenues, even if not proportionately totheir war expenditures,.
and instead of cutting taxes back to previous peacetime levels,.
they increased or added all sorts of “welfare” measures—mainly:
vote-buying hand-outs to pressure groups—to make use of the:
_ mew revenues. What no one sufficiently realized was that once:
these welfare measures were established, it would come to be.
regarded as political suicide by the politicians in power to.
attempt to cut them off or even diminish them.

There has been still a third reason for the increasingly:
wide-spread inflation in recent years. The Bretton Woods Agree-.
ments. as we have seen, gave explicit sanction to devaluation—
provided it did not exceed 10 per cent in any single step. There-
is still a fixed belief on the part of most inflationists that-
devaluation or depreciation of the national currency on the.
foreign—exchange market stimulates exports, discourages imports, .
and helps restore the balance of trade. This is a fallacy and an,
illusion. Exports are stimulated only because there is a tem--
porary drop in their net cost to foreigners. This drop occurs.
because the dollar, say, has fallen abroad faster than our domes- -
tic prices have risen. But domestic prices soon catch up, and~
the so-called stimulus is short-lived.

This is what tends to happen when traders assume that -
what has taken place is once-for-all devaluation. But the effect -
of a long-continued depreciation may be the exact opposite :
it may help to bring about an “unfavorable” balance of trade. .
This appears to be the result at present in the United States.
The reason for this is that depreciation of a currency over a .
long period—because of internal inflation—can lead to the
expectation that the depreciation will continue. When the dollar -
has fallen in the foreign exchange market, for example, and:

“internal prices have not. yet risen enough to offset that external
-depreciation, American goods become more of a bargain than -
before. But foreigners suspect that the dollar may fall still
‘lower next month or the month after, and that they will get
-still greater bargains in American goods by postponing their
purchases. Americans, conversely, fearing that the dollar may
‘be worth still less in the future in terms of foreign currencies,
-may rush to buy foreign goods to avoid paying still higher
-dollar prices for imports in the future.

In any case, the whole process of external depreciation of

‘its currency makes a country poorer on net balance, not
richer. To the extent that its imports are in facc discouraged,
-it is because its nationals can no longer afford them. Their
price jumps on the very day that their currency declines, and
-to the exact extent that it declines. A country with a depre-
-ciating currency is worse off in terms of its ability to buy the
-commodities it needs. It is selling abroad too cheap and buying
-from abroad too dear. All deliberate devaluation does is to
: accelerate domestic inflation. The few who gain on net balance

gain at the expense of all the rest.

There has been still a fourth major reason for worldwide
inflation. This is the fixed idea that inflation is necessary to-
“prevent or reduce unemployment. To the extent that there is
-any truth in this, it is true only for one reason: As long as
-the special legal immunities and privileges now granted to labour

unions in most countries enable those unions to exact wage—
rates higher than the existing market can sustain, more inflation-
higher prices—will seem necessary to make the higher wage-rates _
- payable. Orherwise—as I have shown elsewhere—the belief in the
-necessity for inflation as a remedy for unemployment has no
‘teal basis.

Lord Keynes gets perhaps too much credit—or blame—as the
-inventor of this myth. When his General Theory of Employment,
‘Interest, and Money appeared in 1936, the American government,
-for one, had already been following policies of uninterrupted

deficit spending for six fiscal years. Keynes’s theories simply
=supplied a more elaborate rationale to justify -what politicians

chad alteady been doing. But his authority and prestige prolonged
-and intensified the disease.

‘What, now, is the outlook for the future? I can see now
“nothing to end the inflation, either nationally or internationally.
It is almost impossible to see anything but a continuance of
inflation everywhere, and for the most part at an accelerative rate. >

It cannot be emphasized too often that there is nothing
‘mysterious about inflation, in spite of the efforts of politicians
-and some befuddled economists to make it seem so. Inflation,
-always and everywhere, is brought about by government policy—
‘sometimes by acts of omission, but mainly by deliberate acts
of commission. It is brought about by excessive government
spending, by chronic deficits, and by the printing of excessive

amounts of paper money to pay for the deficits. Inflation is the
‘issuance of too much money and credit. There is no real economic

, ‘ problem about inflation. There is only a political problem. But
that political problem is tremendous, and all but insoluble.

For the great bulk of the spending today, in nearly all inflating
countries, is on handouts to special pressure groups. And once
these handouts have been started and have become established,
under whatever name—food stamps, relief, Medicaid, unemploy-
ment insurance, job creation, revenue sharing, veterans’ aid,
Medicare, Social Security, subsidies of any kind—they come to
be regarded as a right .by their recipients. It is considered to
be an act of political suicide for any officeholder to suggest
abolishing them, or reducing them, or even preventing or slowing
down any further increage.

In fact, once budget deficits come to be tolerated and
accepted, their inevitable tendency seems to be to grow
acceleratively. :

Let me give you just one illustration. The United States
first started to run chronic deficits in the fiscal year 1931. In
the five’ fiscal years 1931 to 1935 inclusive, average Federal
expenditures were $5.2 billion-a year. In the same period the
average deficit was $2.4 billion a year. Let’s skip now to the
five fiscal. years 1975 to 1979 inclusive. (Of course fiscal year
1979. has just begun, but its expenditures and deficit are already

officially planned.) As spent and planned, the average deficit for
those five years comes to $56 billion a year. This is 23 times:
‘the average deficit in the 1931-35 period. In fact, the deficit:
alone is eleven times the total average expenditures in the:
1931-35 period. When we come to the average annual expenditures. -
made or planned for the 1975 to 1979 period, they are
$411 billion a year — about 80 times the expenditure in the-
1931-35 period.

Let’s remind ourselves that we can explain only a very’
minor part of this by the reduced purchasing power of the dollar
in the later period, for each dollar still buys about a fifth as
much as it did in 1931 to 1935. Even if we divide 80 by 5,
we find that expenditures are 16 times as great in a single
year, even in real purchasing power, as they were in the early;
thirties. ,

But worse still, many of our present officeholders in the
administration and in Congress do not regard even this. new:
level of expenditures as nearly enough. They tell us that some-

thing more ‘‘stimulative’—i.e. something more inflationary—-
is needed. Whoily apart from such proposals, we already have-
in prospect record-breaking deficits of $61.8 billion for the-
fiscal year 1978, and $60.6 billion for fiscal year 1979. ( The:
President’s Budget Message for the fiscal year 1979 ). Even these-
official estimates greatly understate reality. Washington has-
developed a new  sstatistical trick—called off-budget outlays..

, When these are counted, the estimated total expenditures for-
fiscal year 1979 are not a mere $500 billion, but $513 billion, and:
the total estimated deficit rises to $73 billion. In addition,.
every once in a while the President may casually ask Congress.
to appropriate a couple of billions more for something. .

Now we come to the problem, what can the individual do
about it? I am not going to try to answer that in detail. ( There
are now in existence, of course, scores of professional services.
which offer such detailed advice.) But I do want to remind the:
reader of some general principles. Authors have been writing:
books in the last few years implying that any individual cannot
merely protect himself in full against the ravages of a severe:
and prolonged inflation, but even that such an inflation offers.

him a special opportunity, not offered bya stable currenéy, for
him. to become: rich. This is just not so. It is true tNat any
individual, considered in isolation—if he is very smart,’ very
alert, and very lucky—may not only be able fully to protect
himself in a severe inflation, but make a fortune out of it. But °
such individuals must necessarily be in a small minority. And
the more severe the inflation, the smaller that minority. Hein-
tich Mann, the famous writer, who lived through the great
German inflation of 1919 to 1923, later declared that none of
his friends, nor even anyone of his direct acquaintance, came
out of that inflation whole. Most of them suffered devastating
losses. ,

’ Let us recall why this is necessarily so. Inflation is a form
of tax. It is a tax levied to pay for a deficit. If the government
prints money to finance a deficit of $70 billion say, then the
rest of us must be paying this $70 billion. Collectively, we have
to forego the equivalent of this $70 billion in goods, services,
or savings. .

A few of us, if we invest shrewdly, and are also lucky, may
escape our proportional share of the payment; but if we do,
we must do it at the expense of somebody else. Those of us
who invest in the right thing at the right time, at the right
price, may achieve a paper profit and escape a real loss, but
we do so by putting up the price for the next buyer, and reduce
ing his opportunities. Every man’s ‘profit from inflation must
increase the proportionate loss of somebody else.

There is a further factor, which also insures that the real
gainers from a serious inflation can be only a small minority.
When a country gets into a hyper-inflation, it becomes more
and more difficult, if not impossible, for the individual producer
to estimate or guess what his future costs and selling prices are
going to be, and what will be the relationship between the two.
It becomes increasingly difficult, in short, for industry to plan,
ahead. Therefore firms everywhere will find themselves producing.
the wrong quantities of the wrong things. There will be great:
waste; there will be increasing misdirection and disorganization,
of output. This is another way of saying that in spite of what.

may be an appearance of- feverish activity, the country as a

whole will be getting poorer than it would under non—inflatio-

nary conditions.

‘What this means is that as inflation gets worse there will

going to earn in the months ahead, and this uncertainty will

nation for the poor performance of the American stock market

The truth is that the cards are stacked today, as never
before, and in almost every country, against all of us who are

prices, the constant commissions, the. taxpayers of every

progressive income tax, and in some countries are forced to pay
formidable ‘‘capital-gains’’ taxes on non-existent gains.

So even those few who have been hither to successful in their
hedges against inflation cannot afford to be smug about it. It
is in the long-run interest of every one of us, in every inflating

. nation, to work to bring the inflation to a halt as soon as
possible.

As mentioned earlier, the critics of the liberal inter-
national economic order accept the Prebisch-Singer theory of the
secular tendency of the terms of trade to deteriorate -for the
LDCs. They rightly regard this deterioration as essential for
their case because without it the thesis of the failure of pros-

hardly be upheld. In other words, a failure of DC growth to
benefit the LDCs would have to reveal itself in a change in
the terms of trade against the LDCs.
It is hardly necessary to discuss why there is a strong pre-
sumption that DC growth will spread to the LDCs. For Classi-
cal as well as Keynesian economics, in rare harmony, teach
that the demand of the DCs for the exports of the LDCs will
strengthen when DC GNP grows; in other words, that the |
marginal propensity to import is positive (barring the most.
unlikely case that DC imports largely consist of inferior goods,
the Giffen case). It is, of course, possible and it often happens.
that DC progress takes a form of reducing demand for parti-
cular imports from LDCs: Synthetics take the place of natural
materials, rayon replaces silk, nylon substitutes for jute and
synthetic rubber reduces the demand for natural rubber. Such
cases have been often cited to help explain the alleged secular
change in the terms of trade agajnst the LDCs.? Individual
industries may suffer from technological discoveries and changes

1. The Changing Mood : From Optimism to Gloom :

The comparatively optimistic appraisal of the world economy,
including the LDCs, will perhaps not be strongly challenged as far
as the first quarter century after the second World War is con-
cerned, although it runs counter to the voices of gloom that
have been emanating from ECLA, UNCTAD, and the chorus of _
supporting voices in the DCs. How about the last four or five
years ? Has not the world recession of 1973-75, the somewhat
sluggish recovery, chronic unemployment, stagflation and the |
breakdown of the Bretton Woods system given the lie to the |
rosy optimism of the 1950s and 1960s ?

The general mood in the industrial countries has certainly
changed since 1973 or so. Optimism has given way to pessimism
and doubt, and the prophets of doom for the third world find
themselves confirmed in their gloomy convictions.

Two major industrial countries, Britain and Italy still suffer

But it must be stressed agian that both in Europe and the

The Fundamental Theorem of Time Series Analysis states
that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the power
spectrum and the autocovariance function (and, similarly, between
the spectral density and the auto-correlation function ) of stoc-
hastic process, since each pair of functions forms a Fourier
transform pair.

Comparison of Autocovariance Function and Power Spectrum

Thus, the Fundamental Theorem of Time Series Analysis
states that knowledge of either one of the autocovariance and
power spectral functions entails knowledge of the other. There
are two main reasons that make it preferable to study the
spectral density in the frequency domain rather than in the
time domain using the autocovariance :

1. The spectral function describes a covariance stationary
process in terms of additive contributions to the variance of the
process of a set of uncorrelated frequency components. In
contrast, the value of J, of the autocovariance function is a
weighted sum of its values at /,, ég,......where Jy, lg,....<l,
and ly is a linear combination of /,, l,,......

The power spectral function thus gives us information as
to the relative importance of the contributions of the different
cyclical movements which have generated the observed time —
series, while the autocovariance function does not.

2. Whereas consistent estimates of the power spectral func-
tion can be made, the sampling distribution of the autocovariance
function is unstable. ,

The ideas of spectral analysis of a single time series are
thus extended to the cross-spectral analysis of two covariance—
stationary time series. This extension is based on a theorem
demonstrating that not only is each frequency component of
one time series independent of all the other frequency components

- of the series, but it is also independent of all such components
of another stationary series except for the letter’s component
that corresponds to the same given frequency.}4 :

The following measures of the association of the frequency
components of two processes ate central in cross-spectral
analysis :

(1) Coherence C(w). It can be shown that o = C(w) =|.
C (w) is analogous to the square of the correlation coefficient.
between two time series. The greater C (w) is the closer is the
association between the two series at frequency .

(2) Phase difference, ¢ (w). The phase difference between the
frequency components of the two series measures the extent to
which at each particular frequency the cyclical movement of
one series leads, coincides with, or lags the corresponding cyclic '
movement of the second series. ;

In other words, cross spectral analysis reveals that (1) agri-
cultural price level exerts very great pressure on general prices and
(2) the general price level exerts very great pressure on the non-
agricultural prices. Indian economic policy recognizes these results
for a proper inflation control policy.

5. Conclusion

This paper represents the first attempt to apply spectral
techniques to Indian price data spanning 106 years. The results
are quite rewarding. Two principal conclusions emerge from the
study, one of theoretical value, and the other of policy use. The
first, theoretical result, is that Indian price data too reveal that the
spectrum is of the Granger discovered “‘typical shape”, a mirrored
J shape. The second, policy result, is that in India agricultural prices
lead the general price level, and the general price level leads the
non-agricultural prices. Thus an inflation control policy which’
concentrates on stabilizing agricultural prices alone can simultan-
eously control general and non-agricultural prices. A policy that
fails to influence the agricultural prices thus will fail to control
any prices in India irrespective of how much development planning :
textbook support there may be, to argue otherwise. Ironically, the
last 30 years of Indian planning and inflation experiences have
failed to persuade the Government of India of its errors, and I
don’t suspect spectral analysis will fare any better.

“In the progress of the manufacture, not only the number

of profits increase, but every subsequent profit is greater

than the foregoing; because the capital from which it is derived:

must always be greater. The capital which employs the weavers,

for example, must be greater than that which employs the

spinners; because it not only replaces that capital with its

profits, but pays, besides, the wages of the weavers; and the
profit must always bear some proportion to the capital.’

In this passage from The Wealth of Nations Adam Smith
makes two related errors. One of them has been noted by several
commentators; the other seems to have gone without comment,
possibly because the combination of the two errors makes it some-
what difficult to understand the argument Smith was trying to
make, and so to see what is wrong with it. I will therefore begin
by explaining what I believe that argument is, and why it is wrong.

The Argument
A farmer grows flax. His capital consists of advances—pay-
| ments for seed, wages, fodder, etc.-that must be made before
, the crop is sold, and that must be recovered, with profits, from
| the payment he receives when he sells it. The flax is purchased
| by an entrepreneur who will employ spinners to convert it into

the farmer sells the flax to him, that part of his advance must: 7” |

The total advances of the entrepreneur must then be larger than.
the total advances of the farmer, and, by the same argument,.

Smith here makes the common error of forgetting time, and.
so confusing a stock with a flow. The total capital required at
each stage depends not only on the amouut of the advances,
but on the length of time for which they must be made. If flax.
is harvested once a year and the advances are made, on average,.
uniformly during the year, then the average amount of capital.
required by the farmer is half the total amount of the advances. |
If the spinner buys flax from the farmer, spins it into thread,. I
and sells it a month after he buys it, then the average amount ,
of capital he requires is one twelfth the amount for which he- !
buys the flax, plus an appropriate fraction of his other advances. ;
If the weaver is working on tapestries which require ten years.

to provide the advances that “replace” the advances of the- /

To avoid confusion, one must note that time enters argu-- ;

payments must be larger than the total of his advances in order:
to provide him with a profit. The total of these payments is a.
part of the total of the advances made by the spinner over the
course of the year. The weaver must buy, each year, as much.
thread as the spinner sells each year, hence his annual payments, .

The neglect of fixed capital is, in context, the less interesting
and less important of the two errors; indeed it is scarcely an error
at all. The passage occurs, early in Book I, and fixed capital is
not introduced until Book II, more than two hundred pages later;
it seems only reasonable to allow Smith, like any modern author,

to begin with a simple model and only later introduce additional D

complexities. When he does discuss fixed capital, Smith explicitly

states that “The far greater part of the capital of all such master
artificers, however, is circulated, either in the wages of their
| workmen, or in the price of their materials, and repaid with a
profit by the price of the work.’® So the factor he ignores has
not only not yet been introduced-it is relatively small in any case.
The confusion between a stock and a flow, on the other hand,
makes the analysis wrong within its own context. Both Cannan
and Hollander comment elsewhere on errors of the same!® sort; it
seems a pity that neither one identified, in his analysis of this
passage, the same error.

PART A

The equilibrium conditions and price rigidity hypothesis in
connection with the Sweezian kinky oligopoly demand curve
may be stated as follows :
In a situation where:

(a) there is oligopoly in an industry;

(b) firms maximise their current profits;

(c) a particular entrepreneur conjectures the reactions of his
rivals but does not think that others conjecture his own
reactions; and

“(d) there is a uniform price ruling in the market at the start
of the analysis;

then there exists a kink in the demand curve of a firm
which leads to a discontinuity in the corresponding marginal
revenue curve.

1. In such a situation if the marginal cost (MC) curve of

Price Rigidity

2. If costs increase by a small amount, demand being unaltered,
then the MC curve continues to pass through the discontinuity
in the MR curve, thus making no change in the price. .

PART B.
General Excess Capacity
Let us start by taking an oligopolist operating under
conditions of a trade depression. There will thus be a lot of
excess capacity in his firm as well as in his rivals’ firms. There
is a certain price at which he is, at any moment, operating,
which may be called the current price. The current price
happens to be his price at a particular moment of time. This
price is the nucleus of all that is to follow. There is a demand
curve facing him; but this is probably unknown to him. In its
place he makes his own estimate of what the demand curve
facing him looks like, and his actions are governed by the
shape of his imagined demand curve. The imagined demand curve
shows the output demanded from him by the consumers if he
were to change his price from the level of the current price. In
estimating the shape of his imagined demand curve he reasons
as follows :

“In a situation of general excess capacity, like the present,
my rivals are in a mood to increase their sales, but not to
decrease them. Asa price cut increases their sales it will be
followed by the rest while a price rise would not be followed.

, “As a price cut will be followed, the price of the indus«
try will decrease, and the sales of all will rise, although
thereby leaving the relative share of each firm in the market
undisturbed. Thus an ordinary demand curve faces me when.
I cut my price.

encroach into my share of the market because others (not having

as given by Joan Robinson.!

that the MC curve continues to pass through the gap. In such a
case, it will be seen that the equilibrium will still remain at the
output directly underneath the kink and the price will remain at
the same level. This explains price rigidity in an excess capacity
situation and establishes proposition II (a) (i).

PART C.
General Limited Capacity

In the next step the state of general excess capacity may be
replaced by restricted capacity as is found in a boom or wartime
or an underdeveloped country. Here an oligopolist expects that his
rivals will now follow a price rise but nota price fall. The wings

' of the demand curve thus move upwards making it steeper above
the kink and flatter below the kink. The Margina 1 Cost has risen
from the slump to the boom but itis assumed that it still passes

However, during a boom, even if for a while the macro-

PART D
Change in Capacity

It finally remains to be seen whether there is any ground for-
believing that there will be price rigidity through a period of change °
in general capacity say either during a slump or a boom or a.
transition from one to the other.

It is important to bear in mind the initial assumption that.
the current price happens to be the price of the oligopolist at
the moment. The level of the initial current price is an external.
datum: it was given when the analysis started. It is in no sense
determined by the inter-action of the curves we have constructed:
later on. From this the only conclusion possible regarding the-
location of the kink is that the level of the kink will coincide
with whatever happens to be the current price. If the current price-
changes, the kink will now automatically be at the new current price
and on the same reasoning as previously the wings of the imagined”
demand curve will be built at the new kink.

George J. Stigler without assigning a convincing reason says ::
“it would be foolish to put a new kink’! at the new price..
In this statement he is forgetting the initial assumption namely-
that the kink is wherever the current price is. By this assumption.
it is no more foolish to find a kink at a new price than it was-
at the old current price. But we have seen that in an oligopoly- -
situation, given the requisite assumption about the working of the-
entrepreneur’s mind in regard to his expectation about his rivals’
reactions, there was some sense in the construction of the kinky-
demand curve at the old current price. There is, hence, the same
amount of sense in, finding a kink at the new level of the current™
price as existed at the time when a kink was discovered at the-
initial current price. It may further be noted that neither the-
economist nor the entrepreneur ‘‘puts’’ a kink deliberately at his.
current price as Professor Stigler thinks he does. A kink is not:
“put”; it is discovered to be there under the assumptions made of
rivals’ reactions. ,

The general price level is determined by macro-economic:
variables. From macro-economic analysis there is no reason to-
think that the price level in an oligopolistic industry will remain.
constant throughout the course of a trade cycle. If macro-economic :

It is thus seen that there is validity in the belief in the
existence of the kink in the Demand Curve under the assumptions:
stated in the beginning. But this is theoretically incapable of
providing an explanation of price rigidity because the hypothesis:

-conditions are unchanged gives any indication of the kink leading

Professor K. W. Rothschild,’ the answer may be that the oligo-

M. P. Bhatt:

Publication of the report prepared by SEVEN-Ol of Lodin.
for a Government Commission in Sweden in 1977, of the U. S..
Treasury’s “BLUEPRINT For Basie Tax Reform” in 1977, of the

This paper tries to examine the advisability and feasibility of
expenditure tax system either as substitute or supplement of the
existing Yt-system, from view point of equity, economic effects. |
and administrative aspects.

Equity Considerations :

Lately, it has been argued that a person’s ‘‘endowment” is.
the best indicator of ability-to-pay. The concept of Endowment
would include consumption (present and future), holding of wealth,

, One of the most repeated equity arguments in favour of
‘the expenditure tax is what is known as the ‘common pool”

‘to note that private inxestment no less than consumpion, is
a withdrawl from the pool. It is worng to say that income

‘Income tax taxes a person because he claims and receives a
‘reward for his services. Consider a business executive who is
-getting salary of Rs. 10,000 per month. When he obtains his
salary, he does not contribute his services, he sells it, i.e.

The argument under consideration may be re-worded as.
follows : An income tax taxes a person as he acquites a right to- —_
the share in the common pool and an expenditure tax taxes a
person as he exercises this right to the share in the common
pool. It is obvious that this amounts to nothing more than stat-
ing that an expenditure tax taxes expenditure and an income tax.
taxes income. The difference in timing of the tax payment is the-
whole problem as the principal difference between an expenditure ,
tax and an income tax is that an income tax taxes savings as they:
accrue but an expenditure tax taxes savings as they are spent.

For the majority of the people the choice between income-
tax and an expenditure tax would make very little difference. For :
most of us, our life-time consumption is likely to be equal to.
our life-time income. The taxation of consumption rather thar.
income would, therefore, but serve to shift the tax burden from
the middle age, when savings are usually at its peak, to youth and!
old age, when funds are usually being borrowed or assets drawn
down. In such a situation, the progressive rate of expenditure
tax, if measured against the income of such an individual, would:
be regressive.

Capital Gains :

One of the most crucial equity argument against existing:
income tax system is that it excludes capital gains and other
casual receipts from its base. As against this under Et capital.
gains if spent would automatically get taxed. However, it can.
be proved that as far as treatment of capital gains is concerned
there does not seem to be any significant difference between Yt:
which exempts the capital gains and an Et in which expenditure:
out of capital gains is subject to the tax. Let us assume that a
taxpayer has Rs. 100 taxable income. The rate of both taxes is.

110 LIBERALISM AND LDCS
50 per cent (gross), Assuming zero consumption (or fixed
«consumption) under an income tax, the taxpayer will have to pay
Rs. 50 immediately to the government. Therefore, his monetary
-savings will be equal to real saving (Rs. 50). Under an expendi-
ture tax monetary saving will be equal to Rs. 100 (assuming
* zero consumption) but real savings will be equal to Rs. 50. The
‘taxpayer can buy Rs. 100 worth of shares under an expenditure
tax and Rs. 50 worth of shares under an income tax. Now suppose
’ share prices double, then, capital gains will accrue. Under an
‘income tax the taxpayer will have Rs. 100 as capital gains (which
-is exempted). Under an expenditure tax, the taxpayer will have
-Rs. 200 worth monetary assets, including capital gains, but real
‘value of these assets (in terms of consumption goods) will be
sequal to Rs. 100. In other words, if two individuals one under
an income tax system and another under an expenditure tax
system, have the same pre-tax incomes, the same amount of
‘consumption, and if they invest their remaining savings and
tealize the same degree of capital gains, then, at the end, they
“will have the same real value of assets. This means that there is
: no real difference between an expenditure tax and an income
tax, as far as the capital gains are concerned.
Fluctuating Incomes :
Income tax creates inequities between stable and fluctuating
‘incomes —as under progressive rate, a person with a fluctuating
‘income will have to .pay a larger amount in tax. As compared
‘to this, a person receiving fluctuating income can without any
difficulty have a steady rate of expenditure, which is obviously
advantageous to the taxpayer unde the Et. However, under the
Et there is a corresponding disadvantage. Under an Yt a taxpayer
-can spend his wealth in any amount at any time without any tax
consequences. This privilege is not available under Et. Under Et. as
soon as he starts spending his wealth his total taxable expenditure
-will increase thus causing ‘fluctuating’ expenditure. Thus a person
will be better off under Et if the fluctuations in his expenditure
‘are less than the fluctuations in his income while persons with
constant income who have saved with the intention of dissaving
in the future will be better off under the Yt as compared to Et. _
It will be appreciated that the problem of fluctuating income
or expenditure is not inherent in the choice of the tax base.

‘The problem arises only because of the progressive tax rates.
| A suitable system of averaging the tax base over a_ period of
| time would reduce the otherwise higher tax liabilities of the
persons with fluctuating tax bases.
Gambling Gains : »

The existing Yt does not tax gambling gains while under Et
expenditure of gambling gains, like any other expenditure, will
be subject to.the tax. Mr. Kaldor maintains that “outlays on betting ;
and gambling is really a form of consumption......there is no
reason in equity for excluding this from chargeable expenditure.

Let us, however, consider the implications of Kaldor’s state-
ment. Assume that there are twenty persons who put down Rs. 10.
each, and agree that one person should get all the Rs. 200, the
lucky person being decided by a game of chance. Now, Kaldor’s
contention leads us to the following curious results: (i) When
each of the twenty persons puts down Rs. 10, he consumes it;
and then the lucky person can consume the whole of Rs. 200
all over again—a physical impossibility. (ii ) Ifa group of persons
Statt gambling and finish in such a manner that on balance none
of them has won or lost anything, then we have the startling
result that there has been no consumption. That is when you
loose something first, you consume it; if you subsequently win
the amount you have lost, what you have consumed somehow
reappears again—a physical impossibility. Alternatively, if you loose
Rs, 150, this amount should enter into chargeable expenditure, if |
ten minutes later you win back the Rs. 50, this amount should
be treated as any other receipt, because what you have consumed .
cannot reappear again. So, a person who on balance has neither
won nor lost anything should, on this view, pay a tax on his
aggregate (not net) losses. It seems highly doubtful that this view
of the tax base would be generally acceptable.

Effects on Savings :

Qut of the various claims of the favourable economic effects
of expenditure tax, the most widely accepted is that about its
favourable effects on savings. Careful theoretical analysis as well
as factual studies on the net impact of taxation on private savings
are inconclusive. Most of the arguments claiming favourable effects
on savings are based on partial micro-analysis, which seems to

112 LIBERALISM AND LDGS

have erred in exaggerating the inducement to save under the

expenditure tax. To the best of my knowledge, no effort has been

made to examine whether or not savings will be higher under an

expenditure tax than under income tax, within the framework of

: general equilibrium analysis. What is required is to make up a

- model and analyse the various functions to find out the direction

and change in the various variables when an expenditure tax is

substituted in place of an income tax. Savings in any economy

, would depend on several economic and non-economic factors,

such as level of income, rate of interest, tax rate, inflation and

motives to save, etc. In the absence of any direct evidence of

marginal propensity to save of different income classes, any con-

clusion about the impact of an expenditure taxon personal savings

would be highly conjectural. Further, in discussion on the effects

of taxes on savings, sufficient attention is not given to the changes

in the real value of income, savings and wealth which takes place

on. account of introduction of expenditure tax or changes in the

rate of expenditure tax. The introduction of expenditure tax or

increase in its rate will reduce the real value of income, savings

‘ and wealth. Normally, people will not accept any reduction in

the consumption level which they are accustomed to. If this is

so, the possibility is that the substitution of expenditure tax

in place of income tax would reduce saving. This is likely to

happen because with given income more funds would be needed

to maintain consumption in real terms, which are likely to be
diverted from that portion of income used for saving.!

Under the expenditure tax the real value of wealth is dependent
upon the tax rate. Under the income tax the real value of wealth
is independent of the tax rate. We assume the price level to be
constant. Since there is uncertainty regarding the future expenditure
tax rate, it follows that under the expenditure tax rate there is
uncertainty regarding the real value of wealth. Since the uncertainty
of the future income tax rate does not affect the real value of
wealth, we may say that there is more uncertainty under the
expenditure tax than under the income tax in this respect. Let us
elaborate this point and study its implications.

The uncertainty of the future expenditure tax rate implies |
the uncertainty of the real value of wealth. Wealth by definition
is the summation of savings from the beginning to the pzesent,
i.e. positive savings are additions to wealth. Uncertainty of the
real value of wealth implies the uncertainty of the real value of >
savings. Now since savings form a part of income, it follows
that under the expenditure tax, there is a greater uncertainty of
the real value of a part of the income than under the income
tax. It follows therefore that there is greater uncertainty of the
real value of a part of the reward a man obtains for his services
under the expenditure tax than under the income tax, the part
referred to is that part of the reward which he saves.

Now it could be argued that a similar uncertainty exists also
under the income tax. Under the existing income tax, certain
items are charged on the previous year basis; i.e. the taxpayer
this year pays these taxes on the relevant portion of last year’s
income at this year’s rates. So, there is a similar type of uncetainty
under the income tax, also. However, two points must be distinguished
between these two cases. Firstly, since the uncertainty under the
income tax arises because certain items are charged on a previous
year basis, the uncertainty involved is that the tax rate one year
hence may be different. Under the expenditure tax wealth
(accumulated savings) carries the uncertainty with it till it is spent,
i.e. the uncertainty involved is the uncertainty of the taxrate as
and when the accumulated savings are spent. The savings obviously
need not be spent one year after they were made, they could be
spent three or five or any number of years hence. Therefore, the
uneertainty involved is greater under the expenditure tax than
under the income tax.

Secondly, under the expenditure tax this type of uncertainty
is inherent and fundamental, while under the income tax it is
neither inherent nor fundamental. The uncertainty referred to
cannot be removed from the expenditure tax, except by taxing
the savings in the year in which they occur and not taxing them
subsequently, i.e. except by turning the expenditure tax into
an income tax.

What we have shown is thatthere is more uncertainty under
the expenditure tax than under the income tax. This does not
imply that there is no uncertainty under the income tax. Of

course, the whole world may be blown to bits in a nuclear war,
the real value of wealth under any conceivable tax will then be
zero; a total loss. The price level may go gallopping up or down,
. technological changes may affect various prices and asset values,
there is uncertainty regarding profits, balance of payments, etc.
The point here is that all these uncertainties are common to
both the taxes. Also, in some of the cases one can more or
less insure oneself against these uncertainties. For example, one
can buy common stock of incorporated companies and insure
onrself to some extent against the price level changes. One
can also insure against untimely death by buying a life annuity,
etc. However, the important point is that all these uncertainties
are common to both the taxes, while the uncertainty of the
real value of wealth due to the uncertainty of the future tax
rate is peculiar to the expenditure tax.
Effects on Investments ;

It is claimed by the advocates of Et that an economic
advantage of the Et is that, unlike Yt it does not discriminate
against tisky investment essentially because the Et does not
reduce the part of the reward for risk-taking that is saved.
Domar and Musgrave! have demonstrated that a proportional

‘income tax with full loss offset equally reduces investors’ risk
. and the reward for assuming risk.

Et as compared with Yt is supposed to encourage saving
mainly because for given interest rate, it increases the value of
interest income net of tax as compared to the inco ne-tax. We
can encourage savings under Yt by raising interest rate but this
would discourage investment. What Et attempts to do is to
increase intcrest income net of tax as compared to the Yt, for
a given interest rate. That is, on the basis of partial micro analy-
sis, the Et encourages savings without discouraging investment.
I believe thet some such mechanism i.e. increasing interest
income net of tax under Yt without discouraging investment
can be used within the framework of income tax. One

Work Incentives :

It is known fact that the gross rate of the expenditure tax
will be higher than the income tax rate to fulfill the condition
of equal yield; therefore a given amount of income will buy less
present consumption under the Et that under Yt. That is, leisure

}  felative to present consumption will be more expensive under
the Yt than under the Et. This situation causes the familiar dilemma
. Of two opposing effects on work incentives. Io the first place,
the return in terms of present consumption for sacrificing a unit
of leisure is lower under the Et than under the Yt, this would
indicate that less work will be done under the Et. Secondly,
because of the very fact that the value of present consumption
is reduced under Et, the tax payer may well increase their work
input : i.e. reduce leisure-—to maintain their existing standard of
present consumption. The net effect on work incentives will be

the sum of the above two effects, the outcome of which is
uncertain. It is known fact that the analysis of effects of Yt on
incentives to work leads to more or less same conclusion. Hence
- there is nothing to choose between Et cr Yt on this account.

Built-in-instability :

Et is likely to affect the time pattern of consumption of the
taxpayers. Under constant Government expenditure substitution
of equal yield ET in place of Yt the tax rate is an endogenous
variable. Therefore, when the general level of consumption is —

high, the tax rate will be low and vice-versa. So, the consumption
value of a given income will be high when the general level of
consumption is high, and vice-versa. It follows therefore that it
would pay a person to consume more when the general level of
consumption is high, and to save more when the general level
of savings is high. Furthermore, higher the level of consumption,
the lower the tax rate; and lower the tax ‘rate, the higher the
level of consumption demand, and so on. Alternatively, lower
the level of consumption demand, higher the tax rate; and higher
the tax rate, lower the demand for consumption, and so on.
That is, here we have built-in-instability.
Transitional Effects :

The transitional effects are the once for all effects, of changing
over from the Yt to the Et. When the Et is introduced, it wilk
have the effect of a once for all wealth tax. If the Et were
introduced at the gross rate (tax ~ inclusive) of 50 per cent; it is
clear that the real value of wealth would fall 50 per cent. Another -
problem will be the effect on a person who has saved during his
earning period under Yt regime with the purpose of spending
it after retirement. Such individual will have to pay Et on the
use of their savings. This obviously would be unfair.

International Aspects :

The Meade Committee and Mr. Lodin have considered interna-
tional aspect of shifting from income base to expenditure base.
The advantage of Yt in this respect is that it is widely accepted
and treaties are signed by several countries to avoid double
taxation. Adoption of Et would create the problem about the

_ treatment of foreign-source income of its’ residents. Providing
relief for Yt paid to other countries would be inconsistent with
the philosophy of Et.

]

Administrative Consideration :

Recent discussion appear to suggest that new insight into
feasibility of Et have been gained. Advocates of Et claim that
the tax based on consumption will be easier to administer than -
the present income tax. However, this claim is based on the failure
to conceive various difficult administrative problems arising in
operation of Et and is likely to burden us with unanticipated
problems. Let us begin with the problem of measurement of
chargeable expenditure under Et. Direct measurement of chargeable
expenditure, i. e., counting up all the rupees spent on consumption
is clearly administratively impossible. The only other alternative
is an indirect measurement of taxable consumption. Consumption
may be calculated by subtracting the increase in wealth between
the beginning and the end of the period in question from the
total receipts during the period. Total assets at the beginning
of the period, plus the total receipts during the period indicate
the total amount that can be spent during the period; subtrac-
ting from this sum the total assets at the end of the period
gives us as a balance the amount actually consumed.

The expenditure tax would remove various arbitrary distinc-
tions present in the income tax, but at the same time would
introduce a few arbitrary features of its own. The principal ~
arbitrary distinction to be made under the expenditure tax is
between chargeable expenditure and investment. Suppose Professor
of Chemistry has small laboratory in his house, where he works
ona research project of his own. Assume the laboratory is financed
through his own funds. Presumably the expenditure and the
laboratory would be considered as investment and taxable con- ,
sumption. If this be so, then do we consider the expenditure on
a child’s chemistry set as a taxable cnosumption? If so then are |
we not discriminating because of age and/or former education, |
and/or intent. In circumstances such as these, how do we draw }
a line between taxable consumption and non-taxable industry, |
which is not arbitrary and which does not create “anomalies” 2
and “inequities” ? Should education be considered as investment |
or taxable consumption ? |
' Under Et purchase of invertment will be a deductable ~ )
For any workable system of the expenditure. tax, it would be |
absolutely necessary to specify explicitly what items are t

118 LIBERALISM AND LDCS
regarded as investment and what items are to be regarded as
consumption; and the circumstances in which a particular item may
be regarded as consumption or investment. It is at this point that

_¢ various arbitrary distinctions have to ke introduced; these arbitrary
distinctions create ‘‘anomalies’” and “inequities”. The arithmetic
involved in ascertaining taxable consumption is elementary, but

; the task of explicitly specifying the content of the words ‘taxable
consumption’ is far from simple.

In general expenditure tax can be avoided by understating
receipts, it can also be avoided by overstating value of purchase.
If receipt is not reported then the value of receipts can be con-
sumed without incurring tax liability. Of course, the income tax
can also be avoided in this manner. However, under Yt all the
receipts are not subject to the tax and hence all receipts do not
have to be reported. Under Et itis essential for the purposes of
accurately calculating taxable expenditure that all the receipts be
reported.

The taxation of gift raises some very serious and fundamental
administrative problems under Et. The Et can be avoided if the
receipt of a gift is not declared by the recipient. The problem
is how do we make sure that all the gifts will be declared by
the recipient? This problem can be overcome without too much
difficulty by system of cross checking. Under this system each
tax payer will be required to furnish the code numbers of all
the persons involved in transactions for each of the items claimed
as a deduction from the expenditure tax. However, this system
can work well under strictly proportionate tax rate. Under the
progressive tax rate, the cross checking system will create several
other problems. Under a progressive Et a tax payer with a high

. marginal tax rate can hire persons, who are either exempt
from tax or have a relatively low marginal tax rate to do some
of the spending for him; the required funds being transferred
as gift. Another possibility of avoidance of Et would be that,
a person in a high marginal tax rate may give a gift to a person
who is exempted, who in turn would buy an object, i. e., car
and keep the title to the object and sell it at nominal and “second

| hand” price to the same high marginal tax rate tax payer.

|
ON ADVISABILITY & FEASIBILITY OF ET IN INDIA 119
Tax Avoidance via Investment Transactions :

In computing taxable expenditure proceeds from the sale
of investment are to be added to the available resources that
can be spent. One way of avoiding expenditure tax is to sell an °
asset and to refrain from reporting the sale, or to underestimate
the proceeds from the sale of the asset. The funds so cbtained
can be spent, and Et avoided. In the modern society, a large
part of investment transactions takes the form of buying and
selling of shares. It is known fact that buying and selling prices
of shares are different at any given point of time and they may .

‘_yary over time. It is also possible that, for one seller, there will
be many buyers and, for one buyer, there will be many sellers.
Furthermore, sellers may have no knowledge of the identity of
the buyer and buyer may have no knowledge of the identity of
the seller. Hence neither the buyer, nor the seller can provide
the code number of the other party. Hence the cross-checking
system will not work. Taking into consideration the fact that
several millions of transactions of this nature occur on the stock
exchange every year, the cross-checking system would involve
colossal amount of work and may fail. Even if an efficient sys-
tem were found, it is likely that such a system would be rather
expensive and cumbersome to operate.

When we introduce other countries into the discussion, the

easier to avoid the expenditure tax i-e. the purchase of invest-

investment could be under-stated. Other possibility is that a
person can consume as little as possible, amass his savings, and
then emigrate and thus avoid the expenditure tax.! Further,
presumably the overseas visitors would be exempted from Et, or
even if they are subject to the tax, their expenditure would be

M. H. Gopal

The fiscal or budgetary policy and its manifestations in any
country play a crucial role in its socio-economic build-up. Not
only the material prosperity, but the social happiness of the
people, is made or marred by a wise or a wayward policy. India
is an illustration of this policy.

This essay analyses India’s experience in recent years in four
different steps, and outlines broad directions of an overhaul:
(i) Policy objectives in retrospect; (ii) the extent of their
achievement in practice; (iii) the reasons for the limited success;
and (iv) the direction of an overhaul. I shall concentrate on
the broad objectives; as presented in the Central budget and its
accessories, with particular reference to the last decade and a
half.

Part Il : The Policy Objectives and their Relations

I shall now examine how far these policy objectives have been
realised. The purpose of any policy is not simply to formuate
it or attempt to operate it; it is, more importantly, to make it
effective in practice.

The period since Independence falls into two sections : 1951—
52 to 1960-61, the years of the first two Plans with fiscal policy
being attuned to them, and the later years, 1961 to 1977 when
inflation and other problems raised their heads. The first ten years
would form the initial years for thinking over socio-economic
and fiscal policies, such as the Industrial Policy Statements of
1948 and 1956, and the Socialistic Pattern of Society aim. This
experience will be a set-off to the later years, largely because
fiscal objectives were still being formulated. I shall, therefore,
concentrate on 1960-61 to 1977-78 for testing the success of the
fiscal objectives.'
