Let us look at two of the more important components of
growth : agricultural and industrial productions.' These, espe-
cially the former, depend also on factors extraneous to fiscal
measures, e.g., floods, droughts and pests. But, by and large,
and after the 1977-78 budget, a closer relationship could be
expected between the growth-oriented policy and the two com-
ponents; therefore, following the changes in production is largely
suggestive and not conclusive of the growth facet of Indian
fiscal policy.

Agricultural production has three components - changes in

"area, output and yield per hectare. What were the changes brou-
ght about in each of these ? With 1950-51 as the base year for
1950-51 to 1966-67, the area index increased by 21 points in 10
years, 1950-60, ie. an average of 2 points a year; in the next
17 years, i.e., half a point a year. Admittedly, there is a very large
element of constraint in area expansion such as socio-economic
limitations on crop shifts and on modifications in cultivation
methods. Nevertheless, the experience in 1960-77 is not very
encouraging.

Agricultural output in 1950-60 increased by 42 points, ice.,
4 points a year, whereas in the next 17 years, the volume was
up 37 points, i.e., 2.5 per year. The yield per hectare increased
by 7.5 points or 0.75 per annum in 1950-60 and by 26 points or
1.7 per annum in the next fifteen years. These performance in
area, output and yield indicate that the objective of growth
vis-a-vis agriculture was not achieved even considerably.

Industrial production did better in 1960-75, the years of the
III, IV and supposedly Fifth Plan periods. The changes averaged
5 per cent a year for these 15 years varying from 0.7 per cent
in 1966-67 to 9.7 per cent in 1962-63.

The overall conclusion, therefore, is that the growth objec-
tive does not appear to have been substantially realised, although
it was the key-stone of fiscal policy and very large outlays from
the public fisc were made in the budgets. My contention is not
that the growth objective was inappropriate and unnecessary,
but that the means to realise it were.

Of the complex reasons for this slow growth four may be
stressed — the private sector’s fear of the capricious fiscal policy
changes and operation, the obsession of the planners that each
Plan must be larger than the predecessor, the faulty plan alloca-
tion of the resources; and finally, the inept administration of
plan projects. In other words, this was the questionable policy of
expansion before consolidation, instead of consolidating the gains
before expanding further.

2. Stabilization :

Stabilization of the price level, the second of the fiscal
objectives, has a two-fold purpose. It influences developmental
outlay, since the greater the price rise, the larger the outlay to )
achieve the same result. The more important impact is on the
common man, his wages and incomes and consumption level,

and on savings and investment in the private sector. Inflation has
been with us since the Second World War, but after Indepen-
dence and particularly in the last 17 years, its pressure has been
mounting. Therefore, budgetary policy since 1950, except for
an odd year or two, has had stabilisation as an important aim.

To ascertain the effectiveness of the policy, let us look |
at the behaviour of prices.! From 1951 to 1960, the wholesale
price index showed an annual average rise of 2.5 points. In a
developing economy and after all the upsets following the war |
and the 1947 holocaust, this level of increase was not much. But
from 1960-61, the price-rise got accelerated. Thus, in 1961-66,
the Third Plan years, prices were up by 66 points, ie. +12.5 a
year, and by 1974, the increase was nearly 300 points in 15 years,
ice. +10 a yearon an average. Even in 1976-77, it was 12 points
up, in spite of the attempted price stabilisation.

Agricultural prices, a component of the wholesale prices,
followed the above trend, though manufacturing prices rose a

164 LIBERALISM AND LDCS
little less. The behaviour of the working class consumer prices
was not different. The inevitable inference from this trend is that
the policy of price stabilization, in spite of controls, imports,
fair price shops, procurement, etc., has not succeeded in even
containing the rise.

Two of the more important reasons for this policy failure
were: (1) The disappointingly low growth rate and (2) the con-

_ tinuous and large increases in money supply with the public. For
instance, between 1963 and 1969, the annual average addition to
money supply was Rs. 333 crores, ranging from +Rs. 180 crores
to +Rs. 475 crores in different years. Thus, in 1971, the total
volume of money with the public was Rs. 7,193 crores but by
1976-77, the volume had doubled to Rs. 15,156 crores, i-e., an
average annual addition of Rs. 1,180 crores, and in some years,
e.g. 1965-76, the addition was as much as Rs. 2,215 crores.

It is amazing that there was so little of co-ordination be-
tween the monetary authorities, largely in control of money supply,
and the fiscal authorities making price stability a policy objective.
The two agencies appear to have run in opposite directions.

Anyway, the Centre’s policy of containing price rise failed.
In a way, the Centre itself contributed to the rise partly by its
rising expenditure and partly by continuously running into defi-
cits. “Budgetary deficit, as a component of changes in money
supply”, warned the Reserve Bank in July 1977,1 “has important
implications for the price level”. And Central deficits have been |
continuous, while in some years their size has been unsettling.
For example, in 1975-76, the amount was Rs. 366 crores and
in the next year (R.E.) it was Rs. 425 crores. In 1977-78, the
budgetary gap apparently was only Rs. 85 crores, but “the Centre.
will borrow from the Reserve Bank Rs. 800 crores against foreign
exchange reserves’’,? supposedly to be balanced by imports. :

4. Social Justice :

The demand for social justice is decades old, prior to the ’
Plans and to Independence; and Gandhiji was one of its apostles.
Such justice is long overdue, but, this apart, it forms an impor-
tant segment of the economic and fiscal policies of the Govern-
ment. It was dramatised in the Congress slogan ‘Garibi Hatao’.

Social justice has many facets, but I shall consider only two
testable ones : (1) changes in the poverty level — numbers and
distribution; and (2) impact of education, housing and health
outlay. Although the letter are nonmonetary facets of justice,
they have their financial and welfare implications, and therefore,
redistributive significance.

The depth and spread of poverty in India are proverbial, and,
repeatedly, claims have been made of improvement in the posi-
tion. But except in 1960-70 very little attempt has been made by
policy-makers even to understand and measure conditions over
the long period. What constitutes poverty level in India and
how it has changed in the Plan period are answered differently
by different studies.! Since my interest is to test broadly a policy

- Objective, I shall consider below only the overall aspects of
Indian Poverty.

5. Self-reliance :

This is a relatively late and not often much stressed fiscal

objective. Its emergence may be traced to the balance of pay-
; ments difficulties and defence and other heavy industry demands.
Appreciable advance has been made in self-reliance in some
directions, but a long way still remains to be traversed. It, more-
over, raises the basic issue if a country of India’s size and
complex problems and with an open economy can both afford
to be and can obtain self-reliance except in a few major direc-
tions. Therefore, we may pass over this fiscal objective.
6. Resources :

Resource raising and spending is the only fiscal objective
that has been achieved, perhaps, more than expected. In 1950-51,
the Central Government’s receipts on revenue account were Rs.
405 crores and by 1975-76, they had increased to over Rs. 6,875
crores, i.e., fifteen-fold in 25 years.! In the five years of the -
First Plan period, the revenue was Rs. 2,232 crores and in the
five yeats of the Fourth Plan, it was Rs. 20,089 crores.

Such a phenomenal growth was the result of five factors :

(1) Price rise which hurt the masses but benefitted the govern-
ment, e.g., in commodity ad valorem taxes; (2) stricter admini-
stration, e.g., of direct taxes; (3) growth in population leading
to growth in consumption and so adding to indirect tax reci€pts;
(4) growth in national income in current prices on which are
based income and other levies, (5) Increase in tax rates and
reduction in tax concessions, as in direct taxes.

tions of the fiscal policy become clearer with a breakdown of
the revenue heads. Thus, in 1950-51 and in 1975-76, the receipts
from personal income taxation for instance, were respectively Rs.

"ILI. Reasons for the Limited Success of Fiscal Policy

The preceding analysis indicates that five out of six objec-
tives have not been much of a success inthe last 27 years. What
could be the reasons for this failure ? The answer suggests what
lacunae should be made good, and which direction any over--
haul should take.

The reasons may be placed in three broad groups : (1):
Overall policy drawbacks; (2) Deficiencies largely of fiscal policy;.
and (3) tax structure limitations. These three may be correlated
to three decision-making levels : The Cabinet which dictates the
outline of the policy, the Finance Minister whose responsibility:
it is to shape fiscally these objectives, and the permanent civil
service — advisers and administrators ~ who, given the policy,
help to formulate the detailed steps. As the overhauling of
policy suggested below is closely linked to these causes, I shall
briefly explain them below :

I. Overall Policy Drawbacks : ©
(a) Lack of continuity :

Fiscal policy, no less crucial for a country than foreign and’
defence policies, insists on its being, in its broad approach, bi-
partisan, the annual budgetary changes being confined to structural’

- and administrative details such as rates and reliefs. Policy, having:

~varied and long-term repercussions on the economy, demands a
continuity of the policy objectives, and also the continuity of
the finance custodian for a few years at a stretch, to formulate
the policy, to see it operate and to understand its limitations.

In India, however, in the last 27 years, in spite of the same
‘party being in power, there has been outwardly a continuity in
broad policy issues, but the changes and uncertainties in the
‘operating details have been many and conflicting. Moreover, in

cand repercussions of the complexity of fiscal policy and of any

4b) Lack of co-ordination : .

The second drawback is the lack of co-ordination between
{1) the Union and the States’ budgetary policies, and (2) the
‘Central fiscal and the banking sector’s monetory and credit
policies and steps. Apparently the Reserve Bank is a part,
though supposedly autonomous, of the Central Government. So

‘co-ordination. This lacuna partly accounts for the excessive
‘money supply and consequent price inflation, which have been

In a sense, the component States are and should be auto-
nomous in many matters, but in economic, especially fiscal,
‘matters both the Union and the States draw from the same re-
sources pool and spend on the same functions. There ‘has not
deen full understanding and co-ordination between these autho-
rities in their budgetary policies and actions, For instance, if a
‘State ‘overdraws’ from the Reserve Bank freely or makes an un-

wise outlay, inflationary pressure would, as has happened, in-

| crease. Further, there is no synchronisation in the timing and.
policy dates, nor among the different States themselves. Much
less previous consultation is there on the broad policy issues.

In a country, such as the United States, where the States.
are more autonomous and act more freely, any Federal State
conflict matters less than in India because of a different economic
structure, different fiscal objectives and vaster Federal resources.
In a developing young federation, lack of reasonable co-opera-
tion between the two sets of governments would be fatal to the
economic ‘growth’ and social justice. A way out of such a situ-
ation is suggested below.

(c) Mix~up of long and short-term policy objectives :

A third drawback is that, apart from the claims while pre-
senting the budget, there is no overall long-term perspective in.
the Central budget. There is a mix-up of the yearly changes,
e.g., in rates and reliefs, and, except in a couple of budzets of
T. T. Krishnamachari, the larger impact of the changes in policy
are not realised and acted upon. Thus, just as fiscal policy is.
repeatedly claimed to be Plan oriented and so resource raising.
these annual changes are presumed to be parts of the same re-
source raising process, and rarely having any other impact. For
instance, the growth objective is secular ~ not in the political.
sense—and so are social justice and employment creation, objectives.
whereas stabilisation is a short-term problem and policy issue,
although its containment has evaded success in the last two decades..

What is the impact of the long and short-term aims on each.
other ? How do the resulting changes in tax structure, for exam-
ple, influence the major objective ? Inflation is an aberration and

| -a temporary imbalance in the economy, but social justice is not.
While the latter is urgent, it will take decades if it can be re-
solved at all through fiscal policy alone.
| There is no recognition of this kind of situation in the
| Indian budgets; there is confusion resulting in a slower than
| need-be achievement of the ‘growth’ objective. As is pointed
out below, policy reorientation demands giving each objective its
relative priority.

{d) Overemphasis on Growth :

. Yet another drawback is the obsession with growth, and the

Government belief till 1977 that the public sector, given the funds
‘can largely by itself achieve the growth target, and thus across
the overemphasis on resource raising. In all non—authoritarian

societies, growth is a function of the public and private sectors
co-operating ~ only that, in a largely competitive economy like

that of U. S. A., private enterprise dominates growth, while in
mixed economies, both sectors play their part. In India, under
its overall economic policy and its component, fiscal policy, the
scope for the private sector has been forced to shrink from Plan
to Plan, through the tax and other constraints, after increasing in

1951-57. So the response of this sector in the growth objective

in terms of saving, investment and risk has been hesitant, and,
. thus, growth itself has -been slowed down.

I reiterate this widely known feature because of my plea
below for giving the private sector a large share in growth and,
therefore, in facilitating stabilization ond other objectives; that
is, a plea for greater relaxation in tax burdens and constraints on
this sector. While the private sector, if given sufficient leeway,
would find for expansion its own resources out of its earnings and
in the open market the public sector must find funds partly in-
ternally and mostly through taxation. Therefore, the emphasis

on growth through the public sector has led to the search for
. "continuously increasing tax resources, especially through indirect
taxation. The repercussions of this overemphasis on taxes have
been overlooked. And since fiscal policy is more than mere
taxation its overall success has been limited.
4e) Lack of stability in policy :

_ A fifth drawback is there has been no policy stability. Appa-
tently the objectives have remained the same, but the manner
in which they have been operated has differed. For instance,
compare the budgets of Mathai, Deshmukh, Krishnamachari;
Morarji Desai and Subramanian—all were able Finance Ministers,
but what a difference in their approaches and measures? Al-
though it was not a strictly policy matter, look at the impact
of the Kaldor taxes on the investing class and on tax administra-
tion. After all, what matters most is not how acceptable the

: objectives or their instruments are to different strata of society,—
no budget proposal-can please everybody,-but how much they
can be depended upon over a long enough period to adjust one’s
investment and production activities.
{f) Confusion between broad policy and details :

Finally, there is the mix-up between overall policy and budget
details such as changes in rates, exemptions, reliefs, commodity
groupings, etc. It is true that the details flow from policy and
are necessarily annual adjustments in applying the policy in the
context of the economic situation. But, these are not of the same
significance as the broader policy directives, spelt not in general
terms as done in Central budgets, but in terms of their specific
and multifaced impact. The impact aspects is largely omitted and
the details facet is over stressed in the budgets.

Further, though the details are to be adjusted annually to
the economic situation in India, there is a too frequent an
alteration in the budget structural details, often depending not on
what the policy requires but who the minister is. For example
changing the income-tax exemption limit, or raising the marginal
tate on the top income slab or the different kinds of profits
taxes, or even the course of the Kaldor taxes. Budget changes
are awaited particularly by the investor with anxiety, which turns
into confusion, when changes depend not on policy but on the
individual custodian’s reactions. Thus, paying greater attentionto © |
structural details and introducing changes too frequently have natu-
tally brought instability into the fiscal policy. Hence, my suggestion
that the Government formulate a long-term, and, even a perspective
broad outline in fiscal policy, into which the shorter, e.g., Plan
term, and annual budget changes can be fitted.

IL. Deficiencies in Fiscal Policy :
(a) Multiplicity of objectives :

These deficiences are at the second level and relate more
specifically to the policy itself.

The most glaring drawback in India is the multiplicity of
fiscal objectives. All of them, and perhaps even a few more, are
important and even urgent, but since a budget is.a practical, |
operating instrument, it is not the prevalence of the problems {
that should determine how many and which are to guide the :

176 LIBERALISM AND LDCS.
policy, but essentially which, given the human and administrative
resouces, are practicable, of greater priority and of greater benefit.
It is this that the Indian policy-makers appear to have overlook-
ed. Too many objectives, though important and interrelated,
have resulted in too little of achievement. In spite of political.
pressures and public demand a selection has to be made and the
fewer the objectives concentrated upon the quicker would the
‘ others, too, be on the agenda.
(b) Mix-up of long and short-term objectives :

When there are competing objectives, a choice has to be
made regarding priorities and some objectives may even have to
be postponed. Such choice has to be of two kinds-(i) between
the long and short-term ones, e.g., growth and social justice are
long-term objectives to be realised in a decade or a generation,
while aberrations like price rise are of short run duration; (ii)
between the above and annual problem.

Another basic defect has been attempting too many things
at the same time, partly because of political necessities and partly
because of inexperience and overenthusiasm. Such a mix-up, when
resources are few, leads; as has happened in India, to failure to
achieve substantially even a single aim. Nobody questions the
legitimacy, e.g., of social justice, but one is not so sure of its
urgency vis-a-vis growth, because adequate growth would pro-

» v.de the resources for welfare and if the economy is rapidly taking
off, economic and social justice would follow with minimum
State control and direction. Therefore, long and short-term obje-
ctives and priorities must be separated, their priorities determined
and dovetai'ed, but this is lacking in India’s fiscal policy.
(c) Dominance of political slogans :

A third deficiency in the second group is the presumption
that political slogans can replace hard reality, e. g., ‘‘garibi
hatao”’ and “Rama Rajya in ten years.’’ Every year, the
Central budget is replete with promises and, often even the hard
facts of the economic situation are slurred over. This has two
effects, first, it gives the unwary reader and the politically biassed
legislator an incorrect idea of the situation, and secondly, it lulls
the policy maker himself into complacence [since it would be a
year more before the next budget is presented and he would
realise, from the economic situation, what happened.

(d) Neglect of the expenditure facet :

The next, perhaps more important, drawback is not adequate
recognition of the importance of the expenditure side. The bud-
get document most often merely narrates the outlay trend and
why perhaps a little more was spent (R.E.) or little more is
needed (R.E). But it really hesitates to enquire (1) the underlying
why of it, (2) if there cannot be greater economies effected, or
(3) the impact of a rise or fall in outlay on other sectors. In
fact, it completely forgets that expenditure is as important in
policy framing and budget making as the presentation of the
revenue position and taxation proposals.

Moreover, it is strange that practically no serious attempt
has been made in the last 30 years to economise, drastically as
is necessary, spending which has been marked by continuous
jumps. For example, the total Central and State outlays were
Rs. 998 crores in 1950-51, Rs. 6,611 crores in 1965-66 and Rs.
18,905 crores in 1975-76, i.e., an annual average increase of Rs.
704 crores; i.e., in 25 years the expenditure has risen nineteen-
fold. The total outlay of the Centre alone was up twenty-four -

| fold in nearly three decades.

| / What is pointed out is that although expenditure determines
the load and direction of revenue, it is markedly neglected by

| the policy maker recalling what a British Indian Finance Member
of old times called the ‘Rake’s progress’.

There is, further, generally a nonchalant approach to bud-
getary deficits. In 30 years there has been practically no year
without an overall deficit, ranging from a few crores to quite a
few hundreds. For. example, it amounted in 1952-53 to Rs. 41
crores, in 1960-61 to Rs. 177 crores, ten years later to Rs. 270
crores and in 1976-77 to Rs. 320 crores. In this respect, the
attitude of the policy maker has been of two kinds, first, to
Over-stress the deficit on revenue account in order to justify
additional tax burden, and second, to under-stress the overall
deficit as not of much import. Thus, for example in 1976, the
Finance Minister concluded “I leave this*gap of Rs. 320 crores un-
covered. It is my considered opinion that this order of deficit
will not accentuate inflationary pressures in the economy.” This

unconcern to an obvious danger is being repeated year after
year. And yet, the Reserve Bank warned in 1977 that deficits
would accelerate inflation.

(e) Frequent tax changes :

Finally, there is the drawback of too many changes in taxes
such as the Kaldor trio, the Super Profits Tax, the Dividends
Tax and now under contemplation, the Value Added Tax. The
old adage that an old tax is a good tax still holds true. All
taxes are ultimately paid by the public, rich or poor, producer
or consumer. Even a burdensome tax or an unreasonable tax
burden tends to be absorbed by the economy financially and by
the tax-prayer psychologically. But, when, under monetary enthu-

: siasm as in the case of the Kaldor levies and in prejudice as with
the Dividends tax, a new burden is imposed, the economic equili-
brium is disturbed, and there is a tremendous psychological impact
on the saver and investor. Novelty is not welcome to the tax
payer or advantageous to the tax administrator. The Indian fiscal

policy makers have often forgotten this since independence. The
budgets of this period leave the impression that the policy maker
itches for novel levies and more burden.

Ill. Tax Structure Limitations.

The third group of causes limiting policy success consists of
details, normally put forward in the budgets and often enquired
into by numerous Committees from Justice Varadachariar Income-

Chowksi Committee. Occasionally, private organisations such as
the Centre for Fiscal Studies in Delhi deal with such problems.
As enquiries are plentiful and suggestions for reform galore and

also as this set of limitations is not totally a policy matter but

. an application of policy objectives. I shall deal with them only
briefly. .

! The tax limitations fall into two groups: (1) Structural;
and (2) Procedural and administrative. The structural group is

| made up of new levies, rate changes, and changes in reliefs,

| exemptions, extensions, etc. The other group relates to rationali-
sation, simplification and tax law.

The other facet. of this limitation relates to tax laws and,

1V. The Direction of Overhauling

The overhauling process should meet squarely these draw-
backs, group by group and deficiency by deficiency.
I. Overall Policy Drawbacks :

: (a) As changing horses in midstream is unwise, the first step
in the reorientation process is to have continuity in the person
formulating policy. The Janata Government, for instance, may be

, expected to be in power for about four more years, and so do
not change the custodian for that period, for, in earlier years,
the Minister’s term was too short and the changes were too
many.

It should even be feasible to give the Finance Minister’s
position a bipartisan colour, as the current overall economic
policy is basically a modified earlier programme, while the fiscal
objectives have been almost the same since 1961.

(b) The second step is to bring about greater co-ordination
between the States and the Centre regarding major policy appro-

aches. This should be possible since many of the States are run
by the same party and also since the Centre can control through
aid, loans and greater firmness any recalcitrant unit.

This involves two means : (1) Normally make the budget
presentation dates synchronise in all the States and the Union.
(2) While the detailed operative budget proposals are confidential
till presented the overall fiscal approach need not be secretive
and prior and closer consultations among the Governments should
be feasible, as in the case of planning.

(c) Another part of co-ordination is with the money and
credit policy formulators. Such an understanding with the Re-
serve Bank exists already, but to a limited extent. Greater co—
ordination is essentiel and may be achieved through two steps
(i) by a little more interference with the policy making powers

of the Bank, e.g., as has been done very recently by appointing

: a competent person, well and truly familiar with the ‘fiscal side’
to head the organization (ii) Yet another device for greater co-
ordination is the Centre itself determining the direction of mone-
tary and credit policies, leaving their application and day to day
adjustment to the Bank. This may convert the Bank, - which in
Central banking theory is supposed to be independent-, a wing
of Government, but in the present circumstances in India such a
step is both necessary and useful.

(d) A further step is to take the cue from the Planning

Commission. The Commission has not only annual plans, but
also five year ones, end with the rolling plan concept, even the
latter becomes a continuous five year plan; it also has perspective
planning, covering a much longer span.

This approach may be adapted to budget policy formulation

as below : (1) the normal annual budget to deal with outlays,
tax changes etc. as of now; (2) a quinquennial perspective or
guideline for policy formulation. This would not involve new
levies, rates or relief and therefore, its confidentiality would be

. limited but its significance in policy making and co-ordinating
with State policies would be important. It would in effect outline
the direction.

(e) The next part of reorientation relates to specific policy
issues. The first of these is to regard the expenditure facet of

the budget as important as the revenue raising or tax levying

II. Deficiencies in Fiscal Objectives :

The second group of reforms relates to fiscal objectives.
Currently these are too many and none can be achieved substan-
tially. Therefore arises the necessity to reduce their number to
two plus one: (1) Growth, (2) Stabilization and, as a necessary
adjunct to the first, (3) Resources. Growth will be the long-term
objective extending, in the first instance, to 10to 15 years, while
stabilization, the short-term objective, may extend to 2 to 3
years, which may be the minimum time to hold and reverse the
price trend, for its success depends largely on the extent of eco- |

_ nomic growth. )
(a) The growth objective should be marked by maximum
returns for the outlay and not by mere outlay expansion and
' spread, as is the case today.
Growth as an objective involves another shift in current fis-
cal policy-greater encouragement to the private sector. Enlarging
GNP involves both the public and the private sectors. While the
former has an overall performance of about 4 per cent on outlay,
the latter has returned around 13 per cent. Also, except in agriculture
and basic industries, the private sector is the major contributor
to GNP and for quite sometime to come, it should not only
continue that role but also must be encouraged to play a larger
part, if the growth rate is to be impressive. This means that the
declining role of this sector-from 60-40 per cent, through 50-50
per cent to 40-60 per cent—must be reversed to enable industrial
production to grow. That is, temporarily at least, political socialism
must be toned down.

If this position is accepted, greater scope is to be given to
the private sector. Three fiscal steps, therefore, become necessary,
—first, gaining its confidence that, for a few years to come, ex-
propriation, unnecessary economic restraints and further taxation
will not be the State policy; second reducing the current tax ,
| burden on business; and third, providing incentives to private
saving and investment from internal sources.

This shift in policy may have its impact.on resources. But
; more taxation is not the only way to raise resources. There are

others: (1) Tighten up the current tax structure and administra-
| tion. (2) As has been almost annually experienced, buyoancy of

ENDIA’S FISCAL POLICY—A SUGGESTED OUERHAUL 185
public especially tax revenue may be expected consequent on
greater private sector co-operation, and larger GNP due to a
higher rate of growth, and (3) greater economy and efficiency in
expenditure. Further, since the expenditure hike is to be halted,
the need for more and more resources would not be so persistent.

(b) The short-term objective of stabilization-holding and even
teversing price rise-is absolutely essential if the economy is not
to get into doldrums. In a way, inflation is a root cause of much
of economic trouble in India- rising public expenditure, priva-
tion in consumption, rising production costs, etc.

The control of expenditure and acceleration of growth
through greater private sector effort-both suggested above—-would
help stabilization. What more is needed is to make it a joint

banking fiscal effort. With the above steps, I guess stabilization
and reversal of rising trend may take 3 to 5 years.

The other policy objectives like employment, social justice
and self-reliance are incidental, and would to some extent follow
from the above three. But their effective and substantial realisa-
tion would take a long long time, for they are secular problems
and require vast resources to solve them. It serves little purpose
to be blind to the difficult nature of these problems. At best,
keep up the present attention, machinery and outlay on them
but do not accelerate or promise too much.

To put the foregoing in different words, the long-term
growth objective is a problem of greater government-—private se-
ctor co-operation, indicating greater freedom to and less burden
on private investment; and the stabilisation objective, one of
fiscal-monetary co-ordination, indicating greater government con-
trol over banking.

Quite a few studies have keen made on them and a few more
are in the pipeline. Partly because these studies,-with which I
do not agree in toto,-partly because limitations lead to the ana-
lysis of details and largely because my concern is with policy,

What is Economics

_ Through much of human history-and this applies to alf |
civilizations-economic thought has been a part of social philoso-- )
phy, governed by what was conceived to be moral principles.. |
The basic ethical ‘laws’ honesty, charity, a sense of responsibi- |

nely ordained. It was the task of the social philosophers - the

The Old Testament, which provides basic ethical principles. }
for Christians, Jews, and, indirectly, Moslems is full of economic
principles presented as moral laws, some dating back to the Law

the prophet Ezekiel, several centuries later, compared the sin of |

The Greek philosopher Plato looked upon economic issues:

For the past two centuries, the Western world has been torn

precisely opposite meaning. For Bastiat and the liberals of his

not a solution to society’s problems, but instead was the pro-
blem itself,

Though the meaning of the word “‘liberal’* has changed great-

ment of our own times. Always quick to defend the consumer __

the forgotten little men of most modern economic analyses, |

be laughed at is the one thing which big government has never |
been able to stand. Zz

“The state quickly understands the use it can make of i

Bastiat was one of those men fated to stand at the crossroads n
of sweeping histrorical events and radically conflicting ideologies.
He lived his life in the turbulence aftermath of the French Revo- Z
lution and personally witnessed the upheavals of 1830 and 1848. ;
He was active in the political and ideological debates of his age. f
The battle he fought as a mid—-nineteenth-century public figure a
were the battles which still mold the events and thinking of the

cades again and again which witnessed the overthrow of several I

poraries that Western men had their destinies in their own hands |

The slender Frenchman spent his life fighting to give all French-

Socialists, communists, visionaries, demagogues, and planners
of every description were all his foes. He stood steadfastly and

had in the struggle were not always in agreement with him. True,

Bastiat and his thought were related to Burke, Mill and the Whig

his resistance to the influences of the French Revolution. It is

Perhaps this is why Bastiat speaks so clearly today: His vision

Frederic Bastiat was far more than an economic journalist.
. In his work there appears a grasp of the broadest social issues.
In a modern world dominated largely by systems builders, Bastiat

Perhaps we should not be surprised that the nineteenth cen-
tury spawned an unusually large number of social architects. The
enormous changes of the Industrial Revolution, coupled with the
political revolution which had begun in France and which had
swept through country after country in the Western world, had
strongly impressed the idea of change upon the European mind.

Since then change was not only sweeping in nature, but was pre-
sumably, change tor the better, the idea of social reconstruction,
of remodelling society in the aftermath of revolution, came to
dominate the minds of many. The idea of evolution, so dear to
nineteenth century thinkers, also played its part in promoting the
idea of progress. Nineteenth-century thinkers tended to see them-
selves living between the old and the new, groping toward radi-
cal change, toward a new society, toward a new world. Men had

required to produce a given monetary service-fiow. Moreover, it
may also increase the precautionary demand for money. In short,
the net effect of the variability of inflation—rate on demand for
money depends upon the relative strength of these two effects,
and no a-priori condition can be put on the sign-derivative of

I Believe ...
Minoo Masani

I believe in the Brotherhood of Man. There are many who
think that the Brotherhood of Man is meaningless without the

' Fatherhood of God. To me there does not appear to be any such
essential interdependence, The Brotherhood of Man involves
human solidarity based on the fact that human nature is essentially
the same everywhere, that people react fundamentally in the same
way to the same incentives and the same pressures. Certain
modifications, of course have to be made to allow for variations
in social heritage, religion, climate, and such factors, but basically

we are all brothers under the skin.

Because of this belief, which I find corroborated by concrete
experience, I am not inclined to accept the plea that the economic
and social policies that produce certain results, shall we say, in
Japan or Germany or the United States would not produce similar

‘results in India. Human nature being what it is, people everywhere
respond to the same incentives and to the same stimuli. I find
nothing unique about the people of our country or the situation
in which it finds itself. I believe that, thanks to the conquest of
space the crashing of the sound barrier and the development of
‘telecommunications, the world is now one organism. Chauvinism
and zenophobia are today, therefore, forces that are as reactionary
as racism. .

A Question of Balance Bo
The belief in Humanism leads to an acceptance of Ethics,

I believe there is such a thing as good and evil. Of course, the

idea of what is good or evil, what is moral or immoral, isa ~
. subjective one. My own belief is that what makes for human

happiness is moral, what makes for misery is immoral. One man’s

food; of course, can be another man’s poison, and one man’s

2

pursuit of happiness may easily cause unhappiness to another.
The test of action, therefore, should be the overall balance of
happiness and unhappiness it produces.

It is obvious that such an approach to the problems of
morality has little to do with traditional or conventional codes ;
of morality. Would such liberty as this approach of mine given
to each individual be exercised with maturity and restraint? I
don’t know. I only know that no other concept of morality appears
to me to make any sense.

The philosophy that appeals to me is the Stoic philosophy.
From my youth, I have responded to the logic of the Meditations
of the Roman emperor, Marcus Aurelius. For instance, it is only
what we ourselves do that can hurt us, nothing that anyone else
does, however beastly, can possibly diminish one’s dignity or
make one shrink. I find that this philosophy helps in making it
possible to tell the truth even when it is unpalatable and builds
resistance to smears and lampooning as also a relative indifference
to popularity, the pursuit of which is the bane of our national
leadership.

From youth onwards, I have responded to Tagore’s
invitation “Ekla chalo re” and the sentiment of James Russell Lowell
in his ‘Stanzas on Freedom’:

. They are slaves who fear to speak o

For the fallen and the weak;

They are doves who dare not be

In the right with two or three. a

My mother tells me that, even as a little boy, I was always’
on the side of the underdog - the servant about to be dismissed
or the woman selling fruit who was being beaten down by some
member of the family inclined to bargain too hard. On such
occasions I was always on the other side of the social barricades.

An Open Letter to My Young Friends

Way back in 1959 when Rajaji and I founded the Swatantra
Party and pleaded for a market economy for India it was considered
politically foolhardy, if not downright foolish for us to go against the
then prevailing dogma of socialism. Nevertheless we persisted because
it was already apparent to some of us that the economic policies being
fqllowed by Pandit Nehru and his party based on the ‘socialistic pattern
of society’ would lead the country to bankruptcy. Our worst fears came
true for the ‘socialistic pattern of society’ did lead to economic disaster
and moral degradation.

Over forty years later, Mr. Narasimha Rao as Congress Prime
Minister admitted that the economy was in dire straits and ‘hard
decisions’ had to be taken. Yet he and his party refuse to admit that
the ‘socialistic pattern of society’ was responsible for the country being
in “dire straits” - to such an extent that we had actually to pawn the
country’s gold with banks overseas to borrow money to run the
Government of India.

This is hardly surprising considering the fact that they have
been the biggest beneficiaries of what Rajaji so aptly described as ‘The
permit-licence-quota-raj’. A cosy arrangement which enabled the ruling
party and its variants in the opposition, in the name of ‘socialism’, to
control the so-called ‘commanding heights of the economy’ and, thus
hold the reins of both economic and political power in their hands. -

If they have now taken the path of economic liberalisation it
is only because there are no other options available to save the country
from economic ruin not to speak of their own political survival.

If the economic reforms fail then the one opportunity the people
of India have had in forty years to look forward to a bettor life and a
fighting chance to reduce poverty and unemployment, will have been
lost and it will be a long long time before another such opportunity
presents itself.

, Why do I lay so much stress on liberalisation? I do so because

I believe that the business of government is to govern and not be in

business. How true that Gujarati proverb: ‘Where the king becomes a
6

trader, there his subjects become beggars’. The policy of involving itself
in industry, trade and commerce has led to the state neglecting its
primary responsibilities: The maintenance of law and order, the
provision of drinking water facilities, primary health care, primary
education, and a network of good roads and rail lines.
These ought to be the objectives of the new economic policy.
And this is the essence of liberalisation. It will enable the government
to live within its means as it will make it unnecessary for governments
to maintain huge administrative overheads. It will eliminate the need
for deficit financing which in turn will help keep prices at reasonable
levels. A government committed to liberalisation will not, even while
' proclaiming its policy of freeing the economy, engage in the dubious
and anti-market act of administering prices as it did recently in the
case of petrol. Such acts make a mockery of economic reforms and
can only hamper the process of liberalisation.

I am personally unhappy with the fact that the Indian voter
today has to make his choice between unwilling liberalisers on the one
hand and those who seek the people’s support through appeals to
religion or caste be it Ayodhya or Mandal. Had I been even ten years
younger I would have taken an active role in educating people on the
real meaning of liberalisation, why it is so important that the economic
reforms succeed. I might even have taken the initiative to once again
organise a movement to put pressure on the government to ensure
that it honestly implemented the reforms.

Since my advanced years and consequent physical frailty
\ prevent me from doing so I appeal to my younger friends and all those
who have faith in the dignity of the individual, their right to live their
lives with the minimum of state intervention, and who wish to see
an India where people have a fair opportunity for self-fulfilment, to
get together and organise a movement. If such a movement does not
emerge soon I am afraid the reforms process will, in the not so distant
future stutter to a stop and when that happens we will once again find
ourselves at the bottom of the heap.

Surely, we do not want that to happen because the people of

India deserve better.
Minoo Masani

The Quintessential Dissenter

M. R. Masani, (Minoo Masani as he was better known)
was an author, politician and an eminent parliamentarian. He
participated in the freedom movement and was a member of the
Constituent Assembly.

° Author of Our India, an all-time bestseller and a
prescribed textbook in schools even in pre-independence India
(the book was withdrawn when he parted company with Pandit
Jawaharlal Nehru and the then Establishment), Minoo Masani
was an almunus of Bombay’s Elphinstone College, the London
School of Economics and Lincoln’s Inn. He joined the Bombay
Bar but soon gave up practice to participate in the freedom
struggle. He courted imprisonment in 1932 and 1933. He joined
Jayaprakash Narayan, Achyut Patwardhan, Yusuf Meherally and
others to form the Congress Socialist Party (CSP) and became
its Joint Secretary. He was elected to the Bombay Municipal
Corporation soon thereafter and, in 1938, presided over the CSP
conference in Lahore.

An admirer of the Soviet Union, he visited that country
in the late ‘twenties when he was a student at the LSE and later
as Secretary of the CSP. The early ‘thirties were the period of
Stalin’s purges of his rivals in the CPSU and the liquidation of
millions of farmers who opposed his, policy of forced
collectivisation of farms. Horrified by Stalin’s brutality Masani’s
disenchantment with Soviet communism led to his questioning
the credentials of the Indian communists. He strenuously resisted
communist attempts to infiltrate and capture the CSP. Unable
to convince the majority of his colleagues in the CSP to support
him he resigned along with Ram Manohar Lohia, Achyut
Patwardhan and Asoka Mehta. A year later the communists were
expelled from the CSP. His disillusionment with Soviet
communism led him to question marxist dogma and to a

8

rethinking of his socialist beliefs. The result was his well known
essay ‘Socialism Reconsidered’.

The freedom movement was gathering movement and
when Gandhiji launched the ‘Quit India Movement’, Masani who
was then an employee in the Tata organisation, resigned his job,
volunteered himself as a satyagrahi, courted imprisonment and
found himself with other Congress leaders in Nasik jail.

On his release from jail, Masani entered legislative politics
via the Bombay Municipal Corporation (he was Mayor in 1943)
and to membership of the Indian Legislative Assembly. Which
was later converted into the Constituent Assembly. He played
his role in the drafting of the Indian Constitution as a member
of the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee and Union-Powers
Committee. ,

Following his renunciation of socialism it was only logical
for Minoo Masani to start thinking of an alternative to socialism
and an economic system for independent India. His was a middle

‘  of-the-road recipe - a mixed economy in a free and open society.
This was the theme of a series of lectures he delivered in 1947
to the Bombay University’s School of Economics which were later
published under the title “Plea for a Mixed Economy”.

.. Nominated by the Government of India as representative
on the UN Sub-Commission on Minorities, Masani invited prime
minister Jawaharlal Nehru’s wrath when he refused to turn a
blind eye to the persecution of minorities in the Soviet Union
and its satellites in Eastern Europe and was sent off in 1948 as
India’s Ambassador to Brazil.

Those were the Cold War years when the Soviet Union
sponsored front organisations to promote its interests worldwide.
Several organisations were set up internationally to counter the
Soviet challenge. One of these was the Congress for Cultural

9

Freedom based in Paris. In India, Masani alongwith Jayaprakash
Narayan, Asoka Mehta and A. D. Gorwala took the initiative in
establishing the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom (ICCF)
and affiliated it to the Congress in Paris. The ICCF was a non-
party organisation of scholars, writers, artists and scientists to
defend intellectual liberty, to cultivate a spirit of free enquiry
and an appreciation of the arts.

° .

Two years earlier he had founded, with the blessings and
encouragement of the then deputy prime minister and home
minister Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, the Democratic Research
Service to educate public opinion on the dangers to India’s
national independence posed by communists who, acting under
instructions from the Comintern in Moscow, were conducting a
violent insurrectionary movement in Telengana in Andhra
Pradesh.

His election to the Lok Sabha as an Independent from
Ranchi in Bihar in 1957 signalled the beginning of his efforts to
implement his thesis of a mixed economy and to combat the statist
policies which went under the name of Nehruvian Socialism. In
1959, he joined C. Rajagopalachari to found the Swatantra Party
which could broadly be described as a liberal-conservative party.

Masani was that rare combination - an intellectual with
tremendous organising competence. During his tenure as general
secretary, the Swatantra Party grew rapidly and in less than ten
years emerged, in the 1967 general elections, as the single largest
party in the opposition in the Lok Sabha with a strength of 44
members; leading a principled coalition government in Orissa;
as the officially recognised opposition in the Rajasthan and Gujarat
Assemblies; and with significant representation in the Andhra
Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Legislative assemblies.

As the party’s ideolgue he was clear that the Swatantra
Party should eschew non-parliamentary forms of protest like

10

satyagrahas, morchas, bandhs and walkouts in the legislatures. He
was largely influential in ensuring that the party did not form
fronts in the trade union and student movements. Perhaps it was
his insistence on discipline and doing the right thing that led to
the party’s exit from electoral politics. In 1971 the so called ‘Indira
wave’ swept all parties aside including the Swatantra Party. He
accepted responsibility for the party’s miserable performance (he
himself failed to retain his seat in the Lok Sabha for a third term
from Rajkot) and resigned from the presidentship of the party
and from party politics.

His was an outstanding performance as member of the Lok
Sabha between 1957 and 1971. He was chairman of the Public
Accounts Committee of Parliament. As leader of the single largest
party in the opposition he invariably opened the debate on the
Finance Bill that follows the introduction of the Union Budget.
Many of his speeches in parliament were later published under
the title “Congress Misrule and Swatantra Alternative”. Masani
kept a close watch on the attendance of members of his group
and their behaviour. He firmly believed that occupying the
opposition benches did not mean opposing for the sake of
opposition. On many an occasion he supported the ruling party
but did not hesitate in going against all other groups in the house
if a particular issue warranted such action. Two instances that
come to mind are the ‘liberation’ of Goa when he opposed India’s
action on the ground that it was unnecessary and that the whole
affair was an effort to ensure Krishna Menon’s return to
Parliament. The other was the abolition of Privy Purses when
the Swatantra Party in Parliament was alone in opposing the move
as it went against solemn assurances given by Sardar Patel and
recorded in ‘Instruments of Accession’. He would often quote
this verse to encourage his colleagues to treat issues on their merit
without being worried about being isolated or in a hopeless
minority:

' “They are slaves who dare not be
“In the right with two or three.”
11

He took over the editorship of Freedom First which he
had founded in 1952. As editor, he fought the censorship imposed
during Mrs. Gandhi’s ‘Emergency’ and sought the court’s
intervention against her censors in what came to be known as
the Freedom First case. Though the court vindicated his stand he
found that there were too many impediments to his exercising
editorial freedom. He suspended publication which was resumed
soon after the Emergency was with drawn. Freedom First, now
in its 47th year is a Liberal Quarterly.

In 1978, when the Janata Party was elected to power he
was appointed Chairman of the Minorities Commission but soon
resigned over differences on principles and approach.

Minoo Masani the socialist agitator in his ‘twenties became
the Liberal par excellence whose contribution to the Liberal
movement was acknowledged when he was honoured as a patron
of the Liberal International. He was a secularist (though he disliked
the word preferring to call himself by the more cumbersome
description ‘Non-denominationalist’) and an uncompromising
champion of individual liberty. Starting out as a friend and
supporter of Pandit Nehru he began to see in his later years the
practical wisdom in Sardar Patel’s policies.

Though he retired .from politics he continued to be active
in public life. In March 1968, he founded the Leslie Sawhny
Programme of Training for Democracy to train young people in ~
citizenship - to be conscious of their rights and their duties as
citizens.

He founded the Society for the Right to Die with Dignity
and enjoyed being in the centre of a minor storm when he
campaigned for passive euthanasia for the terminally ill.

In 1985 he set up the Project for Economic Education in
association with the Leslie Sawhny Programme and Prof. B. R.
Shenoy’s Economics Research Centre to educate public opinion

Introduction
This book is the story of a principled politician—an
oxymoron in current political dialogue. Today the word
politician draws sneer and derision. That it was not always
so we seek to establish in this biography of Minoo Masani
whose life and work spanned the greater part of the
twentieth century.

Masani was a man of many parts. He began asa lawyer
who gave up his practice to participate in the freedom
struggle; an author whose Our India written for the young
brought him popularity and fame; a parliamentarian of
repute with great respect for the institutions of parliamentary
democracy; a crusader for individual liberty who evolved
into a Liberal in the best traditions of Dadabhai Naoroji and
Gopal Krishna Gokhale; an intellectual who traversed the
political spectrum from Marx to Mahatma Gandhi—from
socialism to Swatantra.

In the political game in India success is measured in
terms of offices held. If this be the yardstick then Masani,
like his friend Jayaprakash Narayan, has been a failure. But
how does one measure a man’s achievement if he
deliberately chooses to reject opportunities if acceptance
means compromising with his beliefs. A clue is provided in
Masani’s report of Sri Prakasa’s (an eminent member of the
Congress Party) encounter with Nehru who used strong
language to pull up Sri Prakasa for daring to suggest the

xii © MINOO MASANI

partition of Kashmir. Sri Prakasa, who was then Indian High
Commissioner in Pakistan, lumped the scolding and
continued in office rather than annoy Nehru. Prakasa
narrated this incident to Masani when he was Governor of
Tamil Nadu. Commented Masani: “Here was an example of
one of India’s biggest tragedies—the inability to stand up to

“someone in authority.”

Masani had been very close to Nehru from the early
nineteen thirties and, along with men like Jayaprakash
Narayan and Achyut Patwardhan considered to be part of
Nehru’s inner circle of friends. Immediately after
independence, Masani was very much a part of the then
Congress establishment. Despite emerging differences with
Nehru in economic and foreign policy matters, Nehru
nominated Masani as an expert on the UN Sub-Committee
for the Prevention of Discrimination and the Protection of
Minorities. When Masani crossed swords with the Soviet
Union’s representatives questioning their claims of having
settled the minorities problem in the USSR, he knew fully
well that he was displeasing Nehru. His fears were justified
when he was withdrawn from the UN Sub-Committee. In
the first volume of his autobiography Masani had this to
say about himself: “Swimming against the tide became so
much of a habit, it is almost a part of my nature, I wonder
whether in later life, particularly in my political activities,
the patterns of my habit asserted themselves.”

It is easy to be in the opposition if the individual
concerned sees little prospect of power. But to be near it and
yet reject if it meant compromising with one’s principles,
required courage and integrity of a high order. And these
qualities Masani had in abundance.

Many years later when he had the opportunity to frame
the policies of a political party he brought into it many of
the principles he believed in and fortunately shared with
C. Rajagopalachari or Rajaji, as he was better known. Rajaji

INTRODUCTION xiii
too loved swimming against the tide and often differed with
Gandhiji. For instance, Rajaji preferred to quit the Congress
rather than support the Quit India movement launched by
Gandhiji. So it was natural when Masani sought to set
benchmarks for political behaviour and action, he could
count on Rajaji’s support. .

Masani was both a politician and an intellectual. This
was the norm among politicians in India before
independence. Almost everyone—Dadabhai Naoroji,
Pherozeshah Mehta, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Srinivasa
Shastri, Lokamanya. Tilak, Mahadeo Govind Ranade,
Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru (the list is very
long)—was either a writer or a teacher or both. Qualities
sadly lacking in politicians that have emerged in post-
independent India where the qualities required in the
political jungle are altogether different and not very worthy.

The principles of the short-lived Swatantra Party drawn
up by Masani with Rajaji’s blessings were high on ideals
which, sadly in the Indian context inhibited the
organisation’s growth.

These were: Embargo on the formation of Swatantra
fronts in the labour and students’ movements. Political
parties not to exploit labour and students to attend to their
studies first. No participation in satyagrahas, bandhs and such

. forms of protest as every activity should be within the law.
All protests should be within the framework of legality.
These restrictions were in Indian conditions, prescriptions
for failure.

For Masani, means were important and, if in the process
the organisation collapsed, so be it. For, in his view, the
organisation was not an end in itself but only the means to
an end—the end in the case of the Swatantra Party being
good governance and strengthening parliamentary
democracy.

Dr R. Srinivasan, Professor of Political Science at the

While those who are politically aware do know of

for many others; who know him as the author of Our

India and other books that they read at school either in

What is common to the Liberals, Gandhi and

Masani is the stress they lay on raising the tone of public

life. All of them have emphasized the need to spiritualize

public gaze. This stress on open politics stresses other
values, which are central to Masani—the freedom to opt
out, to choose and to stand by one’s convictions.

Masani’s public life has been spent far more in the
ranks of the Opposition than in the government. This
was the lot of the Liberals in modern India and ina sense
this is something that ought to be praised and
commemorated.

Dr Srinivasan refers to Our India that brought fame and
fortune to Masani. In his life of 92 years of which almost 60
years were spent in public life, he retired from politics thrice
and each time he came out with books mainly for children!
Our India was produced during his first retirement; The
Growing Human Family after his second; his two-volume
memoirs and We Indians after his third retirement.

The Masani classic was Our India. Written in 1940 it
sold over a million copies and was translated into almost
every Indian language. Writing about the book in his
memoirs, Masani described it as “a book for children

something like an economic geography of an elementary
nature. Our India appealed to the national pride of the Indian
and gave expression to his discontent. The book did a
wonderful job for me. A whole generation was brought up
on Our India, and sometime later prescribed as a general
reader in schools and colleges.” Then there was the Growing
Human Family, his next book for children which Masani felt

Masani was a great believer in organisations. Even
‘truth needs wings’ was a popular quote with him. And so
when something needed to be done in the public sphere,
Masani would get the justification ready for such action not
only explaining the cause but proposing an organisation to
deliver the message to further that cause.

Among the organisations he founded were the
Democratic Research Service (DRS) established in November
1950 to disseminate information about subversive
communist activities; another was the Indian Committee for
Cultural Freedom (ICCF) established in November 1951 as
part of an international movement of intellectuals, poets and
writers to combat Soviet propaganda among intellectuals; a
fourth was the Indian Liberal Group set up in 1964 to
promote the principles and philosophy of Liberalism and
function as a think tank for the Swatantra Party; a fifth was
the Leslie Sawhny Programme (LSP) for Training in
Democracy set up in 1968 with a syllabus of training which
included training in leadership, citizenship and in the
principles of Liberal Democracy and finally, in 1985 the
Project for Economic Education as part of the LSP to educate
the common man on economic issues particularly in the
context of a liberalising economy.

There were qualities in Masani which deserve high

INTRODUCTION xvii
praise but which were not taken to kindly by many he had
to deal with particularly in the political arena. For instance,
his obsession with time and punctuality. Even a two-minute
delay in keeping an appointment would invite a rebuke. The
status of the person did not matter. Nor could anyone call
on him without an appointment: For party leaders in India
to meet people by appointment is just not the done thing.
When people dropped in without prior notice or
appointment he would fret and fume and most of the time
the poor person who ‘dropped in’ would get a lecture on
time management. It is common practice in India when the
time for a public meeting is announced, it is earlier than
when it will really start. Therefore it is taken for granted
that if the announcement said that the meeting would start
at 5 p.m. it means 5.30 p.m. or even 6 p.m.; but not for Masani.
He would arrive at the venue of the meeting five minutes
before the announced time and literally explode if it did not
begin as scheduled.

As a chairman of meetings he was hard to beat. While
everyone who wanted to speak got the chance, he was
ruthless in enforcing the time rule irrespective of who was
speaking. If someone, whatever his status, rambled on and
took time, Masani would cut him short in mid sentence and
ask him to make his point. This did not endear him to such
people.

Masani had a quality which many of us lack—keeping
issues and personalities apart. For instance, once he very
vehemently disagreed with K.M. Munshi, then a vice-
president of the Swatantra Party. Munshi even started
walking out when Masani ran after him, brought him back
and pacified him. After the meeting was over I saw him
charmingly and genuinely solicitous over Munshi’s health.
This was not a question of his blowing hot and cold but a
compartmentalised mind responding to specific issues.
Unfortunately not everyone took this kindly. He earned

xviii © MINOO MASANI

epithets ranging from a mild ‘he is a difficult man’ to the
angry ‘he is an arrogant man’. ‘Difficult’ Masani certainly
was but not arrogant instead strong-willed. He was clear in
his priorities, clear in his objectives and did not hesitate to
spell them out in unambiguous terms. He did not make any
conscious effort to be liked.

Above all, he would not permit actions that violated

* party policies or decisions unless there were good reasons
for departures from the norm. If not, then he had no
hesitation in disciplining the member, not very much
concerned with the defaulter’s position in the hierarchy.

Until Minoo Masani joined Tatas in 1941, I knew him

only by name and reputation as a young controversial

socialist politician who, starting as a militant advocate
of Marxism, had gradually turned into an equally

militant opponent, while claiming throughout to be a

firm Gandhian and democrat. This baffled or infuriated

many, including his political comrades and peers of
various parties and hues, who not unnaturally,

considered him either as a dangerous revolutionary or a

I was fascinated by these conflicting aspects of his
personality and political philosophy, which my
politically untutored mind interpreted as those of a born
rebel who, while he saw in the Russian Revolution the
dawn of redemption from the gross injustices and
shameless colonialism of nineteenth century capitalism,
was too intelligent to swallow, wholesale, Marxist
dialectics. Yet, like many other dreamers of the time
including Jawaharlal Nehru, he believed that, somehow,
freedom could be made to co-exist with Marxism.

I will end this introduction on a personal note. My

as head of the Central Office of the Party; then managing

To begin with, it is not easy to work for him. He was
not only a hard taskmaster but could be unreasonable in

Another frustrating characteristic was his penchant to

‘Minoo has a first-rate mind but does he have to be so

India and not in England or USA?’ Many admirers and

I have often wondered what would have happened if

If there was one characteristic that shone above all else
in public life, particularly in post-independent India (again

EARLY YEARS
Religious persecution by Muslim invaders in the 8th century
forced many Zoroastrians to flee their native country, Persia,
and secure refuge in India. As these refugees came from
the plains of Pars in Persia they came to be knownas Parsis.
Many of them who had set sail from Masan in Persia landed
in Sanjan in Gujarat. Hence Masani or those who came from
Masan, belonged to the priestly class.

The Masanis, like so many of their brethren, settled in
Navsari in Gujarat. One of their descendants Pestonji held
a job in Bombay as Head Timekeeper in the Great Indian
Peninsular Railway (better known as GIP, now the Central
Railway) on a monthly salary of Rs. 100. His son Rustom
Masani, a writer and a journalist was also the Secretary of
the Bombay Municipal Corporation and later vice-
chancellor of the University of Bombay. He had distinct
literary interests and wrote ona variety of subjects. He was
knighted by the British colonial rulers but renounced his
title some years later in protest against British repression of
the Quit India movement and the arrest and imprisonment
of Mahatma Gandhi in 1942.

Rustom Masani and his wife Manijeh had four
children—Minoo, Keki, Mehra and Pesi. Though not
wealthy they managed at considerable personal sacrifice to
give their children the best education then available
including higher education abroad in the fields of their
choice. As a result, all four of them distinguished

2. MINOO MASANI

themselves. Minoo Masani became a barrister. Keki
qualified as a psychiatrist; Mehra entered government
service retiring as Deputy Director-General of All India
Radio and Pesi became a mathematician.

This biography is adout Minoo Masani, their eldest
son. For purposes of this biography we shall refer to him as

* Masani.

Masani’s early schooling was at Bombay’s Cathedral
High School and the New High School, now known as
Bharda High School, from where he matriculated in 1921.
Bharda High School produced a number of eminent Indians,
among them Yusuf Meherally, Minoo’s classmate. As a
schoolboy Masani played cricket and hockey and also took
violin lessons from Count Odone Savini, an Italian who had
settled in Bombay. Another of Savini’s pupils was Mehli
Mehta whose son Zubin Mehta was to become a world
famous conductor of classical music.

Masani’s father wanted his eldest son to become a
doctor, but he chose law instead on the advice of Yusuf
Meherally. After passing the matriculation examination
Masani entered Elphinstone College in Bombay, another
educational institution that produced a number of
distinguished Indians including India’s Grand Old Man
Dadabhai Naoroji who was a professor in this college. After
graduating, Masani went to London in 1925 where he
studied Law at the London School of Economics and took
the LL.B. degree of the London University; qualifying as a
Barrister at Law from Lincoln’s Inn. *

As a student in London, Masani took active interest in
student politics. Attracted by the policies of the British
Labour Party he became an ardent socialist. Student unions
in England were organised along party lines. He was an
active participant in the students union of the London
School of Economics, generally referred to as the LSE, and
was soon elected to the Union Executive with the support

EARLY YEARS 3
of the Labour Party. Interestingly, when Masani contested
for the presidentship of the Union as a candidate of the
Labour Party, he was opposed by V.K. Krishna Menon, who
had been an LSE student for some years before Masani.
Krishna Menon contested the electton as an independent
candidate. As a result, both lost, the winner being a
candidate supported by the Conservative Party!

By the time he graduated 1s barrister, Masani also
became a committed socialist 2 41 an admirer of the Soviet
Union. In 1927, ten years afte ‘he Russian Revolution of
1917, he joined a group to vis. ‘he ‘Workers’ Fatherland’.
That was the period of the Nev 3conomic Policy (NEP) in
the Soviet Union introduced by Lenin. The NEP was
somewhat like the mixed economy that prevailed in India
for almost forty years after independence. The NEP allowed
some amount of private enterprise. There were shops run
by private individuals alongside state-owned shops; there
were even private taxis. Masani was deeply impressed by
what he saw and experienced.

1927 was also the year he met, for the first time,
Jawaharlal Nehru who had accompanied his father Motilal
Nehru, to London. Masani was delighted to find Jawaharlal
Nehru an even greater admirer of the Soviet Union!

After completing his education Masani returned to
India in 1928 as a devout socialist and a Marxist and joined
the Bar of the Bombay High Court. He wrote about his
experiences in Soviet Russia in a series of gushing articles
in the Bombay Chronicle edited by S.A. Brelvi, a respected
journalist and a passionate nationalist.
